articles.title: Putin claims that Ukraine has no ‘antidote’ to Russia’s new jet-powered drones. Kyiv has already shown it can shoot them down, but doing it at scale could cost billions.
articles.body:
Putin claims that Ukraine has no ‘antidote’ to Russia’s new jet-powered drones. Kyiv has already shown it can shoot them down, but doing it at scale could cost billions.
Speaking to reporters on the sidelines of the Cultural Forum, Vladimir Putin said Ukraine was seeking an “air ceasefire” out of weakness — especially because it feared Russia’s new jet-powered drones. The Russian president believes Kyiv has no “antidote” to these weapons. They are dangerous, but they lack the chief advantage of the earlier “Geran” drones: low cost. Developing defenses against the faster drones will also be expensive for Ukraine. Here is how the latest turn in the technological arms race could drain — and is already draining — both countries’ budgets.
What exactly was Putin talking about, and is he right?
An “air ceasefire” would mean a mutual halt to strikes on energy and transport targets behind the front lines. Putin believes Kyiv made the request solely because its infrastructure is vulnerable: “Apparently, they particularly need us to stop striking with our modern ‘Gerans.’ At least for now, they have no way to counter them — no antidote.”
By “modern ‘Gerans,’” Putin apparently means a new generation of drones that could more accurately be called small cruise missiles. These jet-powered aircraft are indeed nearly impervious to the layered defenses Ukraine built against older drones. Russia fielded large numbers of the new models from the start precisely because the old ones had become ineffective.
Jet engines have made the new weapons several times faster than their piston-powered predecessors. But that advance came at the expense of the older “Gerans’” main advantage: Estimates suggest the new models cost several times as much to produce.
Still, Kyiv is not entirely without an “antidote.” Ukraine has the technological capacity to build effective defenses. Paying for them is a harder problem.
Why did the old ‘Gerans’ stop being effective?
The Russian military received its first jet-powered drone in early 2025. It was essentially a standard “Geran-2” fitted with a small Chinese Telefly JT80 turbojet engine in place of its piston engine. The modified drone was named the “Geran-3.” Its speed roughly doubled, reaching 300–350 kilometers per hour (about 185–220 miles per hour), compared with its predecessor’s 150–180 kilometers per hour (about 95–110 miles per hour). Its range and payload — its warhead — were smaller, however.
The jet-powered version was developed in response to Ukraine’s increasingly effective air defenses. By then, Kyiv had deployed an effective interception network built around electric-powered interceptor quadcopters. Those drones were connected to a network of sensors: radar; acoustic sensors that located “Geran-2” drones and tracked their direction of flight by the distinctive sound of their piston engines; and optical and infrared sensors that could detect passing aircraft by day and night.
The main source is less than fully reliable: statements from Ukrainian military intelligence and the Security Service of Ukraine. The agencies give detailed accounts of their successes against Russian drones and of the new equipment Russia is using. Ukrainian intelligence officials have an obvious stake in the conflict and are engaged in information warfare.
There is also more objective evidence: photos and videos of downed aircraft and their parts, including engines; videos of interceptions by air defenses; and visual confirmation of the strikes themselves. Russian media outlets and military personnel have also shared technical details of the new weapons, though they, too, have a stake in the outcome. Taken together, this material gives a general picture of the new equipment and how it is being used.
The interceptors themselves had video cameras and onboard computers with some machine-vision capability. Automated systems guided them toward their targets in the final stage of flight, making interceptions much more effective and reducing the skill required of operators: They only had to launch an interceptor toward a Russian drone.
The interceptors also cost less than a “Geran-2” — under $10,000 each, according to Ukrainian and Western manufacturers. Although Ukrainian military personnel said it took three or four interceptors to bring down one “Geran,” the cost was manageable, even before accounting for the value of targets the Russian drones might otherwise have hit. Ukraine’s armed forces used these systems to reliably defend Kyiv and Odesa and their surrounding areas, two of the places Russia attacked most often: Kyiv and its surroundings, and Odesa and its surroundings. By early 2026, attacking those areas with “Geran-2” drones had become entirely uneconomical: It took too many drones to hit a single target.
Hi, I’m Vladislav Gorin.
I’m the host of Meduza’s daily Russian-language news podcast. This summer, the Russian authorities opened a criminal case against me — not for committing a crime, but for telling the truth about Russia and its war against Ukraine.
Because the Kremlin has branded me a criminal, I can’t go home. I also can’t safely travel to countries like Turkey — even though it’s a NATO member — because I could be arrested and extradited to Russia. I can’t even renew my passport at the consulate anymore.
None of this is going to stop me. I know there are hundreds of thousands of people in Russia who don’t want this war and who still believe in freedom and democracy, and they deserve access to independent journalism. Please support Meduza so I can keep reaching them.
What are the new ‘Gerans,’ and what has changed?
The first jet-powered drone, the “Geran-3,” was not very successful. Its Telefly JT80 engine lacked power: With 80 kilograms-force of thrust (about 175 pounds of force), the drone could not reach speeds typical of cruise missiles — more than 500 kilometers per hour (about 310 miles per hour). It also could not carry enough fuel to match the “Geran-2’s” range. The same engine limitations meant it had to carry a relatively less powerful warhead.
Russia therefore quickly began developing new jet-powered drones and miniature cruise missiles. In fact, they are all cruise missiles; the distinctions between them are largely a matter of classification. To address the first model’s shortcomings, developers chose much more powerful turbojet engines, also made in China. By fall 2026, the Russian military had received four models produced in large numbers:
- “Geran-4.” Its delta-wing airframe still resembles the Iranian “Shahed” drone from which Russia’s entire “Geran” family evolved. That wing design distinguishes this model from a cruise missile, though it is probably ill-suited to jet-powered flight. Ukrainian sources say the airframe had to be reinforced for higher speeds. Russia apparently cannot yet abandon the old shape because the factory in Tatarstan’s “Alabuga” Special Economic Zone, which produces thousands of drones each month, is set up to make it. The “Geran-4” uses a Chinese Telefly TF-TJ2000A turbojet engine with 2.5 times the thrust of the Telefly JT80, substantially increasing its speed and range compared with the “Geran-3.”
- “Geran-5.” This jet-powered drone has a conventional aircraft layout and looks like an ordinary cruise missile. It uses the same Telefly TF-TJ2000A engine as the “Geran-4.” It can be launched from aircraft or helicopters as well as ground launchers, increasing its operational range. Judging by the number of videos showing strikes, Russia is using the “Geran-5” more often than the “Geran-4.” The factory in Alabuga also produces this more aerodynamic model. The drone has enough range to strike anywhere in Ukraine. In late September, for example, it was used to attack a border crossing with Poland almost 600 kilometers (about 370 miles) from Russia.
- The S8000 “Banderol” missile. Russia uses it to blockade Ukrainian ports, regularly striking maritime infrastructure and other targets around Odesa. The “Banderol” can be launched from the ground, helicopters, aircraft, or “Orion” attack drones. Unlike the “Geran-5,” its airframe is shaped to make it less visible to radar. Its engine — at least in early examples — is also said to be Chinese. The missile carries a warhead twice as heavy as the “Geran-5’s.”
- The “Dan-T” missile. Based on the “Dan-M” air-defense target drone, it is also used in attacks on Odesa and the surrounding area. Ukrainian sources say it is intended to become Russia’s most widely produced drone, with plans to produce up to 10,000 a year. Some believe the “Dan-T” is a version of the “Banderol” that Russia may be planning to export.
Who else is trying, so far without success, to produce jet-powered drones on a large scale?
Ukraine, above all. Destinus, a company based in the Netherlands and founded by entrepreneur Mikhail Kokorich, who renounced his Russian citizenship, produces the small Ruta cruise missile for Ukraine’s armed forces. Its stated range and payload exceed those of comparable Russian weapons. Ukraine used these missiles to attack the Rostov Optical and Mechanical Plant overnight on September 25–26.
By contrast, Russia is producing and using thousands of jet-powered drones a month, just a year after launching its program. Ukrainian intelligence believes Russia now makes more jet-powered drones than the older, piston-powered “Geran-2.” In that sense, Moscow has achieved something the United States and other countries have spent years trying to do: create weapons that can be produced easily in large numbers and fully meet an army’s needs during a prolonged war.
The U.S. Air Force’s latest version of such a program, planned to run through 2031, is called Family of Affordable Mass Munitions (FAMM). The war with Iran prompted its urgent launch: After just a month of intense fighting, the Pentagon faced an acute shortage of precision weapons, including cruise missiles. The missiles it had used cost tens of billions of dollars, and U.S. officials acknowledge that replenishing the stockpile will take years. The military needs much cheaper munitions capable of striking most targets.
So how cheap are Russia’s new missiles?
The “availability” and “low cost” of Russia’s new missiles are relative. Chinese manufacturers sell jet engines with more than 200 kilograms-force of thrust (about 440 pounds of force) for nearly 10 times the price of the piston engines used in the previous generation of drones. The terms offered to Russian bulk buyers are unknown, but engines of this kind previously sold on Chinese online marketplaces for tens of thousands of dollars apiece. By comparison, piston engines for “Geran-2” type drones cost up to $10,000.
Experts estimate that a finished “Geran-5” costs more than $100,000, over twice the price of a “Geran-2.” Even so, it remains several times cheaper than a conventional cruise missile, such as Russia’s “Kalibr” or Kh-101, the British-French Storm Shadow/SCALP, or the U.S. Tomahawk. Those missiles have powerful, high-performance engines, travel at almost twice the speed, incorporate features that make them harder to detect, use sophisticated navigation systems, and carry warheads several times heavier.
Because the new missiles are fairly expensive, military planners and manufacturers have an incentive to make each one more effective — improving its accuracy, reliability, and resistance to electronic warfare and air defenses. The aim is to make the new missiles more likely to hit their targets than the previous generation of drones. The latest models therefore have features that make them less visible to radar, as well as more advanced navigation systems. “Geran-2” type drones relied for guidance solely on inertial systems corrected by satellite signals. Some “Geran-4” and “Geran-5” drones now have systems that guide them by comparing images of the terrain with a database. All this adds to their cost.
How does Ukraine plan to shoot down the new weapons?
Russia’s new weapons exploit a gap in Ukrainian air defenses: They are too fast for specialized electric-powered interceptors, yet still too cheap and numerous to counter with nearly all conventional air-defense systems, whose missiles cost tens or hundreds of thousands of dollars each.
- Conventional short- and medium-range air defenses: With help from Western partners, Ukraine has acquired many such systems and adapted Soviet launchers to fire foreign missiles under the FrankenSAM program; Kyiv ran out of their original Soviet missiles long ago. But interceptor missiles for conventional air defenses cost at least $70,000 each, even for older systems such as Hawk. More modern missiles, including the AIM-120 and Sea Sparrow, cost over $100,000 each. The missile models Ukraine uses in its FrankenSAM systems are no longer produced and come from U.S. and other countries’ stockpiles. The Ukrainian military has more modern systems as well, but their missiles cost even more. The high price of conventional air-defense missiles is precisely why Ukraine had to develop specialized defenses against the “Gerans.”
- Aircraft: Jet fighters are a reliable way to counter cruise missiles and can therefore be used against the new drones. Air-to-air missiles are more effective against airborne targets than aircraft cannon, but they are also expensive. Kyiv has received inexpensive laser-guided APKWS II missiles from the United States and France for use against drones; they cost up to $20,000 each. The United States uses them against Iranian and Yemeni “Shahed” drones, but they can also bring down faster targets. Ukraine’s main problem is that it has too few aircraft and launchers capable of firing them: Only F-16 fighters and ground-based Vampire systems can use these missiles. The country has received several dozen F-16s and fewer than 20 Vampire systems — nowhere near enough to cover its entire territory. Helicopters and light aircraft make up the bulk of Ukraine’s airborne defenses against drones. They were used successfully against “Geran-2” drones but are too slow to counter jet-powered models.
- Specialized defenses against drones: Ukraine has received electric-powered interceptor drones from Western partners, including private companies, and developed others itself, bringing the total to more than 10 models. They have proved highly effective against “Geran-2” drones and other Russian drones powered by piston engines or electric motors. Around Kyiv and Odesa, where mobile groups equipped with these interceptors formed the layered defenses described above, “Geran-2” attacks have almost ceased. But the interceptors were designed for targets traveling under 200 kilometers per hour (about 125 miles per hour), leaving them almost powerless against jet-powered aircraft. Such a system can bring down a fast target only with considerable luck — for example, in a head-on interception. The detection sensors may pose a problem, too: Acoustic devices were tuned to the distinctive sound of a “Geran-2” engine, while optical sensors were designed for targets with low angular speeds of a few dozen degrees per second. Ukraine’s main defense against Russia’s earlier drones has thus suddenly become ineffective.
Ukraine had prepared for the possibility that its drone defenses would become less effective. Preparations began when its intelligence services discovered Russia’s program to develop new drones for its military. As early as January 2026, Ukrainian military intelligence described the drones’ characteristics and production plans fairly accurately. By September, Ukraine’s armed forces and Security Service had several models of jet-powered interceptor drones. In the past week alone, Ukraine has released videos showing these interceptors successfully bringing down “Geran-4” and “Geran-5” drones. The new interceptors outperform electric-powered models in speed and range and can intercept targets at higher altitudes. Jet engines have an inherent advantage because hydrocarbon fuel has a higher energy density than batteries.
The big questions for Ukraine are how much more the new interceptors will cost and what it would cost to re-equip the hundreds of anti-drone air-defense systems that will use them — including their radars, other sensors, and launchers. The small turbojet engines alone are likely to cost several times as much as electric motors. They are much cheaper than the engines in Russia’s new “Gerans,” however, because they produce less thrust: Ukrainian interceptors do not need to travel hundreds of kilometers or carry warheads weighing tens of kilograms (dozens of pounds).
Bringing down each target also requires several interceptors. According to figures released by Ukraine’s armed forces six months ago, an average of four interceptors were used for every target brought down. Higher interceptor production costs alone — excluding the expense of re-equipping and upgrading air-defense systems — could therefore add hundreds of millions or even billions of dollars a year to Ukraine’s spending.
How is this arms race affecting both countries’ budgets?
Ukraine is already facing severe financial difficulties as it expands production and use of both air-defense munitions and its own strike weapons. A sharp increase in purchases of various drones left a $27 billion gap in the 2026 military budget, President Volodymyr Zelensky said. The military needs to spend $175 billion in 2027, up from $155 billion in 2026, but only $100 billion has been budgeted so far. The government plans to make up the difference with Western help and savings at home. Military spending would thus amount to almost 78% of the country’s GDP.
Russia faces similar problems. Actual military spending rose 30% in the first half of 2026, even though the budget law had called for cuts. Overall, military spending reached 9.4% of GDP, equivalent to roughly $250 billion a year. That increase was the main reason the budget deficit grew. To balance the 2027 budget, the authorities now plan another tax increase and cuts to nonmilitary spending, along with renewed cuts to military spending that would bring it down to $200 billion. So far, the technological arms race between Ukraine and Russia is draining both countries’ finances without changing the balance of power.
At Meduza, we are committed to transparency about our use of artificial intelligence in the newsroom. The story you’re reading was written by one of our living, breathing journalists and translated from Russian using an AI model configured to follow our strict editorial standards. This translation process is the result of extensive testing and refinements to ensure our English-language coverage is timely and accurate. A Meduza editor reviews every draft before publication.
If you find any errors in this translation, please contact us at [email protected].

articles.title: Europe and Ukraine already have the force to stop Russia. What’s missing is the alliance.
articles.body:
For decades, Europe operated on a series of assumptions: that borders were essentially settled; that economic interdependence would constrain major-power conflict; that international law would increasingly regulate state behavior; that military force was becoming less relevant; and that, ultimately, the United States would guarantee European security.
Russia's invasion of Ukraine has shattered those norms, as Moscow attempts to change borders by force and reshape the European security order. NATO now describes Russia as the most significant and direct threat to Allied security, while also identifying sabotage, cyberattacks, disinformation, economic coercion, and other hybrid actions as part of the threat.
The foreign policy of the Trump administration is further undermining past postulations. It threatens to annex Canada, speaks of occupying Greenland by force, and ignores Spain's sovereignty. It disrespects European military contributions, then demands European support for operations of its own choosing, legal justification optional. It negotiates European security over Europe's head while resetting relations with the power that threatens the continent, calls European countries "decaying" and their leaders "weak," and has launched a trade war against its former allies while pursuing business with its former strategic opponent.
Discussing solutions without first agreeing on the problem is meaningless. Yet that is what Europe has done since the war started in 2014.
Eight realities
Analyzing the security environment, before recommending solutions, I have identified eight fixed points that I regard as constants.
1. It was never a Russia/Ukraine war
Russia has offered the West four tales, all unpleasant, one designed to look like an "easy way out." The first calls on Ukraine to give up Crimea, Luhansk, Donetsk, Zaporizhzhia and Kherson, the lie Trump's plan is built on. But Putin's demands transcend Donbas, as his 2024 speech and Russia's operations show. The second, "Novorossiya," adds Kharkiv, Dnipropetrovsk, Mykolaiv and Odesa to the first lie.
The third, "one people, one nation," claims all of Ukraine. In the words of former US National Security Advisor Zbigniew Brzezinski: "Without Ukraine, Russia ceases to be an empire, but with Ukraine suborned and then subordinated, Russia automatically becomes an empire." The fourth, "the Russian World," is the only one formalized in Russian strategic documents, encompassing the "former territories of Kyivan Rus, the Kingdom of Muscovy, the Russian Empire, the Soviet Union, and the contemporary Russian Federation."
Ukraine's defeat is crucial to Russia's broader strategy. Integrated with Belarus, a subjugated Ukraine would give Russia the population, economy and technology to be seen as a near peer to the US and China, project power across the post-Soviet space, and ease its own demographic decline, while handing Moscow the country's defense industry, farmland and mineral, gas and oil deposits, and moving Russian military power nearly 900 km closer to London, Berlin and Paris.
It would create an aggressive, imperialist power on Europe's border, emboldened to force NATO's withdrawal to its 1997 borders and to deny the US the ability to deploy forces and nuclear weapons to Europe. The West, not Ukraine, has been defined as Russia's enemy.
2. A war is ongoing in Europe
Russia has been conducting an ever-escalating hybrid war against NATO's European member states since 2014. The EU Parliament acknowledged as much in September 2021. Its aggressions include sabotage against critical infrastructure, cyberattacks, disinformation, GPS jamming affecting civilian aviation, repeated airspace violations by strike drones, and attacks on Europe's defense-industrial base.
Russia's acts of violence against Western targets are becoming increasingly brazen. In August, Western intelligence sources reported a new wave of attacks on weapons factories in Europe under cover of "plausible deniability," The Telegraph reported. A CIA report shared with European governments warns Russia may attack Spain, France or Italy with Gerbera drones launched from ships, El Mundo reported, citing Lithuanian sources.
It is the same hybrid war Ukraine faced until 24 February 2022, one expected to turn open by 2029. Article 5 could, and probably should, have been triggered years ago. Having failed to respond, NATO has lost credibility, raising the risk of war.
3. The tsunami of ripple effects is changing the political landscape in the West
In May 2022, I began using the term tsunami of ripple effects to describe the cost of not intervening in a war that threatens the security of the Alliance. It is the reverberations that raise the cost of living, undermine food and energy security, and spread famine, recession and inflation, raising the risk of unrest, extremism, and, ultimately, the fall of governments. Europe is living through the biggest refugee crisis since the Second World War.
The international security architecture is being dismantled, our institutions discredited, and NATO no longer deters Russia. Building on public frustration, the tsunami of ripple effects gave us Trump and the rise of right-wing parties across Europe.
4. NATO no longer deters Russia
If Russia were deterred, it would not have launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine. NATO's strategic concept commits it to ending, by political and military means, conflicts that threaten Alliance security, including in Ukraine. Nor would Russia be conducting an ever-escalating hybrid war against NATO's European states, or preparing for a military conflict with the Alliance, as US and European intelligence services warn. Lack of deterrence raises the risk of Russian strategic miscalculation and war, especially since NATO was the only military power able to deny Russia its Great Power aspiration and its demand for a sphere of influence over the post-Soviet space.
NATO used to display readiness and capabilities. Today it has become a religion. Europe begs it is still almighty while Russia is a disbeliever.
5. The transatlantic rupture undermines NATO and European security
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney put it plainly at Davos on 20 January 2026: "We are in the midst of a rupture, not a transition." We "cannot live within the lie of mutual benefit through integration when integration becomes the source of your subordination," he said, calling for countries to organize in the face of great-power rivalry through different coalitions for different issues, based on common values and interests. As he told the World Economic Forum: "We actively take on the world as it is, not wait around for a world we wish to be."
6. The war is existential to both Ukraine and Russia
Ukraine is fighting for its right to exist. Russia is fighting for its Great Power status, strategic parity with the USA and China. If it is defeated in Ukraine, it will forever remain a pariah state, potentially imploding. For a negotiation to succeed, it must solve the cause of the war: Russia's Great Power ambitions, which cannot be negotiated away, only denied through military power.
7. Russia will never accept being defeated by Ukraine
Even with the tools to evict the Russian Armed Forces, Ukraine cannot expect Russia to accept defeat by a nation that, in its distorted narrative, "does not exist." Russia would only accept withdrawal from Ukraine if the alternative were to fight a far superior military power and thereby risk losing the means that secure the survival of the regime and the state.
8. Europe has very limited time to stop the war from escalating
Several European intelligence services warn of war by 2029;
- French intelligence is preparing for large-scale Russian attacks by 2030, and autumn 2027 is now being discussed, France Télévisions reported;
- US intelligence expects Russia may test NATO's resolve with a limited strike against a member state between this autumn and 2029, the Wall Street Journal reported in August;
- Baltic intelligence chiefs told The Guardian on 20 September that an attack could come within "months, not years."
- Worse still, Europe won't be ready until 2035, six to nine years too late, SACEUR warns.
Rules do not enforce themselves
International law, sovereignty, and territorial integrity remain fundamental principles. But without the capability and political will to defend them, principles become aspirations, not constraints on states prepared to use force. Acknowledging the world as it is means acknowledging that power still matters. It means accepting that deterrence requires more than statements of concern: ammunition, air and missile defense, long-range strike and counter-drone systems, secure communications, logistics, cyber resilience, and the industrial capacity to sustain a prolonged conflict.
This is where Carney's second formulation matters: countries must rely not only on "the strength of our values, but also the value of our strength." Values mean nothing unless one is prepared to defend them, as Canada is doing, raising defense spending and strengthening domestic industry. Europe needs to draw the same conclusion: strategic autonomy, not abandoning NATO, but ensuring Europe can defend itself and its interests even when an ally's priorities change.
The European Council already calls Russia's war an existential challenge and demands defense readiness be strengthened by 2030. But acknowledging reality means going further than setting targets.
It means recognizing that Ukraine is not merely the recipient of European security assistance. Ukraine is an integral part of Europe's security architecture. Its battlefield experience, defense industry, intelligence, and ability to absorb and defeat Russian attacks are crucial to European security.
Because individual member states refuse Ukraine as a member, NATO has made itself a liability, and some of the same countries are erecting hindrances to its EU membership too, letting national interest block common security.
The solution
The choice is not between idealism and realism. It is between pretending that the old assumptions still hold and building the capabilities required by the reality that has replaced them.
Acknowledging the world as it is means seeing the threats clearly; defending the world as it should be means acting on that knowledge, and the bridge between the two is strength.
Accept those eight fixed points, and Europe's room for maneuver is gone, along with its present strategy. Europe cannot afford another 12 years of futile diplomacy while Russia exploits our naivety to prepare for war in the next two to three years, diplomacy that has undermined Europe's need to rearm and establish credible deterrence.
European governments have long acknowledged that their armed forces no longer provide credible defense, yet their security policy still assumes NATO guarantees collective security.
Acknowledge reality, and the illusion shatters.
Europe urgently needs a new strategy, one that looks beyond NATO and the EU's inherent weaknesses toward a military alliance credible enough to reshape the strategic environment. This is why I have long argued for a Coalition of Like-Minded European countries (CALM). It offers a path from recognition to action, from acknowledging NATO's failure to building something that works.
Strength is not found in numbers, but in unity: agreeing on the enemy, his aims and strategy, and committing to countermeasures that demonstrate real will and capability to fight.
Unlike NATO or the EU, CALM does not have to wait for Europe's rearmament to reach 2035. It builds on existing NATO interoperability.
The force already exists: Ukraine's battle-hardened army, National Guard, Special Operations Forces, air defense, and Unmanned System Forces, combined with European fifth-generation aircraft and state-of-the-art navies, are credible, combat-proven, and in place.
Russia already struggles to fight Ukraine alone; it would face a different reality entirely if Ukraine formally joined a coalition of European military powers. That is why the declaration matters now, not after the capability is fully built: with the interoperability already proven, it changes Russia's strategic assessment immediately, not in 2035.
This is not only about physical capabilities. It is about changing Russia's perception of its strategic environment. It starts with a declaration; preparing for military intervention comes next. But it begins with the declaration.

articles.title: Report: Eight US Marines wounded in Iranian strike near Strait of Hormuz
articles.body:
Report: Eight US Marines wounded in Iranian strike near Strait of Hormuz
TEHRAN — An Iranian anti-ship cruise missile strike in the Strait of Hormuz has left at least eight US Marines wounded, exposing the mounting operational vulnerabilities of the American military presence in West Asia and puncturing Washington’s carefully curated narrative of naval dominance in the Persian Gulf.
The high-precision strike, which occurred on September 14, targeted an unauthorized maritime vessel deployed within the strategic chokepoint. According to disclosures from American officials, the impact resulted in immediate trauma among the personnel on board, including smoke inhalation and symptoms consistent with traumatic brain injury (TBI) and severe concussions. The injured troops—comprising seven enlisted service members and one officer—were attached to an expeditionary battalion landing team operating covertly aboard a non-naval, commercial-grade maritime vessel rather than a standard commissioned warship.
The incident, concealed by the United States Department of War for nearly two weeks, came to light only after the Pentagon’s Defense Casualty Analysis System (DCAS) belatedly added the wounded Marines to its casualty rosters for Overseas Operations, without disclosing the time, location, or circumstances of the engagement. Both US Central Command (CENTCOM) and the Pentagon declined to formally address the strike, extending a pattern of information suppression and data manipulation that has characterized Washington’s public disclosures since the outbreak of hostilities in late February.
The successful missile engagement serves as a potent reminder of Iran’s comprehensive operational control over the Strait of Hormuz and adjacent littoral waters. Operating under strict rules of engagement, naval units of the Islamic Revolution Guards Corps (IRGC) and the Army have established absolute surveillance over the waterway, through which a significant portion of global petroleum supplies must transit.
Tehran has reiterated that maritime security in the Strait of Hormuz is indivisible and sovereign. Hostile military assets and non-authorized vessels attempting illegal passage, espionage, or the enforcement of unilateral Western blockades against Iranian commerce are treated as legitimate tactical targets. Military authorities in Tehran have repeatedly cautioned foreign powers that any vessel defying Iranian navigational regulations, failing to transmit required identification, or participating in hostile maneuvers will be intercepted or neutralized without hesitation.
Despite Washington’s deployment of vast naval assets to the region—including more than 50,000 personnel, multiple carrier strike groups led by the USS George Washington and the USS George H.W. Bush, and accompanying guided-missile escorts—the Pentagon’s attempt to impose an unlawful blockade on Iranian ports has been systematically frustrated. Iranian coastal defense batteries, armed with advanced radar systems and indigenous anti-ship cruise and ballistic missiles, hold every foreign vessel in the Persian Gulf and the Sea of Oman within immediate targeting range.
US casualties and information blackout
The September 14 strike has renewed scrutiny over the Pentagon’s opaque reporting practices regarding military casualties. Since the United States and Israel jointly launched their aggressive, unprovoked war against Iran on February 28, defense analysts and regional observers have noted an unprecedented level of discrepancy and confusion in official American reports.
While DCAS records show that well over 860 US military personnel have sustained injuries since the start of the conflict, independent observers argue the true figures are substantially higher. Over the summer, the Pentagon abruptly reclassified its casualty methodologies, retroactively lowering official death counts and categorizing combat casualties under vague bureaucratic labels to soften the domestic political impact of the campaign’s escalating human toll. The delayed logging of the eight Marines—justified retroactively by US officials as a standard administrative reporting lag—reflects a broader strategy aimed at downplaying the efficacy of Iranian defensive countermeasures.
Furthermore, the deployment of combat troops aboard an undisclosed “maritime vessel” points to a growing operational shift by CENTCOM. Facing devastating losses and heightened risk to major surface combatants from Iran’s asymmetric swarming tactics, naval drones, and precision coastal batteries, the US military has increasingly resorted to utilizing auxiliary, commercial, or unmarked hulls to evade detection—a strategy that Iranian intelligence and surveillance networks continue to successfully penetrate and neutralize.
Iran’s non-negotiable terms
Iranian political leadership and top military commanders have made it explicitly clear that safe, uninterrupted transit through the Strait of Hormuz remains entirely contingent upon the United States acknowledging regional geopolitical realities and complying with Iran’s legitimate terms.
Tehran has outlined a clear path for the normalization of maritime traffic in the waterway: Washington must bring an immediate, unconditional, and permanent end to the war of aggression it initiated on February 28 alongside Israel. Iranian officials emphasize that no foreign power will be permitted to enforce a state of economic strangulation against the Iranian people while simultaneously demanding unrestricted access for its own war fleet and commercial shipping through Iran’s front yard.
More broadly, senior officials in Tehran have repeatedly affirmed that enduring peace and stability in West Asia and the Persian Gulf can never be achieved under the shadow of foreign occupation. The root cause of regional friction, Iranian authorities insist, remains the destabilizing footprint of extra-regional forces. Real security is attainable only through collective regional cooperation among Persian Gulf littoral states, predicated on the complete, comprehensive, and irreversible expulsion of all American military personnel, bases, and hardware from the region.
As long as the United States continues to pursue a reckless militaristic agenda, sponsor Israeli aggression, and trespass upon Iranian territorial jurisdiction, Tehran has pledged that its armed forces will vigorously exercise their legitimate right to self-defense, ensuring that every act of adventurism in the waters of the Persian Gulf is met with a swift, decisive, and punitive response.

articles.title: Ukrainian Intel Exposes Russia Helping Iran Target US Forces
articles.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has announced that Kyiv’s intelligence services will begin sharing evidence of what he described as a highly coordinated military reconnaissance loop between Russia and Iran.
According to the intelligence, Moscow has utilized its network of spy satellites to monitor Gulf states and critical US military assets in the Middle East. These orbital passes directly correlate with the timing of Iranian drone and missile strikes.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Zelensky offered a striking example. In a 48-hour window between July 19 and 20 alone, four air bases fell squarely within the lens of active Russian satellite surveillance – two in Bahrain, one in Jordan and one in Kuwait.
The intelligence described by Kyiv points to a potentially sophisticated reconnaissance cycle: pre-attack satellite collection, tactical tracking imagery that could assist operational planning, and post-strike battle damage assessment.
“The purpose is clear,” the president warned.
The specific Ukrainian intelligence revelation does not emerge in isolation. Western intelligence officials previously told The Wall Street Journal that Russia had supplied Iran with satellite-derived targeting information for attacks on US forces.
Ratcliffe’s high-stakes diplomacy from Moscow to Shannon
The disclosure also intersects with an unusual sequence of intelligence diplomacy involving CIA Director John Ratcliffe.
Ratcliffe traveled to Moscow on Aug. 25 for previously undisclosed meetings with senior Russian officials – the first known visit to Russia by a serving CIA director since William Burns traveled there in 2021.
Zelensky Warns Russia Is Training North Korea for War, Feeding Iran Satellite Intelligence
The CIA and Kremlin did not publicly detail the agenda.
The White House subsequently played down the significance of the visit.
Less than a month later, Ratcliffe and Zelensky unexpectedly crossed paths at Shannon Airport in Ireland.
Both aircraft were refueling. Zelensky was traveling to New York for the UN General Assembly, while Ratcliffe was returning from a meeting with Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi.
Two sources familiar with the encounter described the conversation to Reuters as informal, with no details of the discussion disclosed.
Congressional scrutiny over a growing axis
The question of whether Russia is providing intelligence that assists Iranian attacks has already been a focal point of intense scrutiny in Washington.
During a high-profile Worldwide Threats hearing in Congress, CIA Director Ratcliffe was pressed by lawmakers about the extent of the Russia-Iran-China intelligence-sharing network.
Confronted by members of the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence, Ratcliffe formally confirmed that Tehran was aggressively requesting advanced intelligence assistance from both Moscow and Beijing to help it evade Western air defense networks.
Though some elements of the findings were withheld for classified sessions, the congressional record highlighted growing alarm over how Russia’s strategic cooperation with Iran directly threatens deployed American personnel.
“The Iranians are requesting intelligence assistance from Russia, from China, and from other adversaries of the United States,” the CIA director told lawmakers.
Asked directly whether Russia was doing so, he responded that he knew the answer but would discuss it only during the classified portion of the hearing.
Trading Ukraine for the Middle East
The deep leverage Moscow holds over Middle Eastern stability was further illustrated by staggering press reports detailing a backchannel proposal from the Kremlin.
According to investigative reports published by outlets such as Politico and The Wall Street Journal, Russian representatives presented a transactional geopolitical trade to the United States.
The reports revealed that Russia offered a bargain: Moscow would halt its intelligence-sharing and targeting-data pipeline to Iran in exchange for the United States severing its vital intelligence support to Ukraine.
The proposal was reportedly floated by Kremlin envoy Kirill Dmitriev to senior US representatives.
While Washington immediately rejected the deal, the transactional offer laid bare Moscow’s calculus – treating its surveillance support of Iranian strikes against US forces as a bargaining chip to isolate and subjugate Ukraine.
Washington now has a new sanctions tool
The disclosure comes shortly after President Donald Trump signed into law the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, a sweeping bipartisan package.
For the first time, this law grants the White House the authority to slap scorching secondary tariffs of up to 100% on foreign nations that continue to act as top buyers of Russian energy or facilitate the Kremlin’s sanctions evasion.
President Zelensky has explicitly called on Ukraine’s Western allies to demonstrate that there can be no “business as usual” with Vladimir Putin, warning that Moscow uses false diplomatic signals to buy time while escalating its campaign of terror.
By turning the screws on Russia’s global financing network and choking off the resources funding both the war in Europe and espionage in the Middle East, the US now possesses the ultimate economic leverage to force the aggressor toward real diplomacy.
In a striking diplomatic paradox, Vladimir Putin – the very leader accused of using satellite surveillance to help target US forces in the Middle East – could travel to American soil if he accepts the official invitation to attend the upcoming G20 summit in Miami.

articles.title: Zelenskyy Warns Of New Russian Mobilization, 10,000 North Korean Troop Deployment
articles.body:
The death toll from Russia's jet-powered drone attacks mounted in Ukraine while Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned that the Kremlin is preparing for a new troop mobilization at home and a fresh deployment of 10,000 North Korean soldiers.
After Zelenskyy spoke, journalists in the Ukrainian capital reported explosions in the city during a missile alert early on September 29. Details were not immediately available.
On September 28, at least two people were killed when a drone hit the National Academy of Sciences building in central Kyiv amid some of the most relentless aerial strikes -- often with new jet-powered drones -- on the Ukrainian capital since the start of the full-scale war in February 2022.
Zelenskyy said at least nine people had been killed and more than 80 injured in Russian drone strikes throughout the country during the day.
In his nightly video address, Zelenskyy said Ukraine was struggling to counter the high-flying Russian jet-powered drones, with the interception rate of just below 60 percent. He said 90 of the 120 drones fired on Ukraine were jet-powered, as opposed to propeller-driven.
"New interceptors are being actively tested," he said in his address.
"Some combat groups are using them, but, of course, some details still need to be refined to achieve enough effectiveness and scale. We are speeding up the developers."
Zelenskyy also cited a report from Ukraine's military intelligence agency, HUR, that he said showed Russia had launched a new wave of mobilization for its military.
"They are increasing the number of people they recruit through various methods," he said. "It is important that the governments of countries from which Russia recruits people for its army take action against this."
Preparations Under Way, Zelenskyy Says
Zelenskyy said some 8,000 North Korean troops, brought in by the Kremlin in 2024 to counter a Ukrainian incursion into Russia's Kursk region, remained in the country and that preparations were under way for the deployment of a further 10,000 soldiers.
Zelenskyy said in a post on social media that the North Koreans -- who reportedly suffered heavy losses during the previous deployment -- were "being selected for training and subsequent deployment to Russia."
Russian President Vladimir Putin has rejected reports of a new mobilization as "utter nonsense," although on September 28 he signed a decree increasing the size of the army by 15,500 troops -- the fourth such order this year.
"The authorized personnel strength of the Russian armed forces is to be set at 2,441,630 units, including 1,550,500 military personnel," the decree said, giving no reason for the addition.
Russia has suffered massive losses to soldiers, weapons, and military hardware since it launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, a venture the Kremlin reportedly believed would take only a few weeks to end in victory.
Putin last ordered a mobilization of reservists in 2022, and another such move would likely prove highly unpopular with the Russian population.
Difficult Reforms
Meanwhile, Ukrainian Prime Minister Serhiy Koretskiy warned that the public finances situation "remains difficult," saying the slow pace of reforms has caused Western partners to hold up financial commitment.
"Part of the planned international funding has not yet arrived. In particular, due to the fact that Ukraine has not had time to fulfill some of the obligations it has undertaken to international partners," without providing details.
Koretskiy has urged Ukrainian lawmakers to pass difficult reforms, including taxation of postal packages from abroad and a comprehensive overhaul of the taxation system.
Zelenskyy said he had held meetings on September 28 with Koretskiy and other officials to discuss "our key priorities in working with partners over the coming weeks in response to this situation. "
"The government, for its part, is doing everything necessary to fulfill its commitments and receive planned international funding. We are working together with the parliament. And here, responsible work from deputies of all factions and groups is important," he added, although he did not cite specifics.

articles.title: Russia is stepping up fake Ukrainian government pages as bait for recruiting agents, Ukraine’s security service says
articles.body:
Russian intelligence services have sharply stepped up building websites and social media pages that impersonate Ukrainian state bodies and media, the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) warned. Moscow uses the fakes to spread disinformation and to steal personal data it can turn into spy recruitment. The SBU says it has already blocked dozens of clones of its own brand.
Counterfeit pages built for propaganda and data theft
The fake sources serve Russian psychological operations and disinformation campaigns, the SBU said on 28 September. Their aim is to destabilize the situation inside Ukraine and damage its position abroad. Russian intelligence also uses them to extract Ukrainians' personal data, the agency said.
Alongside its full-scale invasion, Russia wages war on Ukraine in the cyber domain and through espionage and sabotage. Every agent Russia recruits inside Ukraine can help steer missiles and drones onto targets, and the SBU keeps catching such recruits.
Hacked accounts become recruitment leads
Russians often hack the accounts of users who subscribe to the fake pages and messenger channels, the SBU found. They then use the stolen information for recruitment operations and to collect confidential data.
Moscow is most interested in the combat and operational work of Ukraine's defense and security forces, the agency said. The SBU's cybersecurity department found and blocked more than 50 resources that copied the agency's own branding and positioning.
The fake pages are not Russia's only digital tool. Earlier in September, Anthropic said it had caught Russian spies running a campaign against Kyiv on its Claude AI chatbot.
How Ukrainians can protect themselves
The SBU urged citizens not to follow suspicious links and to rely only on official sources. Anyone who sees a dubious web address, or gets a message from someone posing as an SBU officer, should call the 1516 hotline, the agency said.
What Russia's recruits are sent to do
The SBU's own reports from the past week show what Russia's recruits are tasked with. A mobilized soldier allegedly recruited by the FSB, Russia's Federal Security Service, tried to direct a Russian missile strike on his own unit in Kharkiv Oblast, the SBU said. His repair battalion restores Ukrainian drones.
A Lviv Oblast resident who worked at a drone production site in western Ukraine was allegedly recruited to guide a missile strike on it, the agency reported. The strike was meant to disrupt the steady supply of strike and reconnaissance drones to Ukrainian troops, the SBU said.
A court also sentenced a 17-year-old agent of Russia's military intelligence (GRU), exposed in November 2024, to 10 years in prison, the SBU announced. She tracked Ukrainian air defenses in Chernihiv Oblast under the cover of taxi rides. She talked to her GRU handler through an anonymous messenger chat.

articles.title: New Ukrainian Intelligence Reveals Russia Expanding Military Ties With North Korea, Iran
articles.body:
President Volodymyr Zelensky has issued a stark warning to the international community, detailing expanding networks of military cooperation between Russia, North Korea, and Iran. In his evening address, Zelensky disclosed intelligence revealing that Moscow is actively preparing to absorb an influx of North Korean forces and is leveraging space assets to aid Iranian-backed regional strikes.
North Korean troops heading to Voronezh
According to the Ukrainian president, Russia is seeking to integrate an additional 30,000 North Korean troops into its war effort.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Kyiv’s intelligence indicates that infrastructure preparations to receive these personnel have been underway in Russia’s Voronezh region since June.
Beyond manpower, Pyongyang is reportedly preparing to ship additional ballistic missile launchers to Russian forces.
Zelensky emphasized that this alliance goes far beyond the immediate war in Ukraine.
“Russia is helping North Korea learn how to wage war, improve its weapons, and gain real combat experience in using them,” Zelensky stated, noting that the partnership poses a security crisis for nations across Asia that sit within range of North Korean missile systems.
North Korea has already sent an estimated 14,000 to 15,000 troops to support Russia since 2024, primarily deploying them to Russia’s Kursk region, according to Ukrainian and South Korean assessments. Pyongyang has also supplied Moscow with millions of artillery and mortar rounds, ballistic missiles, long-range artillery and multiple-launch rocket systems.
Mali Army, Russia’s Wagner Committed War Crimes Against Civilians, Amnesty Says
‘Russia is helping them learn how to wage war’
Zelensky warned that Russia is effectively providing North Korea with something difficult to acquire anywhere else: direct experience of modern large-scale warfare.
“Russia is helping North Korea learn how to wage war, improve its weapons, and gain real combat experience in using them,” the Ukrainian president warned.
“All of this is a threat to everyone in Asia who is within range of North Korean missiles.”
Ukraine, Zelensky pledged, “will counter this.”
The battlefield cooperation has already involved North Korean weapons.
Five days after the July warning, Zelensky announced that preliminary Ukrainian findings indicated Russia had used a North Korean ballistic missile in a strike on Radushne near Kryvyi Rih.
A ballistic missile struck an ordinary family home there, killing children and their parents, according to the Ukrainian president.
“The alliance between the Moscow scumbags and the deranged regime in North Korea exists for the sake of missiles, North Korean troops on our borders here in Europe, and killing our Ukrainian children,” Zelensky noted in his July 30 address.
Satellite intelligence funneled to Iran
The Ukrainian president also announced that he has instructed domestic intelligence agencies to share actionable data with international partners regarding Russia’s growing support for the Iranian regime.
Kyiv has recorded active Russian satellite surveillance tracking Gulf states and US military facilities in the region since early July. This intelligence has funneled to Tehran.
“Since the beginning of July, we have recorded active Russian satellite surveillance of the Gulf states and US military facilities located there,” Zelensky disclosed.
“These images subsequently appear in Iran.”
Zelensky highlighted a correlation between Russian satellite passes and subsequent Iranian strikes – noting the imagery is utilized for pre-attack planning as well as post-strike battle damage assessments.
As a specific example, Zelensky revealed that between July 19 and July 20 alone, Russian intelligence satellites focused heavily on four key air bases in the Middle East: two in Bahrain, one in Jordan, and one in Kuwait.
“The purpose is clear,” Zelensky remarked.
“None of us in the world should turn a blind eye to one very simple fact: evil always seeks ways to make things worse and spread further.”
Zelensky presented Russia’s expanding relationships with Pyongyang and Tehran as evidence that the consequences of Moscow’s war against Ukraine are spreading well beyond Europe.
“Russia must be stopped. This war must be stopped. Pressure on the aggressor must work,” he said.
“When we are able to produce PAC-3 missiles in Ukraine, we will help those in the world who need protection with these missiles as well,” the president pledged.
Zelensky closed his warning by broadening responsibility beyond Moscow itself.
“Everyone who is helping Russia prolong this war right now must also be held accountable for all the global consequences of this war,” he concluded.

articles.title: Russian Military Personnel Gap Widens
articles.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky in a Monday evening national video address said the Kremlin’s military was intensifying recruitment and incorporating mercenaries into the Russian Armed Forces in an attempt to fill chronic personnel shortages at the front.
Zelensky stated on Sept. 28:
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Today I received a report from the Defense Intelligence [Ukraine’s military intelligence agency, Головне управління розвідки, or HUR] on the steps Russia is planning next. In practical terms, the Russians have begun new mobilization of conscripts. They are increasing the number of people that they take in [into the military] by various means. They are planning to increase recruiting for foreigners.”
More than 8,000 North Korean soldiers are currently on Russian Federation territory assisting in operations against Ukraine, and Pyongyang is training another 10,000 soldiers to reinforce them, Zelensky said, adding:
“Russia is paying for all of this by various illicit means, and in return, for this this help, for the technical assistance by Russia on North Korean territory, there has been set up a production line for Shahed-type strike drones. This is how evil works together, and how a deadly threat in one end of the world becomes a deadly threat in another end of the world.”
Countries from which Russia recruits foreign soldiers to fight as mercenaries in Ukraine should work with Kyiv and international law enforcement agencies to prevent that, Zelensky said.
EU Might Press Ukraine on Reforms to Unlock Billions in 2026 Aid
Western states also should intensify sanctions against Russia and states cooperating with Russia, because if unchecked, the Kremlin’s attacks against Ukraine and other countries will only increase, Zelensky said.
Zelensky’s comments followed a Monday order by Russian leader Vladimir Putin for a limited increase in the size of his country’s armed forces, and a decree instructing military recruiters to work harder to find men for the Russian Armed Forces.
The Presidential order raised by 15,500 the size of Russia’s armed forces to a total of 2,441,630 personnel, including 1,550,500 military personnel, and directed state funding be funneled to intensified recruitment.
It was the fourth increase in military personnel ordered by the Kremlin in 2026 alone. In 2022, the Kremlin faced with a collapse of its pre-war professional military caused by unexpectedly heavy casualties among mobilized reservists.
The executive decree published on the Presidential register made no mention of increased conscription or mobilization of reservists. In the run-up to national elections earlier in the month, some Kremlin critics had suggested the moment voting was over the Putin regime would implement a wide-ranging draft forcing tens of thousands of civilians into the military to fight in Ukraine.
Putin in early September called reports he was planning to mobilize reserves “utter nonsense” (Russian: “чушь собачья”) and during a Sept. 3 speech in Vladivostok told an audience, “There is no scenario today that would require mobilization… from the point of view of availability of military service members, Russia has no problems whatsoever.”
According to both tracking by the Ukrainian Armed Forces (AFU) and international military observers, Russian forces operating in Ukraine are suffering heavy and sometimes devastating losses in attacks most often carried out by unsupported infantry soldiers ordered to traverse open terrain under continuous observation by Ukrainian drones. According to those sources, Russian personnel shortages are severe and, thus far, Kremlin efforts to fill shortfalls have been insufficient.
According to data published by the Icelandic-based researcher Ragnar Gudmundsson on Tuesday, two days in Sept. 2026 saw some of the highest daily losses by Russian forces of the entire war (Sept. 28 – 2,090 men, Sept. 17 – 1,960 men).
Russian forces have probably suffered more than 405,000 combat deaths in Ukraine since invading in February 2022; and total Russian casualties are on track to pass the 1.6 million mark in mid-November 2026, Gudmundsson estimated.
Heavy losses have made voluntary recruitment of replacements so difficult, that Russia to sustain operations in Ukraine will have no option to force men into service, if not by conscription than by other means of impressment, most western observers say.
Analysis published by the Institute for the Study of War (ISW) on Sept.18 said in part:
“The Kremlin will have to change its recruitment practices and likely conduct some form of involuntary reserve call-up in order to sustain its war effort in Ukraine…Russia’s current casualty rate exceeds its recruitment rate by thousands per month, and the Russian war effort is even so failing to achieve its operational and strategic objectives.”
Petro Andriushchenko, director of the Ukrainian government agency Center for the Study of Occupation (CSO), on Monday possibly confirmed that prediction with a report saying that the Russian state has “factually begun” shadow mobilization of reservists, with recruiters contacting former service members now civilians in the central Sverdlovsk region to “volunteer” for service in drone defense units.
Their mission would largely be in the Svedlodvsk regional capital Yekaterinburg protecting “energy facilities, industrial plants, and other critical infrastructure. Mobile fire teams are also being formed specifically to counter UAVs,” Andriushchenko said in a Monday report published on the CSO public channels.
Key qualifications are minimum nine years of schooling, age 52-62 or less depending on rank, and meeting the third category of physical fitness (Russian: Category “В”) for a recruit, which permits a soldier with moderate medical impairments like reduced respiratory capacity or inability to run for extended periods of time to be accepted into service.
“Russian authorities specifically emphasize that this is not a military service contract and that reservists will supposedly not be sent to the war against Ukraine. Formally, they remain civilian employees who attend training assemblies and receive additional payments,” the CSO statement said in part. Men, including reservists taken into service in 2022-2023, usually found themselves transferred to frontline units, the report said.
Ukraine’s 3rd Corps, a major combat unit in action on the eastern front in the eastern Lyman sector, on Monday announced a wide-front counter-offensive in progress since August had captured more than 250 Russian prisoners of war, and published images of 58-60 disarmed Russian service personnel under Ukrainian guard, reportedly in a northern Donetsk region forest.
Ukrainian mainstream media and Russian milbloggers confirmed the 3rd Corps claims of prisoners of war captured, as well as 2,500-3,000 Russian soldiers killed or seriously wounded. The operation took advantage, in part, of low Russian troop numbers in the path of the Ukrainian attack.
Russian official sources have largely ignored evidence of the defeat and heavy losses and insisted Kremlin forces are continuously advancing.
French researcher Clément Molin’s in a Friday analysis of claimed Russian territorial gains in Ukraine, compared with independently-confirmed evidence of actual Russian control of Ukrainian territory, found that for much of 2026 Russia had “barely advanced in Ukraine but continued to update their official maps and claims. This gives a more than 5,000 square kilometer difference between reality and what Russia claims.”
[KP Note: A land space with an area of 5,000 square kilometers (1,931 square miles) is roughly the size of the British county Northumberland, France’s Bouches-du-Rhône department, or the US Grand Canyon National Park.]

articles.title: The Kremlin calls mobilization talk “nonsense”—Zelenskyy says it has already begun, with North Korean reinforcements
articles.body:
Russia has quietly started a new round of mobilization and plans to bring in more North Korean troops, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said. He cited a new report from Ukraine's military intelligence. The same day, the Kremlin published a decree enlarging Russia's army for the fourth time this year.
Russia widens recruitment at home and abroad
Zelenskyy spoke in his evening address on 28 September, after a briefing from Ukraine's military intelligence (HUR).
"In effect, the Russians have already begun additional mobilization—they are increasing the number of people they recruit through various means," he said.
Moscow also plans to recruit more foreigners, Zelenskyy said. He urged the governments of countries whose citizens Russia recruits to counter it, and said Kyiv would inform each of them.
Ukraine says Russia has been losing soldiers faster than contract recruitment replaces them. If so, an unannounced call-up lets the Kremlin refill its ranks without a formal draft. ISW says Putin may hold off on such a draft until he sees whether his strikes work. Ukrainian intelligence had expected Russia to announce a mass mobilization after this month's State Duma elections.
More than 8,000 North Koreans in Russia, 10,000 more in preparation
More than 8,000 North Korean troops are currently on Russian territory, Zelenskyy said. Pyongyang is selecting another 10,000 for training and deployment to Russia, he added.
Russia is paying, among other things, with technology, according to Zelenskyy. North Korea has launched production of Shahed-type attack drones with Russian technical support, he said.
That is a step beyond what Kyiv reported in June 2025. Moscow and Pyongyang had then only agreed to start preparing such production. In August, Zelenskyy warned that Russia could receive up to 50,000 North Korean troops.
North Korean missile unit deploys to Russia for ballistic strikes on Ukraine, Kyiv says
Kremlin raises the army's size again
Putin's decree sets the authorized strength of Russia's armed forces at 2,441,630, including 1,550,500 military personnel, Vedomosti reported. The decree gives no reason.
The order adds 15,500 troops and is the fourth such increase this year, Euronews said. Since March, the combined increase has reached 47,860 soldiers. Putin's 2022 "partial mobilization" decree also remains in force, the outlet noted.
Russia could open northern front by February if it orders new mobilization, Ukraine intel says
Moscow keeps denying a call-up
In early September, Putin claimed that reports of a coming mobilization were "complete nonsense" and "an information attack on Russia." Russian officials gave similar assurances days before the 2022 call-up.
Ukraine's military and foreign intelligence had earlier said that Russia's General Staff prepared a scenario to mobilize 600,000 people over 2026 and 2027, 300,000 each year.

articles.title: France Just Rehearsed a Nuclear Strike With Rafales—Here’s How Operation Poker Works
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
France Just Rehearsed a Nuclear Strike With Rafales—Here’s How Operation Poker Works
France’s Air and Space Force has rehearsed one of the country’s most consequential military missions: breaking through hostile defenses and delivering a nuclear-armed missile to a precise launch point using Rafale fighters.
The exercise, known as Operation Poker, involved operations linked to the Saint-Dizier and Taverny air bases, both central to France’s airborne nuclear deterrent, Le Parisien reported on September 28.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Saint-Dizier hosts Rafale units assigned to France’s Strategic Air Forces, while the underground command infrastructure at Taverny helps direct nuclear operations.
The exercise is designed to test virtually the entire strike sequence under realistic conditions—with one major exception.
“We use real equipment, we test real procedures in extremely adverse conditions, with around 50 aircraft in the air. The only thing that is prohibited is flying with real nuclear warheads under the wings,” French military personnel explained.
Rafale crews involved in the simulated strike did not carry operational nuclear weapons. Instead, they flew with inert training versions representing France’s ASMP-A air-launched nuclear missile, which could be jettisoned safely if an emergency occurred.
The operational ASMP-A is a supersonic cruise missile carried by the Rafale and forms the airborne component of France’s nuclear deterrent. Public estimates put its range at roughly 500 kilometers, or about 310 miles. France officially confirms that the missile carries its TNA thermonuclear warhead, although Paris does not publicly disclose its current explosive yield.
During Poker, French forces split into opposing teams. The “red” force simulated an enemy trying to detect, intercept and stop the raid, while the “blue” force attempted to penetrate those defenses and deliver its simulated nuclear weapon to the required launch point at exactly the planned time.
“It is about guaranteeing that tomorrow and the day after tomorrow we will still have the ability to conduct such a raid, even as technology evolves faster and faster,” French military personnel said.
For the Rafale crews, that means a demanding mission lasting roughly six to eight hours.
During the nighttime flight, the fighters may refuel several times from aerial tankers before approaching the simulated target area. Crews then have to maneuver at very high speed and, during portions of the mission, at very low altitude to reduce their exposure to enemy air defenses.
The objective is not simply to prove that a Rafale can carry a nuclear missile. Poker tests whether the entire system—command centers, fighters, tankers, crews, communications and supporting aircraft—can function together under the conditions expected during a high-intensity war.
France has conducted Poker exercises for decades, generally several times each year. Earlier 2026 iterations involved around 40 aircraft, including Rafale B fighters and A330 MRTT Phénix tankers, operating against simulated air-to-air and ground-based threats.
For French crews, the exercise is ultimately intended to make sure the nuclear weapon never has to be used.
“The purpose of our mission is to prevent war, and therefore the use of nuclear weapons. Poker is a demonstration of force precisely so that this does not happen,” said Commander Jean-Baptiste, who recently qualified for the mission by participating in the exercise.
Personnel assigned to the nuclear mission must regularly repeat that training.
“Each of them has to participate in at least one such operation per year,” Jean-Baptiste said.
France currently maintains several air bases connected to its nuclear mission, including Saint-Dizier, Istres and Avord. Luxeuil is also expected to regain a nuclear role as France prepares for the future Rafale F5.
Orders for the airborne deterrent ultimately flow through the command structure at Taverny, roughly 200 kilometers from Saint-Dizier, where military personnel operate from a hardened underground command center.
Earlier, Germany and France put their nuclear-deterrence cooperation into practice for the first time, staging a joint air force drill with nuclear-capable French Rafale jets and German Eurofighters.

articles.title: Ukraine just caught a Geran-5 at 425 km/h—the jet drone that has often outrun Ukrainian interceptor drones since January
articles.body:
Ukraine's air defenders now have purpose-built interceptors for Russia's jet-powered attack drones—weapons whose speed and altitude make them difficult for conventional defenses to catch, Militarnyi reported. A crew from the 1020th Anti-Aircraft Missile and Artillery Regiment downed a Geran-5 over Chernihiv Oblast with a newly delivered interceptor, according to the Serhiy Prytula Foundation.
Russia's long-range drone and missile attacks have become central to its effort to wear down Ukraine's air defenses and grid before winter, and the war in the sky now turns on which side scales its answer faster.
The Chernihiv intercept
The crew, callsign Yastrub (Hawk), made its first successful engagement with the new interceptor, hitting the jet drone at 425 km/h and above 3 km, the foundation said, releasing footage of the strike. The Prytula Foundation supplied the interceptors and said it has contracted several manufacturers to counter the jet threat.
"Our task is to scale this up and strengthen units," it said.
Why it kept slipping through
Russia first used the Geran-5 in January 2026. HUR's own specifications put its warhead at 90 kg, cruise speed at 450–600 km/h, and range at 950 km, with a ceiling of 6 km. That mix of jet speed and high altitude kept it clear of machine guns, shoulder-fired missiles, and the cheap interceptors built to swat slower piston-engine Shaheds.
Ukraine's military intelligence estimates Russian plants now turn out around 3,000 jet-powered Geran-4 and Geran-5 drones a month, according to HUR. A monitoring Telegram channel, Polkovnyk HSh, reports a newer variant that steers by ground imagery instead of satellites, which would blunt jamming—though HUR has not confirmed it and lists no such system among the drone's components. Separately, Russia moved the jet engine inside the fuselage, a change aimed at more speed and range.
After Russia hits Kyiv’s Academy of Sciences with jet-powered drone, the Kremlin says Ukraine must “pay a price”
Where the fight stands
Ukraine intercepts about 55% of Russia's jet drones, against more than 90% of the older models, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on 26 September. Since the start of September, Russia had launched more than 2,730 jet drones, and Ukraine had downed or suppressed more than 1,500, he added. Zelenskyy also said Russia plans to spend $12 billion in 2027 on jet drones and loitering munitions alone. Ukraine already has several interceptor prototypes in combat use, and the 1020th crew's kill is one of several jet Geran intercepts Ukrainian units and drone makers have logged this month.
