articles.title: America’s Greenland deal has a radioactive backstory
articles.body:
America’s Greenland deal has a radioactive backstory
The US, Denmark, and Greenland have signed a new agreement to expand American military activity on the island. Washington calls Greenland vital to its security, but an expanded military presence also raises an older question: What risks does the Arctic island take on in return?
The agreement builds on a defense partnership dating back to 1951. That history includes an episode that brought the risks of Washington’s Cold War strategy into sharp focus: An American mission over Greenland that ended in a nuclear disaster.
The nuclear patrols over Greenland
In the 1960s, in the middle of the Cold War, the US Air Force launched Operation Chrome Dome. This mission implied keeping bombers armed with nuclear weapons on continuous airborne alert, ready to strike the USSR if necessary. If you’ve seen the film ‘Dr. Strangelove’, you’ll remember that Major T.J. ‘King’ Kong’s crew was involved in such a patrol mission.
Theoretically, this strategy was feasible: It would have made it impossible for the USSR to disarm the US with a single blow. However, in practice, as the number of nuclear-armed aircraft patrols increased, so did the number of incidents involving nuclear weapons.
Then-US Secretary of Defense Robert McNamara advocated for ending this program, arguing that Americans had already established an effective early warning system for ballistic missile launches, so the US could take fewer risks and cut costs. However, the Strategic Air Command resisted this idea, fearing it would decrease their importance and result in budget cuts.
A horrific incident occurred in 1966 over Spain when a bomber collided with a refueling tanker aircraft, resulting in several fatalities and nuclear bombs landing on beaches and in the Mediterranean Sea. Despite this incident, the US considered the nuclear threat from the USSR a matter of primary importance, one which justified any security measures.
Eventually, after intense debates, a compromise was reached: The number of patrolling bombers would be reduced, but the airborne patrols would continue.
Thule Air Base in northern Greenland was established in the 1950s. A Mercator projection map gives a distorted sense of distance; in reality, its location was very convenient for potentially launching missiles at the USSR and monitoring missile launches from there. It also provided a convenient vantage point for reconnaissance of the Novaya Zemlya Soviet nuclear test site.
Thus, the US Strategic Air Command built a military base in northern Greenland. The name referred to ‘Ultima Thule’ (farthest Thule) – a mythical island at the edge of the world. The base housed bombers, reconnaissance planes, radar systems, missile launch sites, and early-warning radars. In its most active period, Thule base housed about 10,000 personnel. Additionally, the US launched the highly classified Project Iceworm, which aimed to build a wide network of nuclear missile launch sites concealed in tunnels beneath the ice. One could say Greenland became thoroughly inhabited.
Seven men, four hydrogen bombs, and a fire in the sky
On January 21, 1968, a B-52 bomber rose into the air, carrying four megaton bombs. It took off from New York to visually monitor the nuclear alert system, bearing four thermonuclear bombs, each with a yield exceeding one megaton.
The standard crew consisted of five members; however, a third pilot and a substitute navigator were included on the mission.
Everything started out smoothly. But eventually, the factor of human error came into play.
The third pilot, Major Alfred d’Amario, took aboard a few cloth-covered foam cushions to make his flight more comfortable. He placed the cushions under the instructor navigator’s seat and went to replace co-pilot Leonard Svitenko, who went to take his rest period. The cushions remained in place.
Not long after, the pilots opened an engine bleed valve which channeled hot air from the engine to the heater. Unfortunately, the heater was defective and quickly became dangerously hot.
At some point, the pilots noticed the smell of burning rubber filling the cockpit. While they searched for the source of the burning, a fire had already started onboard. The navigator went looking for the flames, and, on discovering the fire, attempted to extinguish it using two fire extinguishers. However, he was unable to put it out.
Captain Haug, the aircraft commander, requested an emergency landing at the airbase. All the extinguishers had been used, but the fire continued to spread. Smoke thickened to the point that the crew could hardly see each other in the cockpit. Ultimately, as the plane neared Thule Air Base, Haug ordered everyone to abandon it.
Out of the seven crew members, six managed to eject relatively safely. Tragically, co-pilot Leonard Svitenko sustained fatal head injuries while trying to escape.
Haug and d’Amario landed directly on the airbase grounds. The base personnel immediately mobilized to search for the remaining crew. A polar night enveloped Greenland, and the weather was dreadful. A representative of the Royal Greenland Trade Department, Jens Zinglersen, significantly eased the search efforts by contacting local Inuit residents who organized dog sled teams. Thanks to their collective efforts, three other aviators were found – they had landed within a mile and a half of the base and were quickly located.
Gunner Staff Sergeant Calvin Snapp was less fortunate. He ejected first and landed nearly 10 km from the base in -30C degree temperatures. Wrapping himself in his parachute, he waited for help for 21 hours before being rescued by a search team. Miraculously, they found him alive, though severely hypothermic.
But the worst was yet to come. The aircraft carrying thermonuclear munitions was still flying northward and burning up. Finally, it crashed onto the ice about 12 km west of the airbase. There was still plenty of fuel onboard; it ignited on the ice, causing spectacular pyrotechnic effects. The bomb’s non-nuclear explosives detonated, partially melting the ice and scattering radioactive debris everywhere.
There was another poignant detail, however. Greenland belonged to Denmark, which had declared its entire territory a nuclear-free zone. And now, a bomber armed with nuclear weapons had crashed there – though the Danes (at least those who didn’t work in the government) were unaware that there was also radioactive debris all over the ground. The Danish government quickly issued a statement claiming that the aircraft was not in Greenland’s airspace and had only entered it due to an onboard emergency. This was a complete fabrication, but it served as a cover-up for the situation.
The US found itself in a delicate situation that urgently needed fixing.
Cleaning up a nuclear disaster in the Arctic night
The cleanup operation was dubbed Project Crested Ice (or unofficially, ‘Project Doctor Freezelove’). The operation was led by General Richard Overton Hunziker, a seasoned veteran and WWII hero.
A team of scientists, nuclear specialists, and a massive number of troops were dispatched to Greenland. Their mission was to remove all radioactive materials before spring arrived and the contaminated ice would be carried off into the ocean. The polar night brought fierce winds and bitterly cold temperatures, making the task even more challenging.
Radioactive elements were scattered across a 1-mile (1.6 km) by 3-mile (4.8 km) area. In the midst of it was an ice hole measuring 50 meters in diameter. A blackened patch measuring 670 by 120 meters and heavily contaminated with uranium and plutonium was clearly visible from the air.
The US suggested to the Danish authorities that they should just wait for spring when the ice would melt and everything would sink into the Arctic waters. But Denmark was outraged. The Americans were given a choice: Either clean up their mess or close down the Thule base and leave Danish territory.
It must be said that Hunziker and his team worked heroically. They established a small town on the ice, complete with igloos, a power station, a runway, a communications hub, and a decontamination chamber. An icy road connected them to the airbase.
Thousands of people toiled under the harsh conditions, illuminated by floodlights as they cut through the contaminated ice, loaded it onto transports, and hauled it to storage, where it was boxed up in tanks for shipping back to the US. Ice was collected using graders, packed into wooden crates, which were then loaded into steel tanks and onto ships. Debris was recovered manually – some pieces were sizable, but the smallest were no bigger than a battery. Contaminated areas were identified using simple Geiger counters.
The cleanup crew worked with minimal protective clothing. Most people simply wore their regular Arctic expedition clothing.
By mid-September 1968, the operation was officially concluded. In total, 1,700 Danes and 700 Americans participated in it. While the disaster was a stark illustration of the consequences of foolish and irresponsible behavior, the cleanup crew – which braved the harsh cold and literally gathered radioactive waste by hand – accomplished real feats, which, however, remained largely forgotten.
What the ice couldn’t bury
It’s believed that around 93% of the radioactive materials were collected, but some remnants remained on the seabed. One hydrogen bomb likely sank among other debris. Attempts to locate it with a submersible were unsuccessful. A heap of wreckage was discovered on the ocean floor, and somewhere down there, it appears that the remains of the nuclear weapon still lie undisturbed.
In the 1980s and ‘90s, a scandal erupted. Danish cleanup workers launched a legal battle against the American government. Though they lost the case, they succeeded in forcing the release of numerous classified documents. Subsequent investigations revealed that cancer mortality rates among Danish workers involved in the cleanup operation were about one and a half times higher than those of the general population. It also turned out that the health monitoring of the cleanup crews after the incident was inadequate. Ultimately, officials concluded that radiation exposure wasn’t significant and found no link between the increased cancer rate and the 1968 accident.
A heated debate arose around the actions of Danish prime ministers Jens Otto Krag and H. C. Hansen. Krag portrayed himself as a naïve yet honest figure, insisting that he wasn’t aware of aircraft carrying nuclear weapons over Greenland. However, declassified US documents indicated that the Danish government was aware of everything. As for Hansen, he was the one who secretly approved the US to use Thule Air Base as part of its nuclear shield. However, by then, both prime ministers had passed away, and were unable to answer to the population.
After the incident, Operation Chrome Dome was officially shut down. After all, it was the second nuclear disaster in three years, and that was too much even for the ‘hawks’. Secondly, both Russians and Americans already had plenty of missiles, and the use of bombers seemed somewhat archaic. Finally, the USSR and the US initiated another period of détente and developed protocols for handling any accidental incidents involving nuclear weapons. While this didn’t help those who suffered or died from cancer as a result of the accident in Greenland, it did significantly reduce the risk of similar events in the future.

articles.title: Are Houthis using new modified cruise missiles in Yemen’s war?
articles.body:
Are Houthis using new modified cruise missiles in Yemen’s war?
Experts say use of modified Iranian defence system could alter the balance in the fight for the Red Sea.
Yemen’s internationally recognised, Saudi-backed government has alleged that the Tehran-backed Houthis have modified Iranian air defence weapons into loitering cruise missiles with the assistance of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).
The Yemeni government has warned that the capability of such missiles – which operate on a heat-tracking system, it alleged – in practice threatens civilian air traffic over Yemen and the crucial Red Sea.
Meanwhile, the Houthis have ramped up attacks on Saudi Arabia as they fight Yemeni government forces. On Thursday, Riyadh said it intercepted six ballistic missiles aimed at Taif in western Saudi Arabia and the Yanbu port area on the Red Sea.
The Houthis also said they attacked “a sensitive target” in the Saudi capital, Riyadh, and Saudi Aramco facilities in Yanbu. Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the group used ballistic and cruise missiles as well as drones in the two operations.
The Houthis were in open conflict with Yemen’s government and a Saudi-led coalition of Arab states from 2014 until a United Nations-brokered ceasefire was declared in 2022, but fighting has reignited in recent weeks with the Houthis taking the Red Sea coast of Yemen along with the strategically important city of Mocha and Mayyun Island in the Bab al-Mandeb strait at the southern entrance to the Red Sea.
In July, the armed group declared a naval blockade against Saudi Arabia in the Red Sea, essentially opening yet another theatre in the US-Israel war on Iran.
Since the closure of the critical Strait of Hormuz during the war, the Red Sea has become a vital alternative export route for the region’s biggest oil player, Saudi Arabia. Its East-West Pipeline, which carries oil from its eastern oilfields to the western port of Yanbu is only just restarting operations after damage inflicted by a drone attack this month.
So what do the Houthis’ latest missile capabilities mean for the region?
What has the Yemeni government said?
Brigadier General Majed al-Nazili, spokesperson for the Yemeni government forces, said the Houthis are using Iranian air defence weapons that pose a danger to all aircraft.
Al-Nazili said the weapons have been modified with the assistance of IRGC experts and are being used to strike aircraft and cruise missiles.
“These missiles move around for a period of up to 25 minutes per missile and operate using a thermal-tracking system and attack any heat source without the ability to distinguish between military or civilian targets,” he said in a statement.
“This constitutes a direct and serious threat to the safety of civil aviation and the lives of passengers,” al-Nazili added.
Why does Yemen’s government think regional airspace is under threat?
Al-Nazili noted that aircraft belonging to the United Nations or humanitarian organisations travelling via air routes over Yemen and the region could potentially be in danger.
“Threatening the airspace over the southern Red Sea and turning it into a danger zone for civilian aircraft and passengers represents an escalation that goes beyond the scope of Yemeni airspace safety alone,” he said.
Al-Nazili also said “this dangerous escalation coincides with the threats” by Iranian officials, including Mohsen Rezaei, the secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, to target aviation services in the region after the US sanctioned Iranian airlines.
Rezaei had initially warned that regional airports could lose flights if they joined US restrictions on Iranian aviation. Two days later, his office later clarified that Tehran was not planning military retaliation over the restrictions although it said nonmilitary countermeasures against specific airports remained possible.
Using “Iranian weapons from Yemeni territory poses a direct threat to international air navigation routes and cannot be considered a purely domestic Yemeni issue,” al-Nazili said, calling on international authorities to take “urgent and decisive action”.
Have the Houthis modified Iranian weapons systems?
Eleonora Ardemagni, a senior associate research fellow at the Italian Institute for International Political Studies, told Al Jazeera that while there is no conclusive evidence that the Houthis have modified an Iranian air defence system, “a series of things suggest this can’t be ruled out.”
“The Houthis have often demonstrated to be able to innovate despite the warfighting scenario, so the evolution of threat capabilities is a constant for the group,” she said.
Ardemagni said years of research have established that “the Houthis don’t receive assembled missiles from Iran but Iranian-origin components to be assembled, so they have significant expertise in assembling weapons.”
She referred to an incident in June 2025 when the Yemeni government-aligned National Resistance Forces, led by Tareq Saleh, seized a 750-tonne shipment of weapons and military equipment bound for the Houthis, including hundreds of advanced cruise, antiship and anti-aircraft missiles, according to the US military’s Central Command.
In July this year, several media reports, including from the Reuters news agency, said an Iranian Mahan Air flight directed to Yemen’s Houthi-held capital, Sanaa, was carrying IRGC commanders, military advisers and weapons. Al Jazeera could not independently verify this report. “The flight was forced to land in Houthi-controlled Hodeidah at last, the same governorate from which the Yemeni government now states the Houthis would launch cruise missiles,” Ardemagni told Al Jazeera.
Brigadier General Mohammed Al-Kumaim, a Yemeni military and strategic analyst, said the Houthis are no longer content with using Iranian ballistic missiles and drones but have begun employing advanced air defence technologies based on “loitering” cruise missiles.
Al-Kumaim noted that these missiles can remain in the air for up to 25 minutes, tracking the flight path of targets from their electrothermal emissions.
Yemeni military and strategic expert Ali Al-Dhahab told Al Jazeera that the effect of these loitering munition projectiles is to create a “permanent threat” to any moving object in the air, which could temporarily restrict military air movements.
AI giant Anthropic has also identified a weapons-development cell in northern Yemen reportedly linked to the Houthis that used its Claude AI to develop guidance, navigation and control software for a guided rocket and several missile programmes.
What are the Houthis’ known missile capabilities?
The Houthis have a multilayered missile force, ranging from short- and medium-range ballistic missiles to antiship cruise missiles and modified surface-to-air missiles.
Research into the armed group’s arsenal suggested it has evolved substantially from the inherited Yemeni military stockpiles it seized when it took Sanaa in 2014, including Soviet- and Chinese-designed missiles, and has incorporated Iranian-designed missiles.
Here is what we know the Houthis have in their missile arsenal, based on their recent statements:
- Palestine-2: a two-stage, solid-fuel missile unveiled by the group that the Houthis claim is hypersonic with a range exceeding 2,000km (1,245 miles)
- Toufan: one of their long-range systems, said to have an estimated range of 1,350km to 1,950km (840 to 1,210 miles). An International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS) assessment said the Toufan appeared to be a rebranded Iranian Ghadr.
- Burkan series: short- to medium-range ballistic missiles based on Iranian designs
- Quds series: cruise missiles cited by Houthi spokespeople after strikes on oil and economic facilities in the region
- Older inventory: The Houthis have historically possessed or modified older variants of missiles that include the Scud-B/-C, Tochka and Qaher-1 ballistic missiles as well as C-802 antiship cruise missiles.
What does this mean for the Red Sea and the Yemen war?
As far as the regional aviation sector is concerned, Saj Ahmad, chief analyst at StrategicAero Research, told Al Jazeera that “critically, air traffic around Yemen is almost nil, and that reduces the propensity of inadvertent threats to passenger airplanes.”
However, “these same missiles are being launched northwards into Saudi Arabia, where there is commercial traffic,” Ahmad added.
That Houthi threat, therefore, poses “a huge dilemma for the Saudis, who will be very reluctant to close off airspace but equally be mindful of the risks of allowing air traffic through when missiles are inbound”, Ahmad said.
He added that the Houthis have “demonstrated that they can hit targets at distance. The attack near Tel Aviv airport last year is but one example.”
When the Houthis’ arsenal is analysed in the context of the crucial Bab al-Mandeb strait, “any missiles that the Houthis have in their armoury can easily decimate ships at will on a much narrower waterway,” Ahmad said.
Yemeni military strategist Al-Kumaim said the introduction of these supposedly new missiles “adds another capability to the military operations theatre south of the Red Sea” and is part of a broader Iranian strategy to exert pressure on regional airspace and energy supply chains.
Analyst Ardemagni noted that Yemen’s government and Saudi Arabia “have an interest in raising the alarm bell for regional security as much as possible given the current ‘loneliness’, in terms of regional and international allies they are experiencing since the Yemen war has reignited”.
She added that if new cruise missiles are demonstrated, “it would certainly contribute to redesigning Red Sea balances in favour of nonstate armed actors.”

articles.title: Ukraine war briefing: Putin orders army expansion as Zelenskyy says more North Koreans to be deployed in Russia
articles.body:
- 
  Russian president Vladimir Putin has ordered an increase in the size of the army to 1.55 million active servicemen, according to a presidential decree on Monday. The order comes as both Russia and Ukraine suffer mounting casualties in the more than four-and-a-half-year Ukraine war. The expansion, which follows a similar increase ordered in August, will put the size of Russia’s armed forces at 2,441,630. Of those are 1,550,000 active servicemen, an increase of 15,500.
- 
  Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on X on Monday there were now more than 8,000 North Korean troops on Russian territory and preparations were under way to deploy another 10,000 troops. Putin and North Korean leader Kim Jong-un confirmed for the first time last year that North Korea had sent troops to fight for Russia in the war with Ukraine, with both leaders describing the soldiers as “heroes”.
- 
  Citing “new data” on the deployment of North Korean troops to Russia, Zelenskyy said they were “being selected for training and subsequent deployment to Russia”. North Korea has sent an estimated 14,000 to 15,000 troops to support Russia’s war in Ukraine since 2024, according to Ukrainian and South Korean estimates, with most deployed in the Kursk region to help repel a Ukrainian incursion.
- 
  Explosions were heard in the Ukrainian capital of Kyiv early on Tuesday, a Reuters witness said, as Russia continues its near-daily attacks. Missile debris fell in the courtyard of a residential building, among other damage, and a non-residential building caught fire in another part of the city, Kyiv mayor Vitali Klitschko said on Telegram. On Monday, Zelenskyy said nine people had been killed and more than 80 injured in Russian drone strikes throughout the country, including in Kyiv.
- 
  Pope Leo urged Russia and Ukraine to sit down and discuss how to end their war, hours after he had urged European leaders seeking to end conflicts to make concessions to achieve peace. Addressing a press conference aboard his flight to Rome on Monday after a four-day trip to France, Leo said the 1.4-billion-member Catholic church had an obligation to call for peace and respect of human life. “The Church has a responsibility to promote these values, continually inviting leaders – from Russia and Ukraine, as well as other countries – to come together, sit down, engage in dialogue,” the pope said.
- 
  Nato’s top military commander said Russia’s sabotage campaign in Europe was failing to put countries off supporting Ukraine. “State-directed sabotage is growing increasingly brazen,” US general Alexus Grynkewich told a committee of EU lawmakers on Monday. Nato’s supreme allied commander for Europe cited recent incidents including the discovery of an explosive-laden drone at a German airport and a Russian naval ship firing flares at a Danish helicopter. “These are clear examples of attempts to instil fear and fracture our unified support to Ukraine. It isn’t working,” he said.
- 
  Ukraine will postpone some spending commitments, including reconstruction work, because of delays in receiving aid from its foreign backers, Ukraine’s prime minister said. The government would carry out these projects eventually, “but for now, all resources must be directed toward critical areas”, Sergiy Koretsky said on Telegram on Monday. Russia’s offensive has battered Ukraine’s economy, causing billions of dollars in destruction and punching a huge hole in its neighbour’s finances.
- 
  Putin has ordered the Russian assets of German retailer Metro AG to be placed under temporary administration, amid Russian-German tensions over the Ukraine war. The order, posted on Monday on the government website, did not state a reason. The step follows similar steps against the Russia businesses of global food company Nestlé and French retailer Auchan under a 2023 decree aimed at businesses associated with “unfriendly countries”. Temporary administration has led to local owners taking over the Russia businesses of French dairy concern Danone and Danish brewer Carlsberg at knockdown prices.
- 
  A Russian jet-powered drone struck a Ukrainian village near the Polish border earlier on Monday, damaging a border checkpoint, a regional Ukrainian official said. The official did not give details about the nature of the checkpoint or extent of damage from the blast. Russia has launched multiple attacks near Ukraine’s border with Poland in recent weeks, drawing condemnation from Warsaw and its European allies.

articles.title: Poland changes rules of engagement for firing on foreign aircraft amid growing Russia threat
articles.body:

Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.
Poland is changing the procedures under which its military can fire upon foreign aircraft, citing the “growing threat from Russia”. Visual identification of targets will no longer be required, with other forms of data to be used instead.
The move follows a series of violations of Polish airspace over the last year by Russian drones, a missile and a helicopter, as well as Russia’s increasing use of jet-powered drones to attack targets in Ukraine close to the Polish border.
Polska zmienia procedury użycia uzbrojenia dla lotnictwa w przypadku zwalczania obcych statków powietrznych. To wnioski Dowódcy Operacyjnego generała Ireneusza Nowaka z ostatnich tygodni.
To także odpowiedź na rosnące zagrożenie ze strony Rosji, doświadczenia wojny w Ukrainie…
— Cezary Tomczyk (@CTomczyk) September 28, 2026
“In the coming days, the defence minister will change the procedures for firing by Polish planes and helicopters at objects flying to us from the direction of Russia,” announced deputy defence minister Cezary Tomczyk on Monday, quoted by news service Defence24.
The change, as Tomczyk explained in a statement later issued on social media, will shift requirements away from requiring visual identification of foreign aerial objects and towards so-called “positive identification”.
The latter involves identifying an object based on a combination of several other, non-visual sources of information, such as using radar and other sensors to determine its speed, altitude, trajectory and flight parameters, as well as a lack of IFF (identification friend or foe) from an object.
Tomczyk said that the change was being made based on the “conclusions from recent weeks” made by the operational commander of Poland’s armed forces, General Ireneusz Nowak.
It is a “response to the growing threat from Russia, experiences from the war in Ukraine, and the emergence of new air attack means – primarily fast jet drones and cruise missiles in the case of which the time for reaction is very brief”, added Tomczyk.
The minister said that positive identification would only be issued when there is a “sufficiently high degree of certainty in determining what we are dealing with”. He noted that accurate target identification is particularly crucial in peacetime, when there are civilian aircraft in Polish airspace.
The change will mean “not less identification, but a different way of conducting it: faster and based on data from multiple sources”.
Poland's government has issued public guidance on how to act in the case of airborne attacks, amid growing concerns over the threat from Russia.
It is also preparing evacuation plans and clearer markings for 85,000 shelters across the countryhttps://t.co/vMEMU6mlRx
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 25, 2026
Defence24 reports that the government, military and many experts have found current rules of engagement to be overly restrictive and not suited to meeting the scale and type of threat facing Poland today.
It points to last week’s violation of Polish airspace by a Russian helicopter, which crossed the border from Kaliningrad and spent around 42 seconds in Poland before returning.
The website also notes that Russia’s growing use of jet-powered drones, which are able to travel much faster than traditional unmanned aerial vehicles, is a further threat.
Such drones have recently been used to attack targets along the Ukrainian side of the border with Poland, including a passenger train travelling between Kyiv and Warsaw.
A drone has struck a passenger train travelling between Kyiv and Warsaw, around 2 km from the Polish border, amid the latest mass Russian attacks on Ukraine.
Separately, a truck around 800 metres from a border crossing with Poland was also hit last night https://t.co/ZbfE2iDLOk
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 13, 2026
“Until now, we have not utilised these [non-visual identification] capabilities because they are typically reserved for a state of war or martial law,” said Tomczyk.
“However, given the threat, and the fact that Poland today struggles daily with the possibility of drones entering our country, we must implement these changes for the benefit of both pilots and national security.”
In July this year, a Russian Kh-101 cruise missile also entered Polish airspace before landing in a field. On one night last year, around 20 Russian drones crossed Poland’s eastern borders. Some were shot down but many struck the ground.
Earlier this month, Prime Minister Donald Tusk warned that, according to intelligence sources, Russia is planning drone and missile strikes on eastern NATO countries, which it would present as accidental.
Russia is planning drone and missile strikes on eastern NATO countries, which it would present as accidental, says Polish Prime Minister @donaldtusk, citing intelligence sources.
The aim would be to create a sense of "NATO's helplessness", he says https://t.co/9MFPiEEkIV
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 18, 2026
Poland has invested heavily in its air defences in recent years, including buying Patriot batteries and fighter aircraft from the United States, as well as developing a new anti-drone system with Norway’s Kongsberg Defence & Aerospace.
The government has also recently moved to expand the network of warning sirens along the Ukrainian border, launched a campaign informing the public how to respond to aerial threats, and started more clearly marking bomb shelters.

Daniel Tilles is editor-in-chief of Notes from Poland. He has written on Polish affairs for a wide range of publications, including Foreign Policy, POLITICO Europe, EUobserver and Dziennik Gazeta Prawna.

articles.title: Why Gaza Flotilla's Thiago Ávila is running for Brazil Congress
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
'We must fight imperialism': Global Sumud Flotilla's Thiago Ávila takes his fight to Brazil's Congress
For more than two decades, Brazilian socio-environmentalist and Palestine solidarity activist Thiago Ávila has campaigned against what he describes as imperialism, colonialism and the exploitation of people and nature.
Now, after years of activism and high-profile participation in Gaza-bound flotillas, he is taking that political struggle into Brazil's electoral arena.
A member of the Global Sumud Flotilla's steering committee, Ávila has helped organise a movement that expanded from more than 40 vessels in 2025 to more than 70 by May 2026, bringing together hundreds of activists from around the world.
He was also among those detained after the flotilla was illegally intercepted by Israeli forces near Crete on April 30, 2026. Along with Spanish-Swedish activist Saif Abukeshek, he was held without formal charges at the Shikma facility in Ashkelon and deported on May 10, 2026, following international pressure and a hunger strike.
Now, Ávila is running for a seat in Brazil’s Chamber of Deputies with the green party REDE in São Paulo.
He says his potential term would bring his activism into parliament, with a particular focus on challenging what he describes as Israeli and Zionist influence over Brazilian policy.
"We believe that our candidacy and possible future term can accomplish an even more expressive role in the struggle for the Palestinian cause, in the fight against imperialism and colonialism," Ávila tells The New Arab.
"One of our key proposals is the rupture of all relations [with Israel]," he continues.
"We intend to establish a term that is vigilant to combat the Zionism lobby in our country, in our political process, and most importantly, in our elections. We are aware that Zionism uses scrutiny times to infiltrate, and that Brazil unfortunately has given in many ways, mostly associated with far-right-wing politicians."
Foreign influence in Brazilian politics
His remarks come days after ABIN, the Brazilian Intelligence Agency, forwarded a report on September 19 to the Supreme Electoral Court (TSE), the Presidency of the Republic, and the Ministry of Justice, pointing to the "risk of influence and interference from the United States of America in the upcoming Brazilian electoral process."
The information was released by Folha de S.Paulo and confirmed by O GLOBO. The report comes amid a wider pattern of closer US-Israeli alignment across Latin America, including the creation of the 'Shield of the Americas', a coalition of 18 Latin American countries plus the United States, which excludes Brazil's Lula and Mexico’s Claudia Sheinbaum.
The shift has also been reflected in relations between Israel and governments across the region.
Argentina's president Javier Milei has praised Benjamin Netanyahu and co-signed the 'Isaac Accords', a branch of the Abraham Accords aimed at furthering public diplomacy and cooperation between Israel and Latin American countries.
In Brazil, congresswoman Tabata Amaral of the Brazilian Socialist Party (PSB-SP) registered bill 1424/26, which supposedly criminalises anti-semitism and includes criticism of Israel as an anti-semitic practice, despite anti-semitism already being a crime in Brazil since 1988.
On September 21, President Lula told CNN anchor Christiane Amanpour that he was "deeply concerned" about possible interference from the United States in Brazil's democratic election process.
As a counterpoint, the United States spokesperson, Amanda Robertson, denied that the United States or its allies had meddled in Brazilian democracy.
Brazilian Zionist backlash
Political candidates who publicly support Palestine and oppose Israel's genocide in Gaza, like Thiago, are commonly attacked by local Zionist organisations.
These include StandWithUs Brazil and the Brazilian Israelite Confederation (CONIB). Journalist Caio Blinder and academic Samuel Feldberg, who are linked to these organisations, have publicly described Ávila as a "professional activist" whose advocacy is motivated by the pursuit of publicity and political gain.
"This sort of attack is not exclusive to Brazil or to me," Ávila explains.
"They attack all those who report on what is done in Palestine, who report on the genocide, and who report on Zionist infiltration in a wide range of countries — similarly how they attacked United Nations Special Rapporteur on the Occupied Palestinian Territories, Francesca Albanese, environmental activist Greta Thunberg, and other prominent figures in the debate for Palestinian liberation," he adds.
"I treat these attacks as part of the process. Threats against me and other advocates have increased dramatically, and our democracy has largely deteriorated due to the influence of Trump and Netanyahu. This is evident in the growing number of far-right leaders occupying positions of power. We must confront these hateful ideologies with all our capacity."
Pathway as a social-environmentalist
Despite support from a significant portion of the Brazilian-Palestinian community and his role in past flotillas to Gaza, Ávila rejects claims that his advocacy for Palestine is motivated by political gain.
He says that, in the electoral process, voters will primarily consider his work as a social-environmentalist rather than his activism in defence of the Palestinian people.
He also adds that his candidacy rests on the intersection of social justice and environmentalism, and rejects claims of appropriation, pointing to the recognition of his advocacy by Palestinian-Brazilian organisations such as the Palestinian Federation and the Palestinian Front of São Paulo.
"I've been an activist for 22 years now, and for 22 years I have been fighting against exploitation, oppression, and the destruction of nature in order to build a 'well-living' society," Ávila tells The New Arab.
"Both environmental disaster and the war machine that profits from genocide originate in the same system. American imperialism, which provides over 80% of the bombs Israel uses in Gaza, is also involved in environmental damage all around the world," he adds.
"It's not a coincidence that the US military, as an institution, is one of the most prominent sources of pollution for the whole planet," Ávila adds.
"In Brazil, some right-wing state governments, but also certain so-called progressive ones, purchase weapons, espionage software, drones and hypersurveillance technology from Israel's arms industry. These are, logically, tools used for mass exploitation, agricultural deforestation, poaching, mining and many other destructive practices," Ávila tells The New Arab.
"The billionaires who profit from these violations, and those behind the legal frameworks that allow this technology to flow into Brazil and circulate around the globe, are the same."
With elections approaching on October 4, and the country’s sovereignty to choose its own leaders at stake, the open question remains: will Brazilian voters pick their representatives based on the Brazil they want to build for the future, or on the Brazil foreign powers want to build for them?
Rogger Oliveira is a multimedia journalist covering geopolitics and social issues in the Middle East and North Africa. He has a previous background as a translator and interpreter working in English, Spanish, Portuguese, Italian, and French

articles.title: Trump denies offering Iran sanctions relief, Tehran says ready for talks
articles.body:
Trump denies offering Iran sanctions relief, Tehran says it is ready for talks
Sept 29 - US President Donald Trump said he has offered Iran nothing to end the war, rejecting media reports that cited US officials saying he was willing to ease sanctions and release frozen funds for "concrete" steps regarding Iran's nuclear programme.
"This is untrue. I offered them NOTHING," Trump wrote on Truth Social on Monday.
Axios and CNN both reported, citing unidentified US officials, that Trump was willing to give Iran sanctions relief and free Iranian funds as part of a final deal on the condition that Iran showed "concrete progress" on the nuclear issue.
Trump has cited preventing Tehran from acquiring a nuclear bomb as a key goal of the war, along with ending its ability to attack its neighbours and creating conditions for Iranians to topple their leadership.
Iran does not have nuclear weapons and denies it wants to develop them, but argues it has the right to a domestic nuclear energy capacity.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, in an interview with the CBS show "Face the Nation", said Tehran was ready for talks on its nuclear programme and other issues, but would not accept "bullying or coercion".
"Iran is not seeking war, but will defend itself against pressure, threats and attacks,” Pezeshkian said, adding that it had already agreed that "we're not supposed to develop nuclear weapons".
US and Iranian officials spoke separately with mediators on Monday as part of a renewed effort to end the seven-month war, according to officials of both countries.
Iran insisted on Sunday that only diplomacy can solve its conflict with the United States and Israel.
"Our conditions are clear, and any move toward reopening the Strait of Hormuz is contingent on these conditions being met," Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi posted on social media. "Only a negotiated solution can get them out of this deadlock."
Araqchi told reporters at the UN on Friday the proposed deal would trigger a seven-day countdown to reopening the strait and a pause in regional fighting.
Trump on Saturday rejected the plan and argued that desperation was driving the Iranians’ push for an agreement on the key waterway.
"They want to make a deal to open the Hormuz Strait immediately because they're losing so badly," Trump told reporters at the White House.
Araqchi said mediators facilitating Tehran's talks with Washington had not officially relayed a US rejection.
"We are waiting for the mediators to convey the definitive views to us, and we will make a decision based on them," Araqchi posted.
OIL PRICES RISE
The war, which Trump launched alongside Israel in February as "Operation Epic Fury", has killed thousands of people, severely disrupted global energy supplies, pushing up oil prices and fuelling global inflation.
Iran and its allies have responded by extending the conflict throughout the region. Iran has struck US allies in the Gulf with drones and missiles, while its Houthi allies in Yemen have hit Saudi interests.
Saudi Arabia, the largest of the Gulf states, has been drawn deeper into the war this month as Houthi fighters have advanced in Yemen, routing forces of the Saudi-backed government and threatening Saudi oil exports through the Red Sea.
Oil prices rose for a second successive session on Tuesday as lingering concern over Middle East supply outweighed signs of recovering crude exports from the region.
Brent crude futures had risen $1.49, or 1.4%, to $106.77 a barrel by 0326 GMT while US West Texas Intermediate crude was at $93.94, up $1.34, or 1.5%. Both benchmarks closed the previous session at nearly $1 a barrel higher. REUTERS

articles.title: France Conducts Nuclear Strike Simulation
articles.body:
France’s Aerospace Force carried out a simulated nuclear strike during the Poker military exercise.
According to Le Parisien, the operation was conducted from the Saint-Dizier and Taverny air bases.
Both bases play a key role in France’s nuclear forces. Saint-Dizier supports the air-based component of the nuclear deterrent, while Taverny houses command and operational facilities for the strategic forces.
Rafale fighter jets took part in the exercise.
“We use real equipment and follow real procedures in highly challenging conditions, with around 50 aircraft in the air. The only thing prohibited is flying with actual nuclear warheads under the wings,” French military personnel shared.
The exercise did not involve real ASMP-A nuclear missiles. Instead, the Rafales carried inert mock-ups designed to match the missiles’ weight and dimensions. These could be safely dropped from the aircraft if necessary.
The missile has a maximum range of approximately 500 km and carries a 300-kiloton TNA nuclear warhead.
Two teams took part in the simulation: the “red” team, representing the enemy, and the “blue” team, which operated against them.
“The aim is to ensure that tomorrow and the day after, we will still be capable of carrying out such a mission, even as technology continues to evolve at an ever-faster pace,” French military officials explained.
The crews were tasked with penetrating the enemy’s defenses and delivering the missiles to precisely designated locations at a specific time.
During the six- to eight-hour nighttime flight, each Rafale crew refueled several times from one of 15 tanker aircraft.
The fighter pilot must maneuver at very high speeds and at low altitude.
“The purpose of our mission is to prevent war and, therefore, the use of nuclear weapons. Poker is a demonstration of force precisely to ensure that this does not happen,” explained Commander Jean-Baptiste, who had just received the necessary qualification by participating in the exercise. “Each of them must participate in at least one such operation every year.”
France already has three air bases with a nuclear role – Saint-Dizier, Istres, and Avord – and will soon reactivate another base at Luxeuil to host future Rafale F5 aircraft.
Orders to the bases come from farther away – from a bunker at the Taverny base, approximately 200 km from Saint-Dizier. The bunker houses the command center, with around 40 military personnel stationed there permanently.
France is currently the only nuclear-armed state in the European Union, and there have been repeated discussions about potentially extending its nuclear protection to the entire bloc.
France is the European country that established a system of “extended” nuclear deterrence, which many countries have already joined.

articles.title: Pentagon orders more fuzes to turn Hydra rockets into drone killers
articles.body:
The Pentagon has ordered another $52.3 million worth of L3Harris proximity fuzes that turn laser-guided APKWS rockets into drone killers, more than doubling the value of a fuze contract signed just four months ago.
The firm-fixed-price modification, announced by the U.S. Department of War, adds to a contract the Naval Surface Warfare Center Indian Head Division awarded L3Harris Fuzing and Ordnance Systems in late May. The work will be done in Cincinnati, Ohio, and is due to be finished by November 2027. The notice does not say how many fuzes the money buys.
A proximity fuze sets off a warhead when it senses a target nearby, so the rocket does not have to hit a small, fast-moving drone directly to destroy it. L3Harris calls the product its Mechanical Proximity Fuze, also known as the FALCO fuze, after the Fixed Wing, Air Launched, Counter-Unmanned Aircraft Systems Ordnance program. It combines radio-frequency sensor electronics from Technology Service Corporation with an L3Harris safe-and-arm device.
The fuze is fitted to the Advanced Precision Kill Weapon System, or APKWS, a BAE Systems guidance kit that turns ordinary 70 mm (2.75-inch) Hydra rockets into laser-guided weapons. The rockets are far cheaper than air-to-air missiles, and a single F-16 carrying six seven-tube launchers can hold 42 of them.
U.S. Air Force F-16s began using proximity-fuzed APKWS rockets to shoot down Houthi one-way attack drones over the Red Sea in 2024. In testing at Yuma Proving Ground, Arizona, APKWS rockets with the L3Harris fuze destroyed Group 3 drones, the larger class of unmanned aircraft, every time, The Defence Blog reported in May. The same fuze arms rockets fired by L3Harris’ VAMPIRE, a truck-mounted counter-drone launcher that Ukraine has used against Russian drones since 2023.
The original May contract was worth $48.5 million, with options that could raise it to about $98 million and deliveries running through July 2027. L3Harris has said demand is pushing it to increase proximity fuze production sevenfold. Most of the new money, $44.8 million, or 86%, comes from fiscal 2026 Defense-wide operations and maintenance funds. Another $3.8 million comes from fiscal 2025 funds of the same type, which expire at the end of the current fiscal year on Sept. 30, and $3.7 million comes from fiscal 2026 U.S. Army ammunition procurement funds. The notice does not say which units will receive the fuzes.
The Pentagon is also developing a newer air-to-air version of APKWS. In February 2026, the U.S. Air Force awarded BAE Systems a contract worth up to $145 million for an APKWS variant with a long-wave infrared seeker and a proximity-fuzed warhead, which lets the rocket home in on a drone’s heat without a pilot having to keep a laser on the target. That version is planned for U.S. Air Force F-16s and U.S. Navy MH-60 helicopters.

articles.title: Over 8,000 North Korean troops stationed in Russia as 10,000 more prepare, Zelenskyy says
articles.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has claimed that more than 8,000 North Korean troops are stationed on Russian territory, warning that preparations are actively underway to deploy an additional 10,000 personnel.
Citing "new data" regarding Pyongyang's military integration with Moscow, Zelenskyy stated that additional North Korean forces are "being selected for training and subsequent deployment to Russia."
The statement comes after the Ukrainian leader warned in August that up to 50,000 North Korean soldiers could ultimately be deployed to fight on behalf of the Russian military, prompting Kiev to urge South Korea to provide air defence assistance.
In July, Seoul committed a $100 million non-lethal aid package to Ukraine.
Pyongyang's arsenal
Zelenskyy's remarks follow diplomatic friction between Seoul and Kiev over his public disclosure last week confirming that Ukrainian forces transferred two captured North Korean soldiers to South Korea.
The South Korean government expressed formal regret over the public disclosure, maintaining that both nations had mutually agreed to keep the transfer confidential.
Seoul also lodged a protest against a statement released by the Ukrainian presidential administration that denied the existence of any confidentiality pact.
North Korea has dispatched an estimated 14,000 to 15,000 troops to bolster Russia's military campaign in Ukraine since 2024, according to assessments compiled by Ukrainian and South Korean intelligence agencies.
The vast majority of these forces have been deployed across the Kursk frontier region to help Russian forces counter a Ukrainian cross-border operation.
Beyond personnel, Pyongyang has supplied Moscow with millions of artillery and mortar rounds, alongside ballistic missiles, heavy long-range artillery systems, and multiple-launch rocket systems, according to Ukrainian officials and independent defence assessments.

articles.title: Russia Closes Airspace Over Kapustin Yar, Launch Site for Oreshnik Missiles
articles.body:
Russia has restricted the use of airspace over the Kapustin Yar test range in the Astrakhan region.
The restriction was announced in NOTAM V5696/26, issued by the Rostov Flight Information Region (FIR).
The airspace will be restricted daily from September 28 through October 3, 2026, between 9:00 a.m. and 7:00 p.m. Moscow time.
The restricted zone extends from the ground surface with no specified upper limit, meaning it formally covers the entire altitude range.
Kapustin Yar is used as a test range for missile technology.
The closure of the airspace has been linked to a possible launch of Russia’s Oreshnik ballistic missile.
However, the airspace restrictions could also be related to tests of other missile systems. Therefore, the issuance of the NOTAM does not establish what specific tests or launches Russia plans to conduct during this period.
In May 2025, Russia similarly closed the airspace over Kapustin Yar ahead of a possible ballistic missile launch between May 12 and 13.
No launches of missile weapons against Ukraine were recorded at the time.
A similar flight restriction was in effect on November 21, 2024, ahead of the ballistic missile strike on Dnipro involving the Kedr (Oreshnik) missile. At the time, the restrictions were in place between 4:00 a.m. and 8:00 p.m. from November 21 to 23.
Similar notices were also issued for December 11–13, from 8:00 a.m. to 12:00 p.m. local time, while a second restriction was in effect from December 16 to 21.
Following this, on December 13, Russia launched a massive missile attack against Ukraine involving ballistic, cruise, and hypersonic missiles.
Kapustin Yar is a large Russian missile testing range in the Astrakhan region of the Russian Federation. Its official name is the 4th State Central Interservice Testing Range of the Russian Ministry of Defense.
The range covers a vast area with launch sites, tracking and measurement facilities, and designated zones where missile stages and warheads land. Its location allows launches over considerable distances and enables monitoring of missile flight trajectories.

articles.title: Era of Iraq without US troops begins as combat presence ends
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
End of an era as US-led coalition forces withdraw from Iraq
Baghdad and other Iraqi provinces hosting military bases used by foreign and US forces are entering a new chapter with the end of the "combat and operational presence" of US forces and the international coalition.
Baghdad no longer has any field barracks or combat camps after Lt Gen Abdul Amir Al-Shammari, director of the office of the commander-in-chief of the armed forces and head of the Iraqi government, announced that the Victory military base, located near Baghdad International Airport west of the capital, is now completely free of US personnel as part of the withdrawal of foreign forces from Iraq.
A new framework based on the bilateral security and political relationship between Baghdad and Washington is set to follow after the withdrawal.
Iraq says it will work to cover the shortfall in military aviation capabilities that will follow the departure of the international coalition, stressing that there will be no foreign combat forces or military bases in the country after 30 September.
Years of US forces in Baghdad
For years, the US military and security presence was distributed across strategic sites inside and around Baghdad, including the Victory military base complex, the largest operations management centre near the capital.
Victory housed headquarters for the general staff, reconnaissance centres, and facilities securing air and logistical transport, as well as advisory headquarters in Baghdad's "Green Zone", the government district.
These forces focused on coordination through the Joint Operations Command to protect the area around the US Embassy and nearby institutions.
In Anbar province in western Iraq, Ain al-Asad airbase was a vital artery for air support, radar systems and supplying equipment and support to fronts near Baghdad.
Harir Airbase in Erbil, the centre of the Kurdistan Region in northern Iraq, emerged as a hub for technical support and logistical movements in the north. Its various roles included intelligence gathering, intelligence coordination through unmanned aircraft, providing air cover, training and equipping Iraqi forces, and carrying out targeted strikes against remnants of the Islamic State.
Iraqi government military spokesman Sabah al-Numan announced on Monday, 28 September, that the international coalition forces had begun withdrawing from the base, saying in press statements that the withdrawal would be completed by 30 September.
Under the 2008 security agreement between Baghdad and Washington, US forces completed their full withdrawal from military bases and cities in December 2011.
The final convoys crossed the southern border into Kuwait, with Baghdad announcing at the time that it had taken over the sites and bases from the Americans and established national sovereignty.
But Iraq soon became compelled to submit an official request to Washington for training and air support after Islamic State occupied about 30 per cent of the country in 2014, amid a security and military collapse of the Iraqi army and armed forces that continues to raise questions without answers.
As a result, the US-led international coalition was formed, comprising 89 countries and international organisations such as the European Union and NATO.
US advisory and combat groups returned to scattered bases, including in Baghdad and Anbar.
The role of the international coalition and US forces in the war against Islamic State from 2014 to 2017 contributed to providing air cover and carrying out direct strikes against the group's headquarters and movements, as well as coordination through reconnaissance aircraft, intelligence gathering and identifying field targets, and training Iraqi military forces, equipping them with modern equipment and weapons, and providing advice on managing battles.
The role of Iraqi forces and Popular Mobilisation Forces brigades was to conduct direct ground combat and carry out raids and operations to liberate villages and cities that had been under the group's control.
But the assassination of Jamal Jaafar, known as Abu Mahdi Al-Muhandis, deputy head of the Popular Mobilisation Forces, and Quds Force commander Qassem Soleimani near Baghdad International Airport on 3 January 2020 marked a decisive strategic turning point like the relationship between armed factions close to the "Axis of Resistance" and US forces and the international coalition in Iraq.
These factions chose to apply political pressure and launch continuous and systematic military campaigns.
This translated into parliamentary demands to expel foreign and US forces as "occupiers", alongside moves to launch strikes and attacks against the US Embassy in Baghdad and vital military bases, including "Victory, Asad and Harir", using missiles and drones.
These attacks led to a state of isolation and heightened security precautions inside headquarters and bases.
The movement of US forces in the field was restricted, and Washington was often forced to redeploy its forces and withdraw some personnel from secondary bases, consolidating them in more heavily fortified camps.
The tensions pushed forward negotiations to restructure the military presence and shift it entirely towards an advisory and bilateral framework.
Baghdad and Washington announced the end of combat missions at the end of 2021, with the missions changing from combat to advisory and training roles, without ground combat forces on the ground.
This followed lengthy rounds of dialogue conducted by the Joint Higher Military Committee between the two sides, which established timetables for evacuating sites, dismantling combat infrastructure and returning full management of the airspace and bases to Iraqi military forces.
In this context, Iraqi Security Media Cell chief Lt Gen Saad Maan said the international coalition had handed over all its bases and headquarters to the authorities and that there would be no coalition combat or training forces after the end of this month.
Maan added that Iraqi security forces were ready to take over the security file and capable of managing it after the international coalition withdrawal.
He said in a press statement that "relations with coalition countries after their withdrawal will become bilateral".
Optimism and objections
For his part, Ali Al-Fatlawi, a member of the Coordination Framework alliance, said to The New Arab, "Iraq's sovereignty is indivisible, and we see ending any US military presence inside Baghdad and its bases as an inevitable step that has been long awaited."
"Previous experiences, beginning with the 2011 withdrawal and the return under the pretext of the Islamic State in 2014, taught us that real stability is not achieved through the presence of foreign forces but through complete reliance on Iraqis," he said. "the withdrawal of the international coalition's combat forces and the complete clearing of Baghdad and its headquarters of any field barracks is a national achievement that reflects the high readiness of Iraqi forces".
"The security situation today is under the full control of our security institutions, and what the agreement stipulated is a smooth and carefully planned transition from a direct military and field role to an equal bilateral security relationship based on training, arms supplies and intelligence sharing to ensure that Islamic State threats do not return," he added.
"Clearing the capital of signs of foreign and US military presence represents a pivotal turning point in the history of security alliances in the region," researcher Adnan Al-Kinani told TNA. "This shift from a field combat presence to institutional partnership tests the state's ability to control the pace of the domestic security scene and remove political and weapons-related pretexts."
"Iraqi forces now face the challenge of proving their direct field capacity to manage the vacuum and sustain stability without direct foreign support," Kinani added.
Despite optimism in Baghdad over the departure of US forces and the announcement of a three-day public holiday after 30 September to mark "Sovereignty Day", the Kurdistan Regional Government has openly expressed its concerns over the US withdrawal.
Kurdistan Region Prime Minister Masrour Barzani described the US military withdrawal from Iraq as "shameful" and said it would leave Washington's Kurdish allies without protection.
He warned that US President Donald Trump risked repeating the mistake of the administration of President Barack Obama, which withdrew in 2011 before being forced to return.
Barzani warned in an interview with the Financial Times that "the US withdrawal is happening at a particularly turbulent time in the region".
"We are weak, and we are under attack. To be left alone now without any proper defence system is shameful," he continued. "And when we are prevented from buying the sufficient weapons needed against these missiles, drones and advanced systems, we naturally become more vulnerable by design."

articles.title: Zelenskyy: Over 8,000 DPRK troops in Russia; another 10,000 being prepared for deployment there
articles.body:
More than 8,000 North Korean troops are currently in Russia, and another 10,000 or so are being prepared for training and subsequent deployment to the country, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said.
“We also have new data on the deployment of North Korean troops to Russia. There are currently more than 8,000 North Korean troops on Russian territory. In addition, preparations are underway to deploy another 10,000 troops – they are being selected for training and subsequent deployment to Russia,” Zelenskyy said in his evening address on Monday.
According to him, the relevant data was presented during a briefing by the Main Intelligence Agency (GUR) of the Ministry of Defense regarding Russia's future plans. The Russian Federation has already initiated additional mobilization and is increasing the number of personnel recruited into the military through various methods.
“They also plan to increase the recruitment of foreigners, and it is important that the governments of the countries from which Russia recruits people into its ranks counter this. We will inform every relevant government,” the President noted.
At the same time, according to Zelenskyy, Russia is compensating North Korea for military assistance, specifically with technology. With technical support from the Russian Federation, the production of Shahed-type strike drones has already been launched within North Korea.

articles.title: Russia Pounds Kyiv Again With Ballistic Missiles Hours After Attacks Kill 2, Injure 26
articles.body:
Russia launched a fresh ballistic missile attack on Kyiv early Tuesday, hours after a day-long barrage killed two people and injured 26 across the Ukrainian capital.
Several loud explosions rang out across Kyiv early hours of Tuesday, Sept. 29, as air defenses activated during a new air raid alert.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“New ballistic missiles are heading towards Kyiv,” Ukraine’s Air Force warned on Telegram as the attack unfolded.
Ukrainian monitoring reports said the new assault began at around 1:20 a.m., with warnings of ballistic missile launches from Russia’s Kursk region as Kyiv again came under missile threat.
Later, shortly before 2 a.m., Mayor Vitaliy Klitschko reported that missile debris had fallen in the courtyard of a building in the Solomianskyi district and that an administrative building at an infrastructure facility in the same district had been hit.
He also reported a fire at a three-story non-residential building in the Pecherskyi district.
After 2 a.m., the mayor added that a strike and fire had occurred at one of the buildings of an educational institution in the Solomianskyi district, with emergency services dispatched to the scene.
In a morning Telegram update, the State Emergency Service (DSNS) reported that one person was injured in the Russian attack.
“A strike on a six-story residential building was recorded in the Holosiivskyi district. One person was injured, and 10 others were evacuated to safety,” the report stated.
‘Science Became a Target’: Europe Condemns Russian Strikes on Kyiv Civilian Sites
Additionally, two private homes were damaged in the Solomianskyi district.
All fires have been extinguished.
According to the Air Force, Russian forces launched a Zircon/Onyx anti-ship missile, two Iskander-M/S-400 ballistic missiles, 152 Shahed-type attack drones – 82 of them jet-powered – as well as Gerbera and Parodiya decoy drones, between 6 p.m. on Sept. 28 and 8 a.m. on Sept. 29.
The Ukrainian Defense Forces repelled the attack using aviation, anti-aircraft missile units, electronic warfare and unmanned systems units, and mobile fire groups.
As of 8 a.m., Ukrainian air defenses had shot down or suppressed 109 aerial targets:
- one Zircon/Onyx anti-ship missile;
- two Iskander-M/S-400 ballistic missiles;
- 106 drones.
“Enemy air attack assets were recorded striking 24 locations, while debris from downed targets fell at 16 locations,” the Air Force said.
The renewed attack came only hours after Kyiv endured waves of Russian strikes throughout Monday, Sept. 28, hitting multiple districts and leaving civilian buildings burning across the capital.
Klitschko said late Monday that two people had been killed and 26 others injured, including three children. Eight of the wounded were hospitalized and one remained in serious condition.
One of the dead was initially reported after a Russian drone struck a non-residential building belonging to Ukraine’s National Academy of Sciences in Kyiv’s historic center.
Rescuers later recovered the body of a second victim from the building during emergency operations.
Russian attacks were reported across the Shevchenkivskyi, Obolonskyi, Solomianskyi, Darnytskyi, Podilskyi and other districts during the day.
In central Kyiv, a strike set part of the National Academy of Sciences building ablaze. Another strike hit a seven-story building housing a Dobrobut medical facility, where seven people were reported injured, six of them employees.
Russia also struck the Darnytsia pharmaceutical plant, while fires and damage were reported at other non-residential and commercial buildings around the capital.
Klitschko continued reporting fresh impacts into Monday evening. A non-residential building in Obolonskyi district was struck more than once, vehicles caught fire after a drone fell into a residential courtyard in Solomianskyi district, and a three-story business center was hit in Sviatoshynskyi district.
President Volodymyr Zelensky condemned Monday’s strikes and said Russia would face consequences.
“Every Russian terrorist attack results in casualties that could have been prevented had the pressure on Russia finally become total,” he said, calling for stronger international action against those financing and producing Russia’s weapons.
Ukraine’s Air Force said Russia launched 124 drones during Monday’s attacks, including 86 jet-powered UAVs, and reported that 86 aerial targets were destroyed or suppressed.

articles.title: North Korea warns UN of Japan’s ‘attempts at rearmament'
articles.body:
Amir Latif Arain
29 September 2026•Update: 29 September 2026
North Korea warned the UN on Monday of longtime rival Japan's “attempts at rearmament” while emphasizing that multipolarity in international affairs was an “irresistible trend of the times.”
Addressing the 81st session of the UN General Assembly in New York, North Korean Vice Foreign Minister Kim Son-gyong accused Japan of taking advantage of the current volatile international environment.
He said Japan has accelerated its attempts at rearmament with an "unprecedented" commitment, including the revision of its Peace Constitution, the abandonment of its "exclusively defense-oriented policy," the reformation of its military structure and an arms buildup.
"Such actions are casting war clouds over the entire region," Kim warned.
He said that “under the signboard of counterattack capability," Japan has moved ahead with the development and possession of long-range attack weapons that put neighboring countries within striking range.
Condemning recent joint military exercises by the US, Japan and South Korea, Kim accused the United States of conspiring "with its allies to systematically amend and update the anti-North Korea nuclear war scenarios through "provocative war rehearsals of all hues and military build-up."
"The US-Japan-South Korea military alliance, unmistakably aimed at the DPRK, is being evolved by the United States into a more offensive and aggressive military bloc with a nuclear element," he said, referring to the Democratic People's Republic of Korea, North Korea’s official name.
He reiterated that North Korea's nuclear status is "uncompromisingly" fixed and can never be reversed in any circumstances.
"I would like to reiterate the official position of the DPRK government: the status of the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea as a nuclear weapons state that has been uncompromisingly and permanently fixed both physically and legally with absolutely no turning back, can never be reversed in any circumstances or by any means, no matter how hard and loudly the hostile forces may deny in chorus with all sorts of rhetoric," he said.
Kim observed that multilateralism and multipolarization have emerged as an “irresistible aspiration and trend of the times based on justice and equity.“
"Gone are the days when an individual member state unilaterally imposed its will on the rest of the world and dominated the international political arena."
Kim also indirectly described the US-Israeli war on Iran as "state-sponsored terrorism.”
"The new year started with the most despicable, world startling act of state-sponsored terrorism, followed by worldwide outbreaks of other appalling incidents and events," he said.
Urging the UN to firmly secure its authority and future by promoting equality and cooperation among sovereign states, Kim said the world body should no longer be misused for the sinister political purposes of ''specific forces.''
He said the effects of a disaster-prone abnormal climate have given rise to a succession of extreme high temperatures, droughts, heavy rains and floods in many countries and regions, seriously threatening the survival of mankind.
This, coupled with the spread of communicable diseases and hikes in oil prices, worsened the socio-economic crisis, he added.

'We will not be intimidated,' Estonian PM says after attributing recent arson attack to Russia
Estonia’s prime minister Kristen Michal does not seem to be convinced by Russia’s denials.
Minutes after we got a response from the Kremlin, he posted on X:
“The arson attack against Milrem Robotics was ordered by Russian special services.
This is part of Russia’s broader campaign across Europe to intimidate us and weaken our support for Ukraine. It will not work.
Our response will be the opposite: stronger security at home, more support for Ukraine and greater pressure on Russia.
We will not be intimidated.”
The Estonian government also published a handy summary of the case so far:
“The criminal investigation into the exact circumstances of the incident is continuing, but the preliminary information gathered so far in the criminal proceedings also indicates that the attack was commissioned. The suspects believed to have directly carried out the arson attack have been apprehended and taken into custody and no longer pose a threat.
On the night of 15 August, a fire broke out in a building used by defence industry company Milrem Robotics on Betooni Street in Tallinn’s Lasnamäe district. Emergency services responded immediately and the fire was quickly brought under control. No lives were in danger.
On 17 August, two Latvian citizens suspected of carrying out the arson attack were detained in Latvia. A third suspect was detained on 18 August. Searches of locations associated with the suspects in Latvia resulted in the seizure of numerous data storage devices and items that may have been used to set fire to the building.
On 17–18 September, Latvia handed over all three suspects to Estonia.”
Burnham to set out 'options' for Britain's EU relationship later this year
In his speech Burnham also talked about his plans to look at Britain’s future relationship with the EU again.
“We will not give Britain the clear path we need into the rest of this century until we decide on a long term relationship with what is still our largest market.
I cannot say to you truthfully that where we are is good enough. Brexit has done more harm than good.
We need to restore a higher level of growth and prosperity for Britain.
So I will take the opportunity around the summit to lay out to you, to lay out to the country, what I believe the different options are for Britain’s long term relationship with our European partners.
And there are different options, and I will see if we can find consensus around one.”
Burnham lays out reforms plans to make Britain 'more resilient to the shocks we will undoubtedly face'
Over in the UK, prime minister Andy Burnham is addressing the Labour party conference this afternoon, setting his plans for the country.
In a brief passage on security and defence, he says:
“A country [reformed] like that will be much more resilient to the shocks we will undoubtedly face in the rest of this century and more able to meet its Nato obligations on defence …
I will be steadfast in my support for Ukraine, and stand up to threats whenever they come from: Russia, Iran, or anywhere.”
If you’re interested in details, my colleague Andrew Sparrow has all of it over on the UK blog:
‘It keeps growing’: the tent camp that stands against Spain’s housing crisis
Ashifa Kassam
in Madrid
Wielding a broom and dustpan, Marta García, 60, darted past the edges of tents, sweeping up bits of litter as she passed a poster that read: “What kind of times are these, when we need to defend the obvious?”
On Saturday, as tens of thousands of people took to the streets of Madrid to protest against the country’s deepening housing crisis, the retired schoolteacher was among a small group who had sought to take the protest one step further.
“At first we were 10 tents,” she said, gesturing to the sprawling encampment set up in the central Puerta del Sol plaza behind her. “Now, we’re more than 300 tents, and it keeps growing.”
The shock soon gave way to anger as the octogenarian was shown being brought out of her home on a stretcher, flanked by protesters on one side and police officers on the other.
Housing campaigners seized on the moment. “The whole country has seen that housing speculation has no mercy on anyone,” said Alicia del Río of the Madrid Tenants’ Union. “We’re not sad, we’re angry. And we’re not going to stop until we change things.”
Two former Hungarian ministers detained over suspected bribery and misuse of public funds
Jon Henley
Two ministers in Viktor Orbán’s former far-right government suspected separately of misusing millions of euros of public funds and taking millions more in bribes have been detained, hours after Hungarian MPs voted to lift their immunity.
Prosecutors said on Tuesday that Balázs Hankó, Orbán’s culture minister and still an MP in the former prime minister’s nationalist Fidesz party, was taken into custody late on Monday. Hankó is suspected of misappropriation of funds. He has denied any wrongdoing.
Miklós Seszták, an MP from Fidesz ally KDNP who served as minister for national development between 2014 and 2018, was also detained on Monday as part of an investigation into alleged bribery. He too has denied wrongdoing.
In more US-Russia relationship news, Interfax reports that Russian economy minister Maxim Reshetnikov will take part in a G20 trade ministers’ meeting in the US which is scheduled to start tomorrow.
Russian president Vladimir Putin’s envoy Kirill Dmitriev had meetings with representatives of US departments of Treasury and Energy during his visit to Washington, sources have told Reuters.
It is a further sign of the Trump administration normalising relations with Russia despite the ongoing attacks on Ukraine and concerns over Russia’s action from Nato allies. Last week US secretary of state Marco Rubio said the US had invited Putin to attend a G20 summit scheduled for Miami in December.

Meanwhile, Ukraine’s foreign minister Andrii Sybiha condemned Russia’s “terror against Ukraine” which he says is “intensifying by the day,” after another night of attacks on Kyiv and Odesa region.
“This is Russia’s deliberate escalation instead of accepting Ukraine’s offers to cease fire, negotiate, and end the war. Putin’s rejection of peace must have consequences for Russia,” Sybiha said.
He said:
“We are grateful to all partners who are strengthening Ukraine’s air defence and providing the systems and interceptors that are saving lives right now. Every successful interception proves that this support works.
At the same time, Russia must face growing pressure for every new wave of terror. Stronger sanctions, fewer resources for its war machine, and fewer opportunities to circumvent existing restrictions.
Moscow should not be allowed to turn another winter into a weapon. Every Russian escalation must bring the opposite of what the Kremlin expects – stronger protection for Ukraine, greater pressure on Russia, and a higher price for continuing this war.”
