Minutes after we got a response from the Kremlin, he posted on X:
“The arson attack against Milrem Robotics was ordered by Russian special services.
This is part of Russia’s broader campaign across Europe to intimidate us and weaken our support for Ukraine. It will not work.
Our response will be the opposite: stronger security at home, more support for Ukraine and greater pressure on Russia.
We will not be intimidated.”
The Estonian government also published a handy summary of the case so far:
“The criminal investigation into the exact circumstances of the incident is continuing, but the preliminary information gathered so far in the criminal proceedings also indicates that the attack was commissioned. The suspects believed to have directly carried out the arson attack have been apprehended and taken into custody and no longer pose a threat.
On the night of 15 August, a fire broke out in a building used by defence industry company Milrem Robotics on Betooni Street in Tallinn’s Lasnamäe district. Emergency services responded immediately and the fire was quickly brought under control. No lives were in danger.

Searches of locations associated with the suspects in Latvia resulted in the seizure of numerous data storage devices and items that may have been used to set fire to the building.
On 17–18 September, Latvia handed over all three suspects to Estonia.”
Kremlin rejects Estonia's attribution of arson attack on defence company to Russia
Meanwhile, the Kremlin rejected what it called Estonia’s “baseless” accusation that Russia ordered an arson attack on an Estonian defence company in August (10:10).
“Such statements are baseless, ill-considered, have absolutely no relation to reality, and lack any form of reasoning. Consequently, we cannot and will not take such statements seriously,” Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov told reporters in response to an AFP question.
How could anyone ever think that Russia could do this, right? Right?
Nato's top figures focus on pushing back against Russia's attempt to undermine support for Ukraine - snap analysis
Jakub Krupa
Rutte’s comments there are (perhaps not surprisingly) very much aligned with what Nato’s top commander Alexus Grynkewich told EU lawmakers last night.
In a rare appearance at the European parliament, Grynkewich warned that “the goal of the Russian activity right now is primarily to break our will to continue supporting Ukraine.”
“The logic of this is if we make the security situation seem dire enough, populations will want nations to withhold from Ukraine for their own protection. …
If there is a hybrid attack on your country, reinforcing the will to support Ukraine will show the Russians that their strategy isn’t working, and maybe have them back off that strategy.”
Top Nato figures appear to be focused on very publicly calling Russia’s tactics out in a bid to stop Moscow from succeeding and having any impact on social attitudes towards helping Ukraine – particularly ahead of 2027, with big elections coming up in France, Italy, Poland and Spain.
Rutte, Sinkevičius warn against Russia's 'campaign of hostile actions' to test Nato's resolve - summary
Nato secretary general Mark Rutte has urged allies to keep calm and carry on supporting Ukraine, saying Russia is “failing to undermine” the alliance’s support for Kyiv despite growing number of sabotage, drone incidents against Nato(11:07).
Rutte warned that Russia “continues its reckless campaign of hostile actions against Nato allies,” trying to “weaken our resolve and stop our support for Ukraine” (10:57).
His comments came at a press conference with Lithuania’s prime minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius who warned that Russia’s actions are “becoming increasingly hostile and less restrained” (10:59).
But Sinkevičius pushed back against recent warnings from Denmark, Poland and Germany about a potential imminent threat, saying there is no evidence of Russia “getting ready” (11:10).
Rutte says Nato has 'options' when responding to hybrid attacks
Pushed a bit further on hybrid attacks, Rutte acknowledges they “are having an impact,” but repeats his point that Nato has “all the response options: sometimes visible, sometimes not.”
He also says it’s important to, whenever possible on the basis of available evidence, publicly attribute these incidents to Russia, as Estonia did today.
“I applaud it,” he says.
He says Nato is acting “in the spirit of staying calm, carrying on.”
Lithuania's PM pushes back against warnings of imminent threat from Russia
Lithuania’s Sinkevičius says Russia “seeks to spread fear, to bring division … but it will not succeed.”
“We are not shaking [with fear]; we are doing what is meant to be done,” he says.
He says countries also do a lot of work in the background that is not publicly seen.
He says it’s important to be open about the challenges posed by Russia, but pushes back against “exaggerations” that something could happen within “upcoming months of weeks.”
“Is there any proof, real proof, that our intelligence services are providing … that Russia is getting ready or something? There is actually none,” he says, stressing “the risk remains,” but it’s not deemed to be escalating at the moment.
He adds “we have to … calmly do our work and we are doing that.”
Keep calm and carry on supporting Ukraine, Rutte tells allies
Rutte gets asked about various recent sabotage actions against Nato allies, including the UK, Germany, and Lithuania.
Should we stop calling them hybrid threats and call them what they are, he is asked. And does he agree with warnings coming from several countries about “decisive weeks and months” ahead?
Rutte says he agrees with the criticism of the phrase “hybrid threat,” as “it sounds a bit cuddly,” and does not reflect the severity of the threat.
But he says the key thing is that Nato “has all the response options we need,” even if “you will not always see them publicly.”
He says allies do a lot to counter the Russian threat.
“I would urge some calm, because we are investing in our defence [and] Russia is not in a good place,” he says.
He adds allies should “carry on, keep the support for Ukraine going, because the best response to any action in this grey zone of what Russia is doing is more support for Ukraine.”
Rutte says “we should not be naive about Russia,” but adds “they know we are stronger and we have to make sure by carrying on with our investments that we are also stronger in two, three, five years from now.”
'Russia’s actions are becoming increasingly hostile and less restrained,' Lithuanian PM warns
Sinkevičius is up next, as he thanks Rutte for today’s talks.
He warns that “the security [situation] in Europe is challenging,” as Russia’s actions are becoming increasingly hostile and less restrained.”
“We see the hybrid attacks: in Lithuania, Poland, Germany, elsewhere. And it’s not a question of proximity now; it’s a question of Russia’s actions.”
He says Lithuania leads the way in Nato as one of the top defence spenders, above 5% of GDP, and invites Rutte to a formal ceremony marking the permanent deployment of a German brigade to Lithuania in 2027.
'Russia continues its reckless campaign of hostile actions against Nato allies,' Rutte warns
Rutte continues saying that “Russia continues its reckless campaign of hostile actions against Nato allies.”
He says:
“[Russia] is trying to weaken our resolve and stop our support for Ukraine. But Russia is failing. It is failing on a battlefield in Ukraine, and it is failing to undermine our unity and support for Ukraine.
Our message to Moscow is clear: we will do even more for Ukraine and not less.”

This translated into parliamentary demands to expel foreign and US forces as "occupiers", alongside moves to launch strikes and attacks against the US Embassy in Baghdad and vital military bases, including "Victory, Asad and Harir", using missiles and drones.
These attacks led to a state of isolation and heightened security precautions inside headquarters and bases.
The movement of US forces in the field was restricted, and Washington was often forced to redeploy its forces and withdraw some personnel from secondary bases, consolidating them in more heavily fortified camps.
The tensions pushed forward negotiations to restructure the military presence and shift it entirely towards an advisory and bilateral framework.
Baghdad and Washington announced the end of combat missions at the end of 2021, with the missions changing from combat to advisory and training roles, without ground combat forces on the ground.
This followed lengthy rounds of dialogue conducted by the Joint Higher Military Committee between the two sides, which established timetables for evacuating sites, dismantling combat infrastructure and returning full management of the airspace and bases to Iraqi military forces.
In this context, Iraqi Security Media Cell chief Lt Gen Saad Maan said the international coalition had handed over all its bases and headquarters to the authorities and that there would be no coalition combat or training forces after the end of this month.
Maan added that Iraqi security forces were ready to take over the security file and capable of managing it after the international coalition withdrawal.
He said in a press statement that "relations with coalition countries after their withdrawal will become bilateral".
Optimism and objections
For his part, Ali Al-Fatlawi, a member of the Coordination Framework alliance, said to The New Arab, "Iraq's sovereignty is indivisible, and we see ending any US military presence inside Baghdad and its bases as an inevitable step that has been long awaited."
"Previous experiences, beginning with the 2011 withdrawal and the return under the pretext of the Islamic State in 2014, taught us that real stability is not achieved through the presence of foreign forces but through complete reliance on Iraqis," he said. "the withdrawal of the international coalition's combat forces and the complete clearing of Baghdad and its headquarters of any field barracks is a national achievement that reflects the high readiness of Iraqi forces".
"The security situation today is under the full control of our security institutions, and what the agreement stipulated is a smooth and carefully planned transition from a direct military and field role to an equal bilateral security relationship based on training, arms supplies and intelligence sharing to ensure that Islamic State threats do not return," he added.
"Clearing the capital of signs of foreign and US military presence represents a pivotal turning point in the history of security alliances in the region," researcher Adnan Al-Kinani told TNA. "This shift from a field combat presence to institutional partnership tests the state's ability to control the pace of the domestic security scene and remove political and weapons-related pretexts."
"Iraqi forces now face the challenge of proving their direct field capacity to manage the vacuum and sustain stability without direct foreign support," Kinani added.
Despite optimism in Baghdad over the departure of US forces and the announcement of a three-day public holiday after 30 September to mark "Sovereignty Day", the Kurdistan Regional Government has openly expressed its concerns over the US withdrawal.
Kurdistan Region Prime Minister Masrour Barzani described the US military withdrawal from Iraq as "shameful" and said it would leave Washington's Kurdish allies without protection.
He warned that US President Donald Trump risked repeating the mistake of the administration of President Barack Obama, which withdrew in 2011 before being forced to return.
Barzani warned in an interview with the Financial Times that "the US withdrawal is happening at a particularly turbulent time in the region".
"We are weak, and we are under attack. To be left alone now without any proper defence system is shameful," he continued. "And when we are prevented from buying the sufficient weapons needed against these missiles, drones and advanced systems, we naturally become more vulnerable by design."

articles.title: Kiev corruption a bigger problem than Russian strikes – Ukrainian poll
articles.body:
Kiev corruption a bigger problem than Russian strikes – Ukrainian poll
Half of Ukrainians place government corruption as among the issues that worry them most, putting it ahead of Russian long-range missile and drone strikes, a new opinion poll indicates.
The survey, conducted in mid-September by the Kiev International Institute of Sociology (KIIS), comes amid a series of high-profile graft investigations involving Ukrainian officials and people in Vladimir Zelensky’s inner circle.
KIIS surveyed more than 1,000 adults living in Kiev-controlled territory using phone interviews. Respondents were shown a list of 12 issues and were allowed to select up to three.
Government corruption was selected by 50%, followed by Russian missile and drone strikes at 40%. Other leading concerns were incompetent officials at 30%, low wages, pensions, and social benefits at 28%, and Ukraine’s military mobilization campaign at 24%. The latter refers to the country’s mandatory conscription system.
The survey showed widespread dissatisfaction over graft amid a string of scandals at the highest levels of the Ukrainian government recently exposed by Western-backed investigators. Some 72% of respondents said corruption has increased since the escalation of the conflict with Russia in 2022. The same share – 72% – said Zelensky bears personal responsibility for corrupt actions by members of his entourage.
Earlier this month, Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko fled Ukraine and tendered his resignation after a senior official in his office was accused of running a protection racket for scam-call criminal networks.
Before that, Zelensky fired Irina Mudraya as deputy head of his office after she was accused of laundering millions to pay bail for former Energy Minister German Galushchenko, who is a suspect in a separate corruption case linked to businessman Timur Mindich.
Mindich, a longtime associate of Zelensky, fled to Israel last November shortly before being accused of running a $100 million kickback scheme at a state-owned nuclear energy company.
Russian forces intensified attacks on targets deep inside Ukraine over the summer after Zelensky ordered a “pressure campaign” involving drone strikes on Russian refineries, civilian ships, and commercial warehouses.
Recent Russian strikes have degraded internet access, digital television broadcasts, and other services used by the Ukrainian public by hitting data centers in Kiev that Moscow says were used by the Ukrainian military and intelligence services.

articles.title: Ukraine is asking for a truce. So why is it preparing for a bigger war?
articles.body:
Ukraine is asking for a truce. So why is it preparing for a bigger war?
Washington is pushing for an energy truce between Russia and Ukraine. Kiev supports the initiative, and Moscow has also responded favorably. Another round of shuttle diplomacy has taken place: US President Donald Trump met with Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky, and a special representative of Russian President Vladimir Putin traveled to the US for talks with his American counterparts. Work is underway to revive the trilateral negotiation format involving Russia, Ukraine, and the US.
Judging by these and other news reports, one might get the impression that things are moving toward a diplomatic breakthrough and a truce between Russia and Ukraine. However, this impression is deceptive: A closer analysis reveals that the positions of the parties have not changed over the past year. On the contrary, Ukraine’s worsening situation has hardened its resolve to fight to the bitter end.
Up the down staircase
In spring 2025, Ukraine, with the backing of its European allies, launched a major campaign for a ceasefire. The expectation was that Trump would force Putin to accept the terms imposed by Europe and Ukraine, freezing the hostilities along the line of contact without any preconditions.
A truce would have cemented Ukraine’s defeat in the conflict. However, Russia’s primary objective would not have been achieved: The anti-Russian regime in Kiev would remain in place, and Ukraine would retain its role as a Western foothold against Russia. A temporary truce would allow Ukraine to recover and prepare for revenge in the future. A year ago, despite major issues, Ukraine still functioned: The remnants of the civilian economy operated, and despite considerable disruptions, steel and agricultural production (two of the country’s main export sectors) continued.
Without Western financial aid, Ukraine would have already faced a financial catastrophe; however, it continued to exist. Despite occasional disruptions, major industrial facilities remained operational, as did the small and medium-sized businesses that supported them – suppliers, transport companies, various outsourced services, construction and repair crews, and so on. Cafes, restaurants, the telecommunications sector, and small businesses stayed open. Ukraine’s robust logistics sector remained active. The government collected taxes from all these businesses.
However, in spring 2026, Ukraine decided to force Russia to conclude a truce by starting a ‘war on cities’ – large-scale strikes on the Russian rear. It first targeted oil refining and export facilities, and then the civilian sector, including the warehouses of companies such as Wildberries and Ozon.
The worst possible moment
Escalation only makes sense when ‘escalation dominance’ can be maintained. Otherwise, the outcome will be detrimental to the party that started the escalation. That is exactly what happened: In response to Ukraine’s attacks, Russia launched a broad offensive against Ukraine’s civilian sector.
From the start of the conflict, Ukraine has not concealed the fact that it uses civilian logistics infrastructure to transport military cargo. Launchers for long-range drones targeting Russia have often been hidden under the guise of civilian trucks.
Ukrainian strikes on Black Sea oil and grain exports gave Russia a pretext to respond in kind and effectively block Ukraine’s shipping in the Black Sea. As with strikes on warehouses, Russia maintained the upper hand in the escalation. There are several reasons for this: Russia’s increased firepower, the depletion of Ukrainian air defenses, and more broadly, Ukraine’s smaller size, its lack of strategic geographic depth, and fewer targets within the country. While the ‘war on cities’ affected Russia as well, Ukrainian strikes did not cause the same amount of damage.
All this prompted Zelensky to propose a truce. What he actually proposed was returning to the way things were before this year’s escalation, and pretending like it never happened. But does he really want a truce? It may look that way. After all, the Ukrainian economy – and consequently the Ukrainian state itself – is beginning to disintegrate; Ukraine’s key exports – its only source of revenue aside from foreign aid – have been effectively destroyed. For the first time in history, steel production in Ukraine has come to a complete halt; restarting it would take months if not years. By all accounts, the country is facing the most difficult winter yet. If this is not grounds for making political concessions, then what is?
The only available option
Zelensky’s calls for a truce are accompanied by opposing statements. One moment, he demands a “winter package” of weapons from Trump; the next, he declares that the war will not end until Crimea is “liberated.” Domestically, he is intensifying the crackdown on the Russian language and the Orthodox Church, even though this only heightens tensions within Ukrainian society. Clearly, given these parameters, Russia will never agree to a ceasefire. So is it all just schizophrenia or a calculated move?
I’d say it’s the latter. It’s true that if we consider Zelensky as the leader of Ukraine, then his actions are insane and amount to suicide. However, if one views him as the military proxy of Europe’s anti-Russia coalition, then everything falls into place.
For Zelensky and his regime, Ukraine is not their own land; it is a resource and an instrument for war against Russia. To save Ukraine, Zelensky must accept Russia’s terms. Yet Ukraine’s masters cannot accept Russia’s terms, as that would mean a crushing defeat for them.Consequently, the war must go on. If the destruction of rear-area logistics and energy infrastructure does not affect the ability of the Ukrainian army to hold the front line, then logistics and energy don’t matter. Of course, left without electricity, heat, and jobs, Ukraine’s civilian population will endure great suffering – but Zelensky doesn’t care about that.
Taking this logic into account, even an energy truce is bad for Ukraine, as a moratorium on mutual strikes would deprive Kiev – or rather, its masters – of the only effective leverage over Moscow.Of course, this is a one-way street. In an earlier article, we analyzed how the Ukrainian state is becoming detached from its own society. Today, I’d like to point out that in its current form, the Kiev regime has no other options: On one side of the scale lies the fate of Ukraine, and on the other, the interests of its masters. Zelensky has no real choice. In the interests of its masters, Ukraine must sacrifice itself and inflict the greatest possible damage on Russia, or if possible, even defeat it.
As long as there remains hope for Russia’s defeat, nothing else matters. Ukraine wants to either freeze the conflict along the line of contact and prepare to take revenge later, or fight to the bitter end. Russia understands this very well; that is why it has once again rejected any idea of a partial truce – this was recently expressed by Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov at the UN, and then by Putin. Even though this year, Russia was seriously affected by Ukrainian strikes, Moscow is only open to ending the conflict on its own terms.
***
What comes next? Both sides are actively preparing for the winter campaign, and it appears that, for the first time since the start of the conflict, long-range air strikes (the war on cities) will become the primary theater of operations. Moscow is confident that the Ukrainian army cannot inflict strategic damage on Russia; consequently, its only option is to maintain escalation dominance by responding to the Ukrainian strikes with even more powerful attacks. Under these circumstances, there can be no talk of either an energy truce or freezing the conflict along the line of contact.

articles.title: Software Deals Move Mobility Fleet Toward Common Operating Picture with Real-Time Data
articles.body:
A recent $21 million contract award to three software companies could give the Air Force’s airlift and tanker units real-time software updates in degraded environments, including aircraft fuel, logistics, and other mobility fleet data.
The Defense Innovation Unit and Air Mobility Command announced Sept. 15 they have awarded deals to Defense Unicorns, Stator Integration Labs, and Air Space Intelligence, each providing different tools to move the prototype software to production and deployment across AMC platforms.
The effort is under the umbrella of AMC’s Open Mission Engine program. Dubbed OMEN, the program is aimed at giving aircrews and mobility commanders better real-time information in denied, degraded, intermittent, and limited environments.
An AMC spokesperson told Air & Space Forces Magazine that the program seeks to have “present, current, and usable” aircrew mission software without a reach back or needing to connect to ground networks or cloud infrastructure to obtain the necessary update.
The program is still in its prototype phase, the AMC spokesperson wrote in an email, so they could not share initial and full operational capability timelines.
Officials have described OMEN as creating a “common operating picture” for mobility forces that have long lacked sophisticated connectivity. Using edge computing, the system will be able to track fuel, deliver software, and fuse data to create that common operating picture across the fleet, which will then load into aircraft cockpits and tablets.
Defense Unicorns CEO and cofounder Robert Slaughter told Air & Space Forces Magazine that’s “what makes OMEN special.”
“There’s a lot of different AMC assets, and they all need a common operating picture,” Slaughter said.
A former Air Force major, Slaughter explained that OMEN will fuse data across multiple inputs to give each user a clear understanding of what’s happening where and when.
“I think the biggest thing is: how do you do that on your worst day, and I think that’s key. How do you get software delivery done?” Slaughter said. “Accelerate the speed of software delivery on the nation’s worst day, and that’s what OMEN’s ultimately all about.”
The goal, Slaughter said, is to get on-demand software updates in the users’ hands.
“That’s measured in hours, not months or weeks,” he said. “That is a gnarly problem.”
Mark Lepczyk, Air Space Intelligence’s vice president of defense, says that as things stand, mobility crews wind up “pulling numbers from separate systems and reconciling them while the situation keeps evolving,”
“Under DIU’s OMEN program we’re reading crucial data like fuel state directly from the aircraft, fusing it on the same screen with the threats, the weather, and mission details, and offering optimal course of action recommendations, so the crew can now make accurate decisions at machine speed,” Lepczyk wrote in an email.
ASI’s application, which creates the common operating picture via data fusion tech provided by Stator Integration Labs, runs on a tablet that aircrews currently carry, Lepczyk said.
“The aircraft and the command center are working from identical information. It connects to existing Air Force systems, shared data services, and beyond-line-of-sight connectivity. A traditional operating picture tells you what is happening right now,” Lepczyk wrote. “Ours projects forward, so if weather suddenly shifts 300 miles ahead, the crew immediately understands all impacts and options to mitigate.”
The OMEN software assesses the “ripple effect” of any disruption to fuel, timing, or mission objectives and then gives the user “executable options” to replan quickly, Lepczyk wrote.
“We configured our solution assuming that any network can fail. Data can be cached locally, and the applications intuitively cue the crew if any information is degraded or stale,” he wrote.
Finding the Tools
DIU sought a software solution with both open-source protocols and a purpose-built capability stack tailored to OMEN’s needs, , unit spokesperson Caroline Thompson told Air & Space Forces Magazine in an email.
The unit works with military organizations such as Air Mobility Command and industry vendors as a kind of middleman, finding the right prototype solutions to military problems.
OMEN fleet software is part of a larger DIU effort to get quickly updatable and upgradable software in action across all Pentagon entities, Thompson wrote.
“The OMEN project exemplifies DIU’s strategy to bridge this gap,” she wrote. “By establishing an air-gapped-native fleet management layer, OMEN is building a repeatable framework to push software updates and AI capabilities directly onto operational aircraft. This project provides Air Mobility Command with a scalable blueprint to keep tactical edge software current and mission-ready.”
Delayed software impacts are felt across the fleet.
“This agility is key because software is only useful if it can be accessed and updated in the environments where it is required, in this case, on aircraft in austere locations or at 35,000 feet in the air,” Thompson wrote.
Defense Unicorns’ Unified Defense Stack-Fleet software is what Airmen will be using through the OMEN program. Components of UDS software have been used to upgrade F-22s, F-16s, and C-17s.
Slaughter, who deployed as an Airman with AMC assets, is keenly aware of what delayed software updates can do to a fleet. Often, software updates on legacy platforms can be a depot-maintenance level task.
“The jet not only goes through a maintenance period on the flight line, but the jet has to fly somewhere and be grounded completely out of the fight,” Slaughter said. “That is huge. I mean, I have vulnerabilities in the system, and I need to patch these. Imagine the entire fleet saying, ‘Hey, all of you have to go to depot-level maintenance, and it’s going to take several days or a week per plane’…You literally couldn’t fight and win wars with that posture.”
While Defense Unicorns’ UDS software will run on large platforms such as airlift assets and tankers, the software can be trimmed down for fighters and even drones, Slaughter said.
And while contractors are running the software updates in the prototype phase for OMEN, Airmen will be taking the reins once it reaches the production phase, Slaughter said.

articles.title: At least 82 Russian regions have banned the publication of photos, videos and reports on Ukrainian drone strikes
articles.body:
Authorities in Russia’s Amur Region have banned the publication of information about Ukrainian drone attacks. Similar bans are now in force in at least 82 of the 89 federal subjects Russia considers part of its territory, The Insider found.
Amur Region governor Vasily Orlov added the restrictions to an order implementing Presidential Decree No. 757, which established a “basic readiness” security level across the region. Media outlets and internet users are now barred from distributing information — including photos and videos — about Ukrainian drone incursions and their aftermath.
The ban covers information that could identify the type of drone, its launch site, location, crash site, flight path, target, and the nature of any damage it may have caused. It also prohibits publishing information about the use and effects of anti-drone measures, including air defenses and electronic warfare systems. The ban also covers information about the locations of Russian military and law enforcement units and related infrastructure.
The restrictions do not apply to publications by government agencies, law enforcement bodies, or local authorities. Other users may redistribute such information if they cite an official source.
Bans now cover almost all of Russia
The Insider reviewed regional restrictions currently in force against disseminating information about drones. The count included only cases in which regional authorities specifically banned or restricted the publication or distribution of information, photographs, or videos about military drone use and the consequences of Ukrainian attacks. Bans on launching or operating civilian drones were not included.
As of Sept. 28, 2026, such restrictions had been identified in at least 82 of the 89 federal subjects Russia claims as its territory. By comparison, at the end of August 2025, state news agency TASS counted such restrictions in only 33 regions, though by April 28, 2026, the number had risen to 64. At that point, restrictions were in force in every region of the Central, Volga, and Southern federal districts. TASS listed Moscow, the Moscow Region, the Murmansk and Kaliningrad regions, the Nenets Autonomous District, and the republics of Kabardino-Balkaria and Karachay-Cherkessia among the exceptions.
The bans, however, continued to spread. Moscow announced restrictions in May, the Krasnoyarsk Region in June, and the Omsk Region and Khakassia in July. Restrictions then appeared during the summer in the Murmansk Region and the Nenets and Yamalo-Nenets autonomous districts. The Tomsk region and Jewish Autonomous Oblast introduced bans in August, followed in September by Yakutia, Yugra (the Khanty-Mansi Autonomous District), and now the Amur Region.
In the Murmansk Region, for example, local authorities banned the distribution of information about the use and effects of drones and other weapons, including details that could identify where an object on the ground was hit and the nature of the damage. In Khakassia, the ban covers “any information” about the use and consequences of drone attacks.
In the Tomsk Region, the restrictions extend beyond attacks inside the region itself, as authorities also prohibit publishing information about drone use and its consequences in other Russian regions. Similar provisions exist elsewhere in Russia as well.
Reports of hits and damage are prohibited
The wording of regional bans is nearly identical in many cases. The most detailed regulations prohibit reporting information that could establish the type of drone, where it was launched, its flight path, its crash site, the location of an attack, the “fact that an object was hit,” and the “nature of the damage caused.”
The restrictions also cover information about air defenses and electronic warfare, the locations of military units and law enforcement forces, and critical infrastructure.
In some regions, the ban goes beyond photographs and videos, with restrictions also applying to text reports and other forms of information. That means not only a photograph of a damaged site but also a written post saying where a drone struck and what damage it caused could potentially be prohibited.
At the same time, regional regulations usually provide exemptions for official sources. In Tatarstan, for example, the ban does not apply to federal, regional, or municipal authorities, and the information they publish may be redistributed provided that the official source is cited. Similar provisions appear in a number of other regional regulations.
In August, the Anti-Terrorism Commission in the Jewish Autonomous Oblast banned the distribution of information about terrorist attacks, drone strikes, and the activities of sabotage groups unless it had previously been published by authorized agencies. The restriction also applies to photographs and videos of the aftermath.
People are fined for publishing information
The regional bans are being enforced. According to a tally by independent outlet Verstka, which reviewed court databases, at least 80 people were punished in 2025 and 2026 for publishing information about the aftermath of Ukrainian drone attacks. Of those, 75 received fines ranging from 1,000 to 30,000 rubles ($12 to $350), while courts issued warnings in five cases.
One of the most extensive enforcement efforts has taken place in the Kaluga Region. According to a report by local newspaper Argumenty i Fakty Kaluga, by late June 2026, more than 70 people and organizations had been fined a combined total of about 700,000 rubles ($8,300). Administrative charges were brought against administrators of websites, Telegram channels, and pages on the Russian social network VK, among others.
St. Petersburg issued its first fine for violating the regional ban in August 2026: a man who posted video of the aftermath of a July 24 drone attack was fined 4,000 rubles ($47). For individuals, a repeat violation in St. Petersburg carries a 5,000-ruble fine ($60); officials face fines of 30,000 to 40,000 rubles ($350 to $470), and legal entities face fines of 200,000 to 300,000 rubles ($2,350 to $3,550).
In the Orenburg Region, courts have imposed fines even when posts were later deleted. In September, a resident of Orsk was fined 5,000 rubles ($60) for posting a photograph online showing the aftermath of a drone attack. Another woman in the region was previously fined 3,000 rubles ($35) for video showing the aftermath of falling drone debris. She said she had mistaken the fire for the result of a gas boiler explosion and deleted the post once she realized what had happened.
In the Omsk Region, after a July 6 drone attack on an oil refinery, the FSB and police identified several residents who had posted videos of the strike on social media. They were charged with administrative offenses. Shortly beforehand, the regional Anti-Terrorism Commission had banned the distribution via media outlets, social networks, websites, and messaging apps of text, audio, photographic, and video material about drone use and the consequences of drone attacks.
No ban found in seven regions
The Insider found no regional ban on distributing information about drone attacks in seven federal subjects: Buryatia, Kabardino-Balkaria, Karachay-Cherkessia, the Kamchatka Region, and the Kaliningrad, Magadan, and Moscow regions. (Some of those regions do have bans on launching or operating civilian drones, but The Insider did not include such restrictions because they do not prohibit publishing information about attacks.)
However, the absence of a regional ban does not mean similar restrictions do not exist at a lower level. In the Moscow Region, for example, the city of Dubna has its own rule. On June 9, 2025, the city district’s Anti-Terrorism Commission prohibited photographing or filming drone use and its consequences, along with drone crash sites and damaged objects. It separately banned the publication or distribution of any information that could identify the type of drone, its launch or crash site, flight path, target, whether an object was hit, and the nature of the damage. Violators are subject to administrative penalties.
In Kamchatka, the Anti-Terrorism Commission in Petropavlovsk-Kamchatsky issued a notice in August 2025 titled “On the ban on publications about drone attacks.” It did not, however, impose a legally binding regional ban, as the commission recommended that residents “refrain from publishing” photographs and videos showing the aftermath of terrorist attacks, including drone strikes.
The situation in the Kaliningrad Region — the Russian exclave squeezed between Lithuania and Poland — is unusual. The Insider found no regional legal act banning publication of information about drone attacks. However, the regional branch of Russia’s Emergency Situations Ministry notified residents in October 2025 of a “ban on posting” photographs and videos online showing the aftermath of terrorist attacks, as well as certain military and critical infrastructure sites.
The Emergency Situations Ministry itself said the requirement was based on a recommendation from the National Anti-Terrorism Committee that had been sent “to all regions.” The ministry said violating the recommendation could result in administrative or criminal liability.
That points to the existence of federal recommendations instructing regions to prevent the dissemination of such material, even though there is no single federal ban on publishing information about drone use and the consequences of attacks.
No single federal ban, but common guidance exists
Regional authorities impose the restrictions in different ways — through governors’ decrees and resolutions, as well as in the form of decisions by operational and anti-terrorism commissions.
Many documents cite Presidential Decree No. 757 of Oct. 19, 2022 as their legal basis. That decree established different security response levels across Russian regions and authorized regional authorities to take additional security measures. However, the decree itself does not contain a direct nationwide ban on publishing information about drone attacks.
The similarity in the wording of regional regulations is striking even in documents adopted in different parts of the country and at widely separated times. They repeatedly list the same categories of information: the type of drone, launch or crash site, flight path, attack location, whether an object was hit, the nature of the damage, the operation of air defenses and electronic warfare systems, and the locations of military and critical infrastructure.

articles.title: Ukraine’s Zelensky says North Korea prepares to deploy another 10,000 troops to Russia
articles.body:
Ukraine’s Zelensky says North Korea prepares to deploy another 10,000 troops to Russia
- Ukrainian President Zelensky stated that over 8,000 North Korean troops are in Russia, with plans to deploy an additional 10,000 soldiers.
- North Korea has sent 14,000 to 15,000 troops and supplied Russia with artillery and missile systems to support its war effort in Ukraine.
- Tensions arose after Ukraine transferred two captured North Korean soldiers to South Korea, leading to disputes over confidentiality agreements between Seoul and Kyiv.
AI generated
SEOUL – Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Sept 28 there are more than 8,000 North Korean troops on Russian territory and preparations are underway to deploy another 10,000 troops.
Citing “new data” on the deployment of North Korean troops to Russia, Zelensky said in a post on X they were “being selected for training and subsequent deployment to Russia”.
The Ukrainian president said in August that up to 50,000 North Korean soldiers could be sent to fight for Russia, and called on South Korea to provide support for Ukraine’s air defence.
South Korea announced in July a US$100 million (S$128 million) aid package for Ukraine, although it excluded lethal weapons.
Zelensky’s comments on Sept 28 came after Seoul and Kyiv were at odds over his announcement last week that Ukraine had transferred two captured North Korean soldiers to South Korea.
Seoul expressed regret over his announcement, citing an agreement to keep the transfer confidential. South Korea also protested against what it called a false statement from the Ukrainian presidential office denying that such a confidentiality agreement existed.
North Korea has sent an estimated 14,000 to 15,000 troops to support Russia’s war in Ukraine since 2024, according to Ukrainian and South Korean estimates, with most deployed in the Kursk region to help repel a Ukrainian incursion.
Pyongyang has also supplied Russia with millions of artillery and mortar rounds, as well as ballistic missiles, long-range artillery systems and multiple-launch rocket systems, according to Ukrainian and independent assessments. REUTERS

articles.title: North Korea accuses US of undermining global nuclear non-proliferation system
articles.body:
PYONGYANG, September 29. /TASS/. The United States is undermining the international nuclear non-proliferation system and increasing the risks of a new arms race with its actions, North Korea's Foreign Ministry said in a memorandum released by the Korean Central News Agency (KCNA).
"The open US steps toward vertical and horizontal nuclear proliferation are destabilizing the cornerstones of the international non-proliferation regime and becoming a key factor threatening the world peace and security," the document reads.
Pyongyang mostly means the US nuclear force buildup and modernization under "vertical proliferation." The North Korean Foreign Ministry referred to the US efforts to develop the LGM-35A Sentinel intercontinental missile, B-21 strategic bombers, the Columbia class submarines, and the latest modifications of the B61 nuclear bomb as well as a planned Golden Dome missile defense system in the memorandum.
A separate section of the memorandum covers "horizontal proliferation." North Korea’s MFA accused Washington of transferring nuclear weapons technology to its allies, deploying nuclear attack means in foreign territories and developing extended deterrence mechanisms jointly with its European and Asian partners. It cited NATO, AUKUS, and cooperation with the Republic of Korea and Japan as examples.
Pyongyang will proceed from the need to protect its national interests and regional security, the North Korean Foreign Ministry emphasized. "The DPRK's option of action as a responsible nuclear weapons state will be strictly based on the grave reality in which no international body or treaty is deterring the US from bolstering up its nuclear power and going on its nuclear proliferation," the ministry concluded.

articles.title: Ukraine’s F-16s have downed over 3,150 Russian targets
articles.body:
- Ukrainian F-16 pilots have shot down more than 3,150 aerial targets, including 666 cruise missiles and about 2,500 drones, Ukraine's Air Force commander said.
- Ukrainian officials and Lockheed Martin discussed a possible move to the newer F-16 Block 70/72.
Ukraine’s F-16 pilots have shot down more than 3,150 Russian aerial targets, including 666 cruise missiles and about 2,500 drones, the commander of Ukraine’s Air Force said during a meeting with Lockheed Martin.
Lt. Gen. Anatolii Kryvonozhko gave the figures when a Ukrainian Air Force delegation he led met with representatives of the U.S. company, the Air Force said. He said Ukrainian F-16s have also flown more than 650 strikes against Russian ground targets. Kryvonozhko said the pilots are getting the most out of the jets despite a limited supply of weapons, using several different types of munitions.
The Ukrainian Air Force did not say when or where the meeting took place, or over what period the kills were counted.
Conor McGuire, who leads F-16 capability development at Lockheed Martin, praised how Ukrainian pilots and ground crews have operated and fought with the jet, and said the company intends to help Ukraine improve the capabilities of the F-16s it already flies, according to the Air Force. The two sides also discussed the possibility of Ukraine moving to newer versions of the Fighting Falcon, including the F-16 Block 70/72.
The Block 70/72 is the latest production model of the F-16, built by Lockheed Martin in Greenville, South Carolina. It adds an AN/APG-83 active electronically scanned array radar, which can track more targets at longer range than older radars, along with new cockpit displays and a longer structural service life. Ukraine currently flies older F-16s donated by European countries, which were upgraded in the 2000s but were not built new for Ukraine.
The first F-16s arrived in Ukraine in the summer of 2024, supplied by the Netherlands, Denmark, Norway and Belgium. Ukraine has used them mainly to intercept the Russian cruise missiles and Shahed-type attack drones that target its cities and power grid, often firing guns and short-range missiles at drones to save more expensive weapons. Ukraine has also lost several F-16s and pilots in combat and accidents since the jets entered service.
Ukraine is also looking beyond the F-16. In October 2025, it signed a letter of intent with Sweden for up to 150 Saab Gripen E fighters, and in November 2025 it signed a similar agreement with France for up to 100 Rafales. Neither deal has produced deliveries so far.

articles.title: US ‘too late’ to boost missile production – WSJ
articles.body:
US ‘too late’ to boost missile production – WSJ
The US faces a major hurdle replenishing key missile stocks after burning through huge quantities of Tomahawks and Patriot interceptors during the Iran war, the Wall Street Journal reported on Sunday. According to the paper, the manufacturing push is coming “too late,” with the industry hollowed out by years of underinvestment.
The US fired more than 1,000 Tomahawk cruise missiles at Iranian targets, or around one-third of its prewar inventory, the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimated in late May, adding the stocks are expected to be replenished only by late 2030 or early 2031.
CSIS also estimated that Washington has used roughly half of its high-end Patriot interceptors, with the stockpile below 1,000 as of late July.
Faced with the shortage, defense contractors are spending billions of dollars on factories and expanded production capacity, but the investment has yet to translate into major gains, the Wall Street Journal reported, adding that the additional missiles will arrive too late to substantially improve US inventories in any conflict over the next several years.
“Ministers of defense have fat wallets – they walk into the shops, and there are empty shelves,” Rob Bauer, former chair of the NATO Military Committee, told the newspaper.
According to the WSJ, the issue precedes the Iran war. An Army Science Board study launched after the escalation of the Ukraine conflict in 2022 found that the US munitions industrial base had been hollowed out. “It’s a miracle that we have anything that blows up,” Mackenzie Eaglen, who helped coordinate the study, told the paper.
For instance, Pentagon orders for the Tucson, Arizona factory – a key facility producing Tomahawks – plunged so low that the line producing the missiles was at risk of being completely shut down. In August, the facility received a $23 billion seven-year Tomahawk order, but it took more than a year to negotiate the terms, and the final agreement is still pending congressional approval.
Washington has also awarded RTX a provisional $20.7 billion multiyear contract for AMRAAM medium-range missiles as part of the Pentagon’s “Arsenal of Freedom” initiative. RTX earlier said it has invested about $900 million in three missile production facilities over the past three years.
Earlier this year, the Pentagon also struck a $58.6 billion deal for Patriot interceptors with Lockheed Martin.
The Iran war has been a costly affair for the Pentagon, with a US Central Command estimate putting the overall expenditure at $43.6 billion as of early September, including $28.1 billion to replace expended ammunition. However, unnamed US officials told NBC in July that overall cost could be nearing $100 billion if damaged bases and destroyed aircraft are taken into account.

articles.title: Iran’s Araghchi meets Qatari mediators as US calls for nuclear talks
articles.body:
Iran’s Araghchi meets Qatari mediators as US calls for nuclear talks
Tehran awaits reply on Hormuz plan as a US official says there will be no deal unless nuclear issues are addressed.
Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has met with Qatari mediators in New York to discuss a proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, while a United States official said there would be no agreement to end the war unless Tehran’s nuclear programme is addressed.
Araghchi told Iranian state media on Monday that the Qatari mediators would carry the ideas discussed at the meeting to the US and that he hoped to receive Washington’s final response by Tuesday.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Pezeshkian says Iran ‘no longer trusts talks with Washington’
- list 2 of 4Iran shifts trade north to Caspian Sea as war impairs Strait of Hormuz
- list 3 of 4‘Better deal’: What’s behind Trump’s rejection of Iran’s truce offer?
- list 4 of 4Strait of Hormuz tensions linger as Iran and US move further from a deal
“We talked about ideas and how to find solutions to fulfil Iran’s conditions and how to implement those conditions,” he said. “They had some ideas, and we had a discussion that they will also present to the American side.”
Asked whether he would stay in New York to await the reply, Araghchi said he would fly to Tehran within hours.
“Whenever the Qataris have a response, they know how to get it to us,” he said.
He described the meetings as part of an existing exchange of messages through Qatari and Pakistani mediators, which he said had taken on “a more serious form” since Iran submitted its proposal.
The Iranian plan, announced on Friday at the United Nations General Assembly in New York City, calls on the US to release frozen Iranian funds, lift sanctions and end its naval blockade of Iranian ports. Araghchi said those steps could be completed within four or five days, allowing the strait to reopen and negotiations on a final agreement, including on Iran’s nuclear programme, to begin by the seventh day.
US President Donald Trump, however, rejected the proposal on Saturday, calling it “unacceptable”.
‘Positive, constructive’ talks
The US official, who spoke to Al Jazeera, said indirect discussions were continuing.
The talks were “positive and constructive”, the official said, but stressed there would be no agreement unless Iran’s nuclear programme is addressed. The official said Trump is willing to relieve sanctions and release Iran’s frozen funds in exchange for progress on nuclear issues.
“Iran has indicated they are flexible on the nuclear issues, but the sides still remain apart on the timing of the commitments and who takes which steps first,” the official said.
The official also expressed scepticism of Iran, saying it had broken the memorandum of understanding signed in June by firing on commercial vessels. Tehran denies the accusation and says it was Washington that broke its commitments by failing to halt Israel’s attacks on Lebanon and by seeking to establish alternate shipping routes through the Strait of Hormuz.
Iran had closed the strait, which handled roughly 20 percent of the world’s oil and gas supplies before the war, shortly after the US and Israel launched their offensive on February 28. Iranian attacks on vessels since have sharply curtailed shipping, and oil prices have risen above $100 a barrel.
Even so, crude exports from major Middle East producers rebounded in September to 12.8 million barrels per day, their highest level since the war began, the Reuters news agency reported, citing data from the maritime intelligence firm Kpler.
That is still well below the 18.8 million bpd exported in February.
Some ships have used the US military-supervised route hugging the coast of Oman, travelling at night with tracking systems off and offloading oil to tankers outside the strait. Admiral Brad Cooper, the head of US Central Command, said on Saturday that American forces had assisted 2,000 transits and more than 1 billion barrels of oil in recent months.
The US has also imposed a blockade on Iranian ports and threatened secondary sanctions against airports and companies that do business with Iranian airlines. The United Arab Emirates, Iraq and Oman have already cancelled related flights.
Trump says US will win
Speaking to reporters on Monday, Trump said US officials had also spoken with mediators but insisted that Washington would prevail.
“We’re going to win,” he said. “It’s going to go pretty quickly.” He added that gas prices would fall once the US won the war.
In Tehran, officials struck a defiant tone.
Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, in a message marking the Iran-Iraq War and Israel’s killing of Hezbollah leader Hassan Nasrallah in 2024, said that the days of foreign domination were over.
“Having suffered painful blows from our valiant combatants and the guardians of the Strait of Hormuz, they [the enemy] dare not venture beyond the Arabian Sea,” Khamenei said in the message carried by Iranian media.
“Whenever they have risked doing so, they have only inflicted harm upon themselves, and the time is fast approaching when the Arabian Sea, too, will be cleared of their presence.”
Major-General Ali Abdollahi, the armed forces chief of staff, meanwhile, warned that Iran and allied forces would deliver a “decisive and devastating response” to any threat against the country.
Rear Admiral Habibollah Sayyari insisted that the Strait of Hormuz remains closed and said Iranian forces were ready to prevent enemy forces from entering the country.

articles.title: Trump denies offering Iran sanctions relief for nuclear concessions
articles.body:
Trump denies offering Iran sanctions relief for nuclear concessions
- US President Donald Trump denied offering Iran sanctions relief or releasing frozen funds in exchange for nuclear concessions, calling such claims "untrue."
- Reports from Axios and CNN suggested Trump was willing to provide relief if Iran showed "concrete progress" on its nuclear programme.
- US and Iranian officials held talks on Sept 28 to try to end a seven-month conflict involving strikes and casualties, amid ongoing disputes over Iran's nuclear activities.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – US President Donald Trump denied on Sept 28 offering Iran sanctions relief and the release of frozen funds in return for nuclear concessions from Tehran.
“This is untrue. I offered them nothing,” Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform, responding to an Axios report citing US officials who said he was willing to give Iran sanctions relief and release Iranian frozen funds in return for “concrete” Iranian steps regarding the nuclear programme.
The Axios report did not identify the US officials.
CNN also reported, citing an unidentified US official, that Trump was willing to give Iran sanctions relief and release frozen funds as part of a final deal on the condition that Iran offered “concrete progress” on the nuclear issue.
Trump has offered shifting goals and timelines for the Iran war that began on Feb 28, when the US and Israel attacked Iran and Tehran responded with its own strikes on Israel and Gulf states that host US bases.
US-Israeli strikes on Iran and Israeli attacks on Lebanon have killed thousands and displaced millions.
US and Iranian officials spoke separately with mediators on Sept 28 as part of a renewed effort to end seven months of war, according to officials from both countries.
Trump has cited weakening Iran’s nuclear capabilities as one of his war objectives.
Iran, which does not have nuclear weapons, denies seeking them. The US is nuclear-armed.
Tehran says it has the right to develop nuclear technology for peaceful purposes as a party to the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty. REUTERS
