articles.title: New pharaohs: How Egypt combines high tourism numbers with the world’s largest population of political prisoners
articles.body:
The Arab Republic of Egypt is expected to set two new world records by the end of 2026: for the number of tourists it attracts and for the number of political prisoners it locks up. Until recently, Egypt had trailed Syria in the latter ranking; however, after the fall of the Assad regime and the release of tens of thousands of Syrian prisoners of conscience, the Egyptians seized the lead, surpassing even the misanthropic regimes of Myanmar and Iran. Meanwhile, most foreigners visiting the Pyramids or spending a few days at an Egyptian resort never stay long enough to notice that the regime in Cairo rules by repression, fear, propaganda, and the personality cult of usurper president Abdel Fattah el-Sisi.
In the winter of 2011, amidst the Arab Spring protests, the streets of Cairo were patrolled not only by the army and police but also by Bedouins from neighboring Giza. On Feb. 2 of that year, armed with sharpened sticks, stones, and rebar, they staged a bloody attack on the protest camp. Eleven people were killed and several hundred wounded.
Later, the attackers explained to journalists that because of the revolution, tourists had almost stopped coming to the Egyptian capital. As a result, the Bedouins, who made their living giving tourists camel and mule rides along the roads of the world’s most famous necropolis, were left without income and could no longer support their families or feed their animals. The Bedouins hoped that breaking up the protest on Tahrir Square would calm things down and bring tourists back to the pyramids at Giza.
“Virginity tests” for protesters
At around the same time, the military was setting up torture chambers and special “medical rooms” in the famous Egyptian Museum — just a few hundred meters from the main revolutionary camp on Tahrir Square. At the Museum, intelligence officers carried out so-called “virginity tests” — sexualized violence against female protesters, who were forced to undergo gynecological examinations in public.
State propaganda at the time claimed that the women taking part in the revolution were all, without exception, prostitutes, and that the “virginity tests” were meant to prove this. But the public did not believe the state-sponsored stories, so the authorities tried to walk it back — claimed the tests were carried out solely to confirm that the detainees had not been subjected to sexual violence by soldiers or police, arguing that the revolutionaries were making baseless accusations of rape against security forces and that it was necessary to prove those accusations false.
The job of saying so publicly went to one of the generals leading the crackdown on the protests: Abdel Fattah el-Sisi. This was the first time many Western journalists heard his name.
According to one theory, it was el-Sisi himself who allowed the armed Bedouins onto Tahrir Square, since at the time he headed the country’s branch of military intelligence, which was responsible for carrying out acts of sabotage and provocation, among other things. However, it has never been definitively proven that el-Sisi personally issued the order.
What is not disputed is the fact that, in 2011, the general failed to live up to the expectations that then-President Hosni Mubarak had placed on him — he was unable to crush the revolution, which toppled the regime and led to Egypt’s first-ever democratic presidential election. But Mohamed Morsi, the Muslim Brotherhood Islamist who won that vote, saw a kindred spirit in the relatively young (he was 56 in 2011) and conspicuously devout general. It was Morsi who appointed el-Sisi as commander-in-chief of the armed forces.
Just two years later, in 2013, el-Sisi would “repay” Morsi for that trust by overthrowing him and sending him to prison for life. The list of charges against Morsi was seemingly endless, but at the top of it was treason. Egypt’s first — and, so far, only — democratically elected president died behind bars in 2019.
El-Sisi, who took Morsi’s seat soon after his overthrow, presented himself as the savior of the nation. According to the military command’s version of events, he had saved Egypt from Islamist terrorists who had propelled their own man, Morsi, into power. Ever since, Abdel Fattah el-Sisi has ruled the country through propaganda about “revolutionary prostitutes,” mockery of the opposition, and outright violence.
Brother against “Brother”
On Aug. 14, 2026, the World Coalition of Egyptians Abroad published an appeal to the authorities in Cairo calling for the release of political prisoners and an investigation into the circumstances under which thousands of people had been jailed for their personal views. The appeal was backed by the Association of Families of Egyptian Political Prisoners and by the International Association of Families of Political Prisoners, which was founded in London that very week.
The date was not chosen at random. It was on Aug. 14, 2013, that Mohamed Morsi’s rule in the country came to an end. That July, Morsi and his entourage were taken into custody by soldiers under el-Sisi’s command. State television ran round-the-clock footage of the arrests of the country’s top officials and their supporters, captioned: “Egypt is fighting terrorism.” The deposed president was declared an agent of Hamas and Hezbollah, and his followers were branded accomplices of terrorists. Those followers had set up a protest camp on Rabaa Square, demanding the president’s release.
On Aug. 14, the military destroyed the camp with extraordinary brutality. At dawn, soldiers opened fire with automatic weapons against the sleeping camp residents. Armored vehicles and bulldozers were then sent in to raze the protesters’ tent city. At least 817 people died that day (Egyptian authorities themselves acknowledged 638 deaths). Thousands ended up behind bars. They were later joined by tens of thousands more, detained in raids on opposition party headquarters, in apartments, and in mosques.
Most of those arrested 13 years ago remain behind bars, many still awaiting trial. The Morsi supporters rounded up in the summer and fall of 2013 are the demographic that makes Egypt the world leader in political prisoners.
The Morsi supporters rounded up in 2013 made Egypt the world leader in political prisoners
Still, new prisoners are constantly being added as Egyptian authorities wage a genuine war on those they deem to be religious extremists (above all, followers of the Muslim Brotherhood movement, which Morsi himself came from). Every year, hundreds more people are put behind bars, often on unfounded charges of terrorism or espionage. According to human rights organizations, Egypt holds between 50,000 and 70,000 political prisoners.
For years, Egypt was second on the list of countries with the largest numbers of political prisoners — behind only Bashar al-Assad’s Syria, which had sent more than 130,000 people to prison on political grounds. However, after Assad’s overthrow in 2024, the new authorities in Damascus emptied entire prison complexes, granting Egypt the lead in this shameful contest.
Incidentally, Egypt also has prison compounds built specifically for political prisoners. The most notorious is Scorpion Prison, which holds 2,000 people and was specifically designed so that sunlight never reaches the cells. But deprivation of vitamin D is just one — and probably the most innocuous — form of torture faced by its inmates.
Human rights reports state that Egypt’s political prison complexes are overcrowded and lack adequate medical care. Poor food, non-functioning ventilation, and prison staff brutality often lead to mass hunger strikes and suicide attempts. Among those who have tried to take their own lives because of abuse suffered in confinement was Mohamed Morsi’s nephew, arrested in 2022 without any justification.
Not all political prisoners in the country are Islamists. The prisons also hold members of democratic movements who actively opposed Mohamed Morsi and staged mass protests against the unconstitutional actions of Egypt’s first popularly elected president. In 2013, they demanded that Morsi abandon his attempts to appropriate parliamentary powers for himself.
Paradoxically, it was the actions of democratic groups like the April 6 Youth Movement that gave el-Sisi a pretext to arrest Morsi and take his place. As a result, in 2013–2014 many of these democrats ended up behind bars, charged with participating in the activities of banned parties and movements. Thousands of detainees remain in prison to this day.
Man of the hour
It was also in 2013–2014 that it became clear el-Sisi was preparing for a long personalist rule. The new authorities set about building the aforementioned prison complexes (officially called “correction and rehabilitation centers”), which were clearly intended for political opponents. Sure enough, dissidents began to be arrested en masse based on even the slightest suspicion of disloyalty.
Then a campaign was launched to transform the little-known figure of el-Sisi into Egypt’s leading man — an irreplaceable, wise ruler without whom the country would be doomed to collapse. The construction of the general’s personality cult began before his presidency — even before he announced his intention to run for the top office. Just days after the Rabaa massacre, the streets of Cairo and other cities were decorated with giant portraits of el-Sisi bearing captions like “Conqueror of terrorism” or even “Lion of the nation.” Street vendors — whether picking up on the trend or acting on direct orders from the military — pulled T-shirts and other souvenirs commemorating the 2011 revolution from their stalls. New merchandise soon appeared in its place — this time bearing the portrait of the “savior general.”
The biggest musical hit in the summer of 2013 was a song by pop artist (and head of the musicians’ union) Mostafa Kamel, glorifying the heroism of the army and el-Sisi personally. The general is never named in the song — instead, it features an anonymous “hero” who “will sacrifice everything for the homeland.” Still, to make sure everyone understood exactly who was being described, the music video for the song cuts to el-Sisi every few seconds. As of today, 13 years after its release, the video has 38 million views.
In state and semi-state media, el-Sisi was called “blessed” and “long-awaited.” His looks were compared to the pharaohs of antiquity — his strength to Greek gods and heroes. Within a matter of weeks, a petition calling on el-Sisi to run for president gathered millions of signatures.
Over the years since Mohamed Morsi’s overthrow, his successor’s personality cult has evolved further. The Sisi-mania of 2013–2014, which at times took on comical forms, is now tightly controlled. Stories about saving the homeland and heroic battles against terrorists have given way to reports that presidential oversight is doing wonders for the economy, that from the very start of his rule el-Sisi has shown a “modern vision of statehood,” and that he governs Egypt skillfully and confidently, with the full approval of all Egyptians.
In state propaganda, the president remains, as ever, Egypt’s sole hope and mainstay. However, today, el-Sisi is portrayed less like a military superman and more like a merely visionary official. After all, the state no longer dares to irritate people with fairy-tale stories about an all-powerful el-Sisi at a time when Egypt is going through one of the most severe economic crises in its modern history.
Old friends, new enemies
El-Sisi has tried-and-tested methods for dealing with those unhappy with his presidency: torture, blackmail, intimidation. He has used this arsenal even against people who considered themselves the president’s associates and allies.
In 2018, a military tribunal sent Egypt’s former chief of staff Sami Anan to prison for announcing his readiness to run against el-Sisi, who was then seeking a second term. Anan spent nearly two years behind bars on charges of violating military statutes, and since his release has led a quiet life, making no attempt to return to politics.
Another prominent military figure, Air Marshal Ahmed Shafik, made it to the second round of the country’s first-ever democratic election in 2012, losing to Morsi by just a few percentage points. In 2018, Shafik withdrew his candidacy after Morsi’s people showed him documents allegedly proving his involvement in Mubarak-era corruption schemes. The compromising material also included several intimate videos of the marshal, filmed by hidden cameras installed in his bedroom.
However, these methods have not helped shore up el-Sisi’s popularity — a fact that presents a major challenge for the general-president. In 2023, on the eve of el-Sisi’s reelection to a third term, protests swept across Egypt, with participants demanding the president’s resignation and even burning posters bearing his photo. People were driven to protest by inflation, unemployment, and the authorities’ indifference to the fate of their neighbors in the Gaza Strip, who had become hostages of the war between Israel and Hamas.
People were driven to protest by inflation, unemployment, and the authorities’ indifference to the fate of fellow believers in the Gaza Strip
In the past three years, these problems have only gotten worse, and people blame the person who holds the most power in the country — the president — for the catastrophic rise in prices, for the state’s default on its social obligations, and for its foreign-policy failures. In this context, el-Sisi is changing both his propaganda narratives and his strategy for political survival. No longer a president backed by mass popular support, he now leads a clique of people strong and influential enough to keep the army and security services, if not the public, under his control.
The people in uniform have become the regime’s true mainstay. El-Sisi has not merely preserved the economic system formed under Mubarak, in which the military plays a key role across a whole range of sectors — construction, banking, telecommunications, and insurance among them. He has literally turned officers into the country’s economic elite. Companies run by military officers get priority in the allocation of state contracts. They have access to preferential loans. And state auditors give them the benefit of the doubt. In addition, an abundance of free labor — conscript soldiers — makes officers’ construction firms far more profitable than those that actually have to pay wages to their workers.
On top of that, under el-Sisi officers have gained effective immunity from prosecution, pensions far higher than those for civilians, and priority access to senior government posts after leaving the service.
City of dreams
El-Sisi and his inner circle understand that if a new popular revolution were to break out — one resembling the uprising that toppled Mubarak in 2011 — they would not stand a chance against it. Western analysts put the probability of mass protests breaking out in Egypt before the end of this year at 15–20%, and even in the more-than-likely event the regime makes it to January, nothing suggests public discontent will subside anytime soon — not with the currency devaluing at a near-record pace and modest economic growth failing to lift living standards or wages.
The situation has not yet ripened into an open revolt, but much could change in the easily foreseeable future. Through manipulation of the constitution, el-Sisi has not only secured the ability to run for president an unlimited number of times, but has also extended the length of a presidential term from four to six years. The next election is due to take place in Egypt in 2030, and by then el-Sisi is supposed to move — along with his government, parliament, and security agency — to an entirely new city currently being built in the desert 45 kilometers from Cairo.
This city is still unnamed — in official documents it is called the New Administrative Capital. Officially, it is being built to relieve overcrowded Cairo and free the city of smog and endless traffic jams. But the new capital has several features that indirectly underscore the authorities’ fear of a new revolution.
For one, the city under construction has no separate neighborhoods planned for the middle class or workers (the main actors of the 2011 revolution). It has no narrow streets (only wide avenues that cannot be barricaded). Every square and plaza is designed so that any crowd gathering there could be dispersed with machine-gun fire from the roofs of nearby buildings (which are all linked by underground passages). And on top of all that, the new capital has no public transit links to Cairo or other cities.
The new nameless city will have no narrow streets — only wide avenues that cannot be barricaded
In other words, Egypt is building a new “Tahrir-proof” capital — in part with money from foreign tourists. That same money also goes toward building prisons for political prisoners, funding propaganda, and paying the salaries of security officers who blackmail and intimidate dissidents.
One could say that Egypt’s two records — for tourists and for political prisoners — are interconnected. The more people come to Egypt, and the more money they spend, the bigger the budgets available to the military and security services that guard Abdel Fattah el-Sisi’s regime.

articles.title: Board without peace: The club of Trump’s friends has made no progress on Gaza peace settlement
articles.body:
Donald Trump’s Board of Peace will finally get its first American money: more than $206 million to build an international military contingent in the Gaza Strip. The first practical result of an organization created to demilitarize and rebuild the region was not a peace agreement, but a preliminary contract to build a military base on Israeli-controlled territory. In seven months, a body with nearly unlimited powers has launched neither demilitarization nor full-scale reconstruction of Gaza. Instead, it has become a commercial club of politicians loyal to Trump.
“We don’t want to fund anything having to do with the bloodshed, hatred, or terror,” U.S. President Donald Trump said in Egypt in the fall of 2025 at a summit aimed at achieving a peace settlement for the Gaza Strip. “We’ve agreed that Gaza’s reconstruction requires that it be demilitarized.”
The “we” Trump was referring to was the summit participants — the leaders of 20 countries who gathered at the resort of Sharm el-Sheikh to discuss Gaza’s post-war future. Their decisions laid the foundations for the Board of Peace, which emerged in early 2026 as a supranational “executive committee” responsible for rebuilding Gaza.
A body with unlimited powers
Trump, as the mastermind of the Board, speaks as if his creation could assume responsibility for the whole world, not just one small region. Conveniently, the Board’s charter specifies no geographic limits at all, even though it is associated primarily with Gaza.
The mandate for creating it was issued by the UN Security Council specifically to establish peace in the Gaza Strip. Or rather, the board gave those powers to itself and its members, since the Security Council merely approved the creation of the Board of Peace to implement the U.S. president’s fairly general peace plan. The Board, once created, then adopted its own charter containing these broad powers.
The Board of Peace also gave itself the right to oversee the technocratic Palestinian administration that would govern Gaza during the transitional period — between the cessation of hostilities and the formation of fully functioning elected authorities. The Board distributes humanitarian aid, is responsible for rebuilding infrastructure and the economy, and has even secured the right to form its own International Stabilization Force (ISF) — a quasi-army meant to maintain order in the region until Gaza has effective police units in place.
The Board of Peace gave itself the right to oversee the technocratic Palestinian administration
As chairman of the Board, Trump holds nearly unlimited powers, including veto power over any decision and the authority to personally appoint his successor without input from other officials. He can also select the ISF’s commander and create or dissolve bodies within the Board. What’s more, Trump remains at the head of the Board indefinitely, as the founding documents provide neither term limits for the top post nor any mechanism for removing him from it. The chairpersonship is not even tied to his presidency.
By and large, the charter and structure of the Board of Peace resemble those of a commercial company rather than those of a supranational organization responsible for resolving one of the world’s longest-running and bloodiest conflicts. Even the name itself points to the corporate world.
The “board of Trump’s friends”
How did Trump manage to get the UN Security Council to sign off on the creation of an almost openly commercial structure accountable to virtually no one? How did he entice the leaders of more than two dozen countries to join his new board? Several factors were at play.
First, Trump’s peace plan, though written in a “something for everyone” style, is virtually the only option that was marginally acceptable for Israel, Hamas, and the leading regional players all at once (though not without caveats, of course). Even Trump’s fiercest critics, such as Hillary Clinton, publicly praised the plan as the only realistic roadmap to peace. In principle, that was enough for the Security Council to approve the creation of a new body (with China and Russia abstaining).
Second, for several national leaders — like, say, Belarusian strongman Alexander Lukashenko — joining the Board offers a chance to curry favor with Trump and leverage his weight to solve their own problems. On top of that, Trump all but openly advertised his creation as a structure whose members could gain access to the budgets allocated for rebuilding Gaza.
As a result, the composition of the Board of Peace resembles a roster of Trump’s friends and those aspiring to join their ranks. Aside from Lukashenko, the list features the leaders of Azerbaijan and Armenia, the king of Jordan, and the emir of Kuwait — but no representatives of the United Kingdom, France, Japan, or Germany. Also telling is the presence of Trump’s favorite, Viktor Orbán, still listed on the Board of Peace’s official website as prime minister of Hungary, even though Hungary’s government has been led by Péter Magyar since May 2026.
The Board pays little attention to such nuances, as it has convened in full only twice — both times for ceremonial receptions rather than working sessions. After the first meeting in January 2026, when the Board’s charter was signed, the so-called inaugural session followed less than a month later. No decisions were made at that meeting, which merely laid out the organization’s purpose.
Importantly, all heads of state sit on the Board in their personal capacity, meaning that the body does not create obligations for the countries involved. It is better described as a club of Trump-loyal politicians assembled under the pretext of helping Gaza. For this reason, many major world powers are absent from the Board, and the European Union is represented by just two members — the already-mentioned Orbán and Bulgarian President Iliana Iotova.
Leaders of states with solid, well-established standing in long-running institutions such as the UN, the G7, and NATO are in no hurry to join Trump’s club. They prefer to operate in settings they already know and to use more traditional models of interaction with one another. They see the Board of Peace as a new, alternative UN in which Trump takes on the roles of chairman, Security Council, and supreme judge all at once. Unsurprisingly, he has even spoken openly about the possibility of replacing the UN with his creation.
Vladimir Putin’s possible membership on the Board of Peace is also a cause for concern. The Russian dictator was officially invited to join Trump’s club immediately after it was created, but he has yet to provide an official response to the offer. The dictator may be holding off on joining because he does not want to play second fiddle in an organization built around Trump. But he cannot say so openly either, for fear of damaging relations with the American leader.
In any case, the invitation has not been withdrawn, and in theory Putin could join the Board at any moment — and would almost certainly try to use it to pull Trump to his side and discredit other international institutions.
No structure, no budget
All of the above is just a fraction of the Board’s many troubles and risks. The organization appears to lack funding to carry out what it envisions: forming and sustaining the International Stabilization Force, rebuilding thousands of homes and infrastructure facilities, creating a favorable investment climate in Gaza, and all the rest of the aspirations laid out in Trump’s peace plan.
While the Board was being set up, Trump urged its would-be members to contribute to the organization’s fund. One billion dollars would buy a lifetime membership and veto power. Members could skip the contribution, but then their membership was limited to two or three years — and no veto power. Since the Board’s budget was empty as of this past May, it appears that neither the members’ contributions nor the $10 billion Trump promised from the U.S. Treasury ever actually arrived.
At the end of the day, the Board of Peace is a body with enormous powers on paper but no budget of its own, no clear deadlines, and no clear division of responsibilities among its members — in other words, none of the things integral to the functioning of such international organizations.
Still, the Board continues to exist simply because Trump wants it to. He has yet to tire of his creation and shows no intention of abandoning the cockamamie unfinished structure. The Board still is not really functional and has not even published a report for the first six months of its existence — most likely because there is nothing to report.
In August, almost a year after the Egypt summit at which the U.S. president promised Gaza’s demilitarization, Trump’s club signed its first preliminary contract to build a military base in Gaza. Instead of the promised demilitarization, implementation of the U.S. president’s peace plan is set to begin with the construction — in the Israeli-occupied part of the Gaza Strip — of a barracks and a number of support buildings for a Moroccan ISF contingent. Morocco was one of the first countries (along with Kazakhstan and Kosovo, among others) to announce its readiness to send troops to Gaza to help form the International Stabilization Force.
The initial plan suggested sending 500 Moroccan service members to Palestine. Then reports emerged that there would be 200 — supposedly to guard a refugee camp while also training the Palestinian security forces. But all of this remains at the level of speculation and guesswork. There are still no concrete documents specifying the numbers or the exact mission of the Moroccan troops in Gaza, and the source and size of financing for the construction of their base is just as vague. The contract reportedly went to Arkel International, a Louisiana-based company that has built multiple U.S. military facilities abroad. But the funding sources, the contract’s value, and its timeline are not mentioned anywhere in open sources.
And that’s not even the biggest problem with the first real initiative of the Board of Peace. What matters far more is the glaring gap between the institution’s grand plans and its actions. The Board, which presents itself as the main instrument for turning a war-torn region into a flourishing land, has managed to issue just one contract — and even that a preliminary one — for building a decidedly modest outpost to house a single reinforced army company.
Moreover, news of the Arkel International contract coincided with the Board of Peace’s first serious internal conflict. On August 9, Israeli Prime Minister and Board of Peace member Benjamin Netanyahu called Trump’s plan for establishing peace in Gaza unacceptable.
Prior to that, Trump announced in late July that the Board of Peace had secured a promise from Hamas to lay down its weapons, and that it was time for Israel to begin the gradual withdrawal of its forces from the Strip. Netanyahu, for his part, argued that no agreements with Hamas existed, and that Israel therefore had no obligation to pull back its troops.
If the Board of Peace were a normally functioning diplomatic organization, this scandal would have seriously damaged its reputation. After all, it was the Board that, according to Trump, reached an agreement with Hamas, and it was the same Board that, according to Netanyahu, never agreed to anything at all. However, in the absence of a reputation, even such a scandal did little to tarnish the Board’s name.
In the absence of a reputation, even a real scandal did little to tarnish the Board’s name
Obviously, putting a complete end to the war in Gaza and bringing stability and prosperity to the region is a monumental task. It cannot be solved with just a club of Trump’s friends — a good number of whom, one can assume, have little concern for Gaza’s fate. From the very start, this initiative by the U.S. president bore the mark of political adventurism and differed little from his promises to end the war in Ukraine in 24 hours, to make Canada a U.S. state, or to make Mexico pay for a border wall.
The Board of Peace could perhaps be compared to the American president’s previous pet project: the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE), created specifically for Elon Musk. It was conceived as a tool for sharply cutting government spending and shrinking the federal workforce, and at the start of his second presidential term, Trump praised DOGE almost daily. But over time, the president’s interest in the new department faded, Musk fell out of Trump’s favor, and DOGE stopped operating.
It is reasonable to assume something similar will happen with the Board of Peace. Once Trump realizes that its members are in no hurry to fill its coffers — and that the decisions made and even the contracts signed are not bringing the transformation of Gaza’s ruins into a “Middle Eastern Riviera” any closer — the U.S. president will lose interest in the project and move on to his next quixotic grift.

articles.title: Zircon and ballistic missiles launched by Russia neutralized over Ukraine - details from Air Force
articles.body:
Zircon and ballistic missiles launched by Russia neutralized over Ukraine - details from Air Force
Kyiv • UNN
During the night of September 29, Russia launched a Zircon-type missile, two ballistic missiles, and 152 drones at Ukraine. Air defense destroyed 109 targets, including the missiles.
Russia struck Ukraine during the night of September 29 with a Zircon-type missile, two ballistic missiles, and 152 drones; all the missiles—the Zircon and the two ballistic missiles—as well as 106 drones were shot down or suppressed. UNN reports this, citing data from the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine.
What Russia attacked with and from where
According to the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, during the night of September 29 (from 18:00 on September 28), the enemy attacked with a Zircon/Oniks anti-ship missile from Russia’s Kursk Region; two Iskander-M/S-400 ballistic missiles from Russia’s Kursk Region; and 152 Shahed-type attack UAVs (82 of them jet-powered), Gerbera UAVs, and Parodiya-type decoy drones from the following directions: Oryol, Millerovo, Kursk, Primorsko-Akhtarsk—in Russia; the temporarily occupied territory of Donetsk; Hvardiiske; and Chauda—the temporarily occupied territory of the Autonomous Republic of Crimea.
How many were destroyed
The air attack was repelled by aviation, anti-aircraft missile forces, electronic warfare and unmanned systems units, and mobile fire groups of Ukraine’s Defense Forces.
According to preliminary data, as of 08:00, air defense forces shot down/suppressed 109 targets:
-  1 Zircon/Oniks anti-ship missile; 
-  2 Iskander-M/S-400 ballistic missiles; 
-  106 enemy Shahed-type and Gerbera UAVs and drones of other types. 
Hits by the enemy’s air attack weapons were recorded at 24 locations, as well as the سقوط of downed targets (debris) at 16 locations.
The attack is ongoing; several enemy UAVs are in the airspace.

articles.title: NATO Chief Mark Rutte Warns Russia Is Testing the Alliance With Hybrid Attacks
articles.body:
- Category
- World
NATO Chief Mark Rutte Warns Russia Is Testing the Alliance With Hybrid Attacks
NATO is strengthening defenses against drones after repeated incursions along its eastern flank, Secretary General Mark Rutte stated, according to The Guardian on September 29.
Speaking alongside Lithuanian Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius at NATO headquarters in Brussels, Rutte recalled a drone shot down in Lithuanian airspace by NATO fighter jets two weeks earlier.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The warning comes amid growing concern over Russian hybrid operations against NATO states, including drone incursions, sabotage, cyberattacks, and attacks on critical infrastructure. UNITED24 Media recently detailed how such operations have escalated across Europe while often remaining below the threshold of conventional war.
The Guardian reported that he described the incidents as evidence of the changing security threat facing the alliance.
“The repeated drone incidents along our eastern flank showed the evolving nature of the threat, and we are strengthening our integrated air and missile defense,” Rutte stated. “We are adapting and reinforcing our posture against drones.”
Rutte also accused Russia of continuing hostile activity against NATO members and attempting to weaken allied support for Ukraine, The Guardian wrote.
“Russia continues its reckless campaign of hostile actions against NATO allies,” Rutte stated. “It is trying to weaken our resolve and stop our support for Ukraine. But Russia is failing.”
“It is failing on a battlefield in Ukraine, and it is failing to undermine our unity and support for Ukraine,” he added. “Our message to Moscow is clear: we will do even more for Ukraine and not less.”
The warning follows a series of drone incidents along NATO’s eastern flank that have increased pressure on the alliance to strengthen air and missile defenses against threats reaching member states bordering Russia and Belarus.
Mark Rutte had also recently stated that the alliance deliberately keeps its Article 5 response to such threats ambiguous to prevent Moscow from exploiting fixed red lines.

articles.title: Warheads of two ballistic missiles neutralized near residential buildings in Kyiv
articles.body:
Warheads of two ballistic missiles neutralized near residential buildings in Kyiv
According to Ukrinform, this information was reported by the Main Directorate of the National Police in Kyiv.
“Following an overnight enemy attack on the capital in the Solomyanskyi district, Kyiv police bomb disposal experts defused the warheads of two ballistic missiles. Both fell in close proximity to residential buildings. Each warhead weighed about half a metric ton,” the statement said.
Police bomb disposal experts rendered the warheads safe. Subsequently, using specialized equipment, these fragments will be transported to a special testing range for further disposal.
The Kyiv Police are urging citizens who discover suspicious or potentially explosive objects not to approach or touch them and to immediately report the find by calling 102 or 101.
As reported by Ukrinform, President Volodymyr Zelensky stated that over the past 24 hours, 11 regions of the country came under enemy attack; specifically, in the capital, the Russians damaged the depot at the “Kyiv-Pasazhyrskyi” station, as well as data centers, business centers, and residential buildings.

articles.title: In Poland, preparations are underway for a possible Russian hybrid attack on the border with Ukraine
articles.body:
In Poland, preparations are underway for a possible Russian hybrid attack on the border with Ukraine
Kyiv • UNN
In the border town of Dorohusk, traffic was suspended three times due to the threat of drones or missiles. Warsaw fears new hybrid attacks by Russia.
In the eastern regions of Poland bordering Ukraine, readiness is being strengthened for possible hybrid attacks by Russia involving drones or missiles. Associated Press reports this, UNN writes.
Details
In the border town of Dorohusk, local residents received warnings three times in a single day about a possible drone or missile crossing the border. People were urged to be prepared to take shelter in the event of a threat.
Traffic through the border crossing with Ukraine, located approximately 2 km away, was suspended three times that day. During one of the warnings, checkpoint personnel were even evacuated, while military helicopters flew over the settlement.
Poland fears new Russian attacks
Anxiety in the region intensified after the events of September 13, when two Russian drones exploded on the Ukrainian side of the Dorohusk–Yahodyn crossing. The explosions were clearly heard in Poland.
New anxiety and fear have emerged because those explosions were heard very clearly in our village that night. We had never experienced anything like this before. It was the first time the sirens sounded
On September 17, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk warned that Russia could be preparing hybrid strikes involving drones or missiles against European countries supporting Ukraine. According to him, Polish regions near the Ukrainian border could be particularly vulnerable in the coming months.
Warsaw's concerns relate both to the possible accidental crossing of the border by Russian weapons during attacks on Ukraine and to deliberate provocations. European countries have also previously accused Russia of using other methods of hybrid warfare, including sabotage, cyberattacks, and disinformation.

articles.title: Ukraine's defence minister urges EU not to wait until 2027 and provide Ukraine with defence funding this autumn
articles.body:
Ukraine's defence minister urges EU not to wait until 2027 and provide Ukraine with defence funding this autumn
Ukraine's Defence Minister Yevhenii Khmara has called on EU member states to provide Ukraine with defence funding from an EU loan this autumn, rather than waiting until 2027 as planned.
Source: Ministry of Defence of Ukraine
Quote from Khmara: "The funds are needed this autumn to give manufacturers enough time to purchase components and produce drones on time. This is especially important given the mobilisation that the enemy is already planning."
Details: Khmara stressed that Ukraine has a number of priority needs to strengthen its defence capabilities.
In particular, around one-third of Ukraine's additional defence funding requirements amounting to US$27 billion is attributable to advance payments for drones due to be delivered in early 2027.
The minister therefore called for the disbursement of funds from the EU loan to be brought forward from 2027 to this autumn, for the remaining funds under the SAFE programme to be used for Ukraine's procurement needs and for additional funding to be provided as part of bilateral assistance.
Khmara also said that Ukraine is looking for affordable and effective solutions to counter jet-powered Shahed drones. He added that such targets are already being shot down, in particular by interceptor missiles.
The minister therefore called on the EU to help fund this area so that interceptors could be delivered to the defence forces in sufficient quantities as soon as possible.
He also stressed to partners the importance of providing Ukraine with air-to-air missiles, man-portable air-defence systems and ammunition for F-16s.
As for countering ballistic missiles, Ukraine's request remains unchanged, Khmara said. The defence minister called on EU member states to transfer some missiles from their own stocks in exchange for those Ukraine is due to receive later under existing contracts.
Background:
- On 14 September, Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said that the situation with public finances was close to critical due to Ukraine's failure to meet some of its commitments to partners on time. In particular, the country risks losing a significant portion of the US$29.5 billion in planned international funding.
- On 27 September, Koretskyi said that delays in some international aid had resulted in a US$27 billion shortfall in the country's defence budget.
- The government plans to secure around US$7 billion through strict austerity measures in public finances, including expenditure optimisation and the reallocation of funds.
- Ukraine is working with partners to find mechanisms and sources to cover the remaining US$20 billion shortfall. Koretskyi pledged to implement all government decisions necessary to secure international financial assistance by 15 October.
- On 28 September, the Cabinet of Ministers decided to postpone budget funding for non-critical expenditure on building, major repairs, urban improvements and other areas due to a lack of funds. From October onwards, the State Treasury Service of Ukraine will draw up a daily forecast of cash flows in the single treasury account and the financial resources available for each ten-day period.
- If there are insufficient funds to cover all planned monthly expenditure, the Treasury will make payments in order of priority. The government has designated defence and national security, the servicing of state and local debt, pensions, salaries, social benefits and assistance as priorities.

articles.title: Russia warns UK and NATO of nuclear response over Kaliningrad blockade
articles.body:
Russia warned on Tuesday that any attempt to blockade the Kaliningrad Region by the UK or NATO will be met with a response using all means, including nuclear weapons.
In a statement on Telegram, the Russian Embassy in London said this while responding to UK media reports that discussed the possibility of a NATO blockade of Kaliningrad or non-recognition of Russian sovereignty over the region.
“Those advocating plans to blockade Kaliningrad or launch a strike against it should have no illusions about the consequences. Any military action by the UK or NATO against Russian territory will be met with a response using all means available to Russia, including nuclear weapons,” it stressed.
The embassy reiterated that Russia “does not seek confrontation with NATO and Europe and does not intend to attack them,” adding that those who choose to initiate such a conflict “should not be under any illusions” that Russia would respond accordingly.
Russia will use all means to defend its territory
The Kaliningrad Region is a Russian exclave on the Baltic Sea, situated between Poland and Lithuania and separated from mainland Russia by Lithuanian territory.
Last week, in remarks to Anadolu, the Russian Embassy in Paris also commented on what it described as "provocative statements regarding the possibility of NATO forces striking the Kaliningrad region or blocking access to it."
"We wish to emphasise that Russia will use all means at its disposal to defend its territory and that, should any attempt be made to carry out such plans, the retaliation will be inevitable and overwhelming," the embassy said.

articles.title: Trump denies Iran concessions in ‘hoax’ report
articles.body:
Trump denies Iran concessions in ‘hoax’ report
US President Donald Trump has denied offering any concessions to Iran after indirect negotiations resumed in New York on Monday in the hopes of ending the war he launched alongside Israel against the Islamic Republic seven months ago.
Trump took to social media to refute an Axios report claiming that he was prepared to lift some sanctions and release frozen Iranian funds in return for “concrete Iranian steps” regarding its nuclear program. AP published similar claims early Tuesday morning, also citing US officials.
“This is untrue. I offered them NOTHING! Axios’ story, like most others, is a HOAX, used only for purposes of satisfying their Trump Derangement Syndrome,” he wrote on Truth Social, demanding that the “fake story” be taken down.
US and Iranian officials met separately with mediators on the sidelines and are expected to focus on a revised proposal submitted by Tehran last week during the UN General Assembly, according to Reuters.
Trump confirmed on Saturday that he had rejected Iran’s proposal for a seven-day ceasefire that would have reopened the Strait of Hormuz, arguing that he sought a better deal. The US president has emphasized that his primary goal is to dismantle Iran’s nuclear program and ensure that Tehran never acquires nuclear weapons.
Iran, meanwhile, has maintained that its nuclear program is entirely peaceful and that uranium enrichment is its right as a sovereign state.
The situation remains tense around the Strait of Hormuz, where disruptions to shipping are driving up energy prices worldwide. On Wednesday, an Indian sailor was killed after a projectile struck the Antigua and Barbuda-flagged cargo ship Cape Dao. Although Iran has not claimed responsibility for the attack, it has previously warned vessels passing through the strait not to use the “illegal” routes designated by the US Navy.

articles.title: Latvia Plans to Purchase U.S. Barracuda Cruise Missiles
articles.body:
Latvia plans to purchase long-range Barracuda family cruise missiles from U.S. company Anduril Industries.
Latvian President Edgars Rinkēvičs announced this after visiting an Anduril facility in the United States.
It is currently unknown which Barracuda version Latvia plans to purchase, how many missiles it will buy, the contract value, or the potential delivery timeline. At the same time, TWZ considers the Barracuda-500M, the longest-range variant in the family, the most likely option.
“We expect the procurement of Barracuda missiles to be completed and further development of Latvian-U.S. cooperation in the defense industry,” Rinkēvičs stated.
Militarnyi previously reported that the Barracuda-500 is a jet-powered unmanned platform capable of carrying a payload, reconnaissance equipment, or electronic warfare systems. Its Barracuda-500M combat variant is essentially a compact cruise missile.
These cruise missiles have a range of more than 920 km. They can carry a payload of over 45 kg, have a flight endurance of more than two hours, and can reach a maximum speed of approximately 926 km/h, depending on the mode of operation.
Anduril positions them as relatively inexpensive, mass-producible long-range weapons. The expected manufacturing cost of a serial-production platform is estimated at no more than $150,000, while about 70% of the missile’s components are commercially available.
The company plans to significantly increase production of this weapon. In 2027, Anduril plans to produce around 7,000 Barracuda-500 missiles.
Separately, the U.S. Department of Defense has signed a framework agreement with Anduril for the delivery of at least 3,000 SLB-500M systems over three years. In 2027, the company is also expected to deliver more than 60 corresponding launchers.
The missile was initially developed as an air-launched weapon, but Anduril has already developed a surface-launched SLB-500M version. In 2025, the company successfully tested a Barracuda-500 prototype with a ground launch using an additional solid-fuel booster.
The surface-based launcher is housed in a standard 20-foot ISO container and can accommodate up to 16 ready-to-launch missiles. The system can be transported to the required area and deployed without combat aircraft. It is particularly important for Latvia, which does not have its own fleet of combat aircraft.
Acquiring Barracuda would significantly expand Latvia’s long-range strike capabilities. The country has already ordered ATACMS tactical ballistic missiles for its M142 HIMARS systems, with a range of around 300 km, while the Barracuda-500M could potentially engage targets beyond 900 km.
Militarnyi previously reported that Poland’s PGZ defense group and Anduril had agreed to localize Barracuda-500M production in Poland.
In July 2026, Anduril and Polish company Wojskowe Zakłady Lotnicze Nr 2 agreed to establish production facilities in Bydgoszcz. Poland became the first European country to sign such an agreement with Anduril for the Barracuda. In addition, the share of Polish-made components is expected to gradually increase over time.

articles.title: Russian Tu-95 bomber crashes, killing six crew – MOD
articles.body:
Russian Tu-95 bomber crashes, killing six crew – MOD
A Tu-95 strategic bomber has crashed during a training flight in the Amur Region in the Russian Far East, killing six crew members and injuring another, according to Moscow’s Defense Ministry.
The injured crew member was evacuated to a medical facility, the ministry said.
The aircraft was unarmed and crashed in an uninhabited area, the MOD added.
A Russian Aerospace Forces commission has been sent to the site to investigate the cause of the crash.
The Soviet-designed Tu-95, which first flew in 1952, remains the world’s fastest production turboprop aircraft. The long-range strategic bomber has been used extensively by Russia to launch Kh-101 cruise missiles at targets in Ukraine during the conflict.
The bombers are part of the Russian nuclear triad and are capable of carrying missiles with thermonuclear warheads.

articles.title: Poland to Change Rules for Shooting Down Russian Aircraft
articles.body:
Poland’s Ministry of Defense will change, in the coming days, the procedures for using weapons against Russian aerial objects that violate Polish airspace.
Deputy Defense Minister Cezary Tomczyk announced the changes, according to RMF24.
Major General Ireneusz Nowak, the Operational Commander of the Polish Armed Forces, made the decision.
The new rules will apply to Polish fighter jet and helicopter crews responsible for protecting the country’s airspace.
Under the new procedures, pilots will no longer be required to visually identify an aerial target before taking action. This requirement normally applies during peacetime.
Under the current rules, a pilot must approach the object at close range and visually confirm what it is before opening fire.
Under the updated rules, the military will switch to so-called “positive identification” based on radar data.
To decide whether to destroy a target, the pilot or operational commander will only need to rely on radar readings.
The new protocols will allow fighter jets to shoot down enemy drones and missiles significantly faster.
As previously reported, Russia is planning drone and missile strikes against countries that support Ukraine, including Poland.
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said that similar threats had been discussed before, but that the information available now is more convincing.
Poland’s Ministry of the Interior is also testing a new mobile app designed to quickly alert the public about emergencies.

articles.title: Honeywell gets $25.6M for nuclear-tough navigation gyro
articles.body:
- The U.S. Air Force Research Laboratory awarded Honeywell $25.6 million to mature a compact, radiation-hardened strategic gyroscope, with work due by July 2029.
- The contract follows a $41.6 million laboratory award in 2020 for Honeywell to design a Compact Strategic-Grade Gyroscope.
The U.S. Air Force Research Laboratory has awarded Honeywell Aerospace $25.6 million to keep developing a small, radiation-hardened gyroscope accurate enough for “strategic” use, the class of navigation sensor that has to work in space and survive the effects of a nuclear environment.
The cost-plus-fixed-fee contract covers what the Pentagon calls the compact strategic gyroscope maturation project, the U.S. Department of War said. Honeywell will do the work in Clearwater, Florida, and is expected to finish by July 1, 2029. The laboratory’s office at Kirtland Air Force Base, New Mexico, is managing the contract.
Combined with accelerometers in an inertial navigation system, it lets a missile, satellite, ship or aircraft work out where it is and which way it is pointing without GPS or any other outside signal. “Strategic-grade” refers to the most accurate class of these sensors, used where drift has to stay extremely low for long periods, such as in ballistic missile guidance and satellite pointing. Radiation hardening means the sensor and its electronics are built to keep working when hit by the radiation found in space or produced by a nuclear blast.
The notice does not say which weapon or spacecraft the gyroscope is intended for.
The award builds on earlier Air Force Research Laboratory work with the same company. In early 2020, the laboratory’s Space Vehicles Directorate at Kirtland gave Honeywell a $41.6 million contract to design a Compact Strategic-Grade Gyroscope, Military & Aerospace Electronics reported. That five-year effort, carried out at Honeywell’s Phoenix site, called for building and testing four prototypes, refining the design into six strategic-grade units, developing a radiation-hardened custom chip and software for the gyro, flying it on an experimental satellite for a one-year mission in low Earth orbit, and laying out a path toward a gyroscope that could keep operating through the radiation and electromagnetic pulse of nuclear explosions. The earlier contract was scheduled to run through August 2025.
The Department of War did not say how much of the first project’s goals were met or whether the space flight took place. The new work is described as “maturation,” which in defense research usually means taking a design that has been shown to work and making it more reliable, easier to build and closer to use in a real system.
The contract was competitively awarded, and the government received two offers. Only $500,000 in fiscal 2026 research and development money was committed at the time of award, with the rest of the $25.6 million to be added in later years.
Honeywell’s Clearwater site is one of the company’s main centers for navigation and inertial sensor work. The notice did not name the second bidder.

articles.title: British warship hits frigate with live Naval Strike Missile
articles.body:
The Royal Navy used both of its newest anti-ship missiles during a joint US-UK live-fire exercise off the Hebrides that ended with the sinking of the decommissioned American frigate USS Klakring, firing the Naval Strike Missile from HMS Portland and Sea Venom from a Wildcat helicopter of 815 Naval Air Squadron operating from her flight deck.
The round Portland fired carried a warhead and was aimed at a real ship rather than a range target, which the service describes as the first Royal Navy firing of a Naval Strike Missile, although HMS Somerset launched one off Norway in September last year.
Lieutenant Commander Louise Kirkaldy, HMS Portland’s principal warfare officer, said: “The successful firing of Naval Strike Missile marks a significant milestone for the Royal Navy, demonstrating our ability to deliver credible, modern maritime strike capability. This achievement reflects the professionalism, dedication and teamwork of all those involved, whose hard work has ensured we remain ready to meet the challenges of today and tomorrow.”
Petty Officer James Kenyon, an above water warfare specialist aboard the frigate, fired it. “To be involved in such a high-profile exercise is the highlight of my career,” he said. “Being the first person to fire war-shot Naval Strike Missile and achieve a hit is a very proud moment, and one that will stay with me for the rest of my career. This was the culmination of over a year’s effort in planning and bringing the drills into service, and I am glad that I was able to contribute.”
Commander Dafydd Bryden, the ship’s commanding officer, said: “The opportunity to fire anti-ship missiles against a decommissioned warship is an important test of our warfighting capability. This engagement proved the effectiveness of these systems as well as the sailors and aircrew who operate them. We remain ready to fight and win at sea.”
Sea Venom was fired from the Wildcat during the same serial, and Captain Kelechi Ndukwe, commander of Task Force 65, confirmed to journalists that it was the missile’s first live firing since reaching initial operating capability, and that it hit the target. According to the Royal Navy, the helicopter completed the full kill chain by detecting, identifying and striking the target rather than simply releasing the weapon.
Lieutenant Commander Rhydian Edwards, test and evaluation commander at the Maritime Aviation Strike Operational Advantage Group, said: “This was a landmark moment for the Wildcat Force. For the first time we demonstrated the live firing of an operational Sea Venom missile against a representative maritime target. More importantly, we proved our ability to execute the full maritime strike kill chain under realistic operational conditions.
“This was about giving commanders confidence that Wildcat can find, fix and strike maritime targets using Sea Venom as part of a wider task group. The lessons learned from this activity will directly inform future tactics, training and operational capability development, ensuring Maritime Aviation Strike remains ready to fight and win when called upon.”
The Naval Strike Missile was brought into Royal Navy service under an interim arrangement to replace Harpoon, which left service in 2023, and has been fitted to Type 23 frigates and Type 45 destroyers using equipment transferred between hulls as ships enter and leave refit. Built by Kongsberg, the weapon is a sea-skimming missile with a low radar signature and a range well beyond that of the system it replaced, and it can strike land targets as well as ships. The service says it carries an advanced warhead, travels close to supersonic speeds and can reach targets more than 100 miles away while evading detection by skimming the sea, and that it will be complementary to the Future Cruise Anti-Ship Weapon, intended to become the fleet’s premier long-range anti-ship missile aboard the Type 26 and Type 31 frigates through the Mk41 vertical launch system.
Sea Venom, built by MBDA, is the Wildcat’s principal anti-ship weapon and replaced the Sea Skua carried by the Lynx. The Royal Navy describes it as designed to defeat corvette sized vessels or disable frigates, destroyers and other larger ships, with a Wildcat able to carry four at once, and says it can also be used overland against bunkers, buildings and vehicles. Readers will have seen the same missile turn up this week on a very different platform, fitted by STARK to an uncrewed surface vessel built near Plymouth.
The two British weapons were part of a wider engagement in which USS Paul Ignatius demonstrated the maximum damage and range capability of an anti-surface variant of the Standard Missile 6, and the submarine USS Massachusetts engaged the target with the Mark 48 Advanced Capability Torpedo, which delivered the final hit and sank the ship, as we reported.
Weapons were used in order of reach too we understand, with the longest range ordnance going first. Ndukwe said the American side started with the SM-6 before moving in to shorter range systems, a sequence designed to get the most out of the sensors fitted to the hull for battle damage assessment.
Atlantic Thunder 2026 was led by United States Sixth Fleet and drew in forces from five American task forces alongside the Royal Navy, the Royal Air Force and the United States Air Force. Lieutenant Commander Paul Atkins, the United Kingdom lead project officer for the exercise, said: “Atlantic Thunder 26 demonstrated the enduring strength of the UK-US alliance and the close partnership between the Royal Navy and the United States Navy. Operating together in a demanding environment, we showcased our ability to integrate seamlessly, share expertise and deliver a highly capable, interoperable maritime force. Through combined training and operations, we have strengthened our collective warfighting capability, reinforcing our ability to deter potential adversaries and deliver maritime combat power whenever and wherever it is required.”

articles.title: Why is South Korea so angry with Ukraine over two North Korean prisoners of war?
articles.body:
South Korea and Ukraine are locked in an escalating diplomatic dispute over who agreed what regarding the circumstances of two prisoners of war captured fighting for Russia.
Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, told the UN general assembly last week that his country had “sent two North Korean prisoners of war to the Republic of Korea”.
Seoul had long said it would take the men. But rather than celebrate, on Monday South Korea summoned Ukraine’s most senior diplomat in Seoul and demanded an apology.
Here’s a brief guide to what has happened, and why.
Who are the PoWs and what has happened to them?
Ukrainian forces captured the two men in Russia’s Kursk region in January 2025. They were among thousands of troops Pyongyang sent to fight for Moscow. Both men later said they wanted to go to South Korea, which regards North Koreans as its own citizens.
In July, Zelenskyy and South Korea’s president, Lee Jae Myung, agreed to resolve the issue while respecting the soldiers’ “free will”. The captured pair reportedly arrived in South Korea via a third country earlier this month.
North Koreans arriving in the South as defectors are usually questioned by the National Intelligence Service before being sent to a state resettlement centre, although sensitive cases can reportedly bypass the centre.
Why is Seoul so angry?
Seoul says Kyiv requested secrecy about the transfer, fearing domestic criticism for passing up the opportunity to exchange them for “a large number” of Ukrainian prisoners. South Korea says it agreed, citing the safety of the two men and their families as well as diplomatic and security considerations.
After Zelenskyy revealed the transfer in his UN speech, Lee said on X that Ukraine had broken a “non-disclosure agreement” and that this was regrettable. Zelenskyy’s adviser Dmytro Lytvyn responded on Facebook that there had been no such agreement, prompting accusations from Lee’s critics that the president, whose approval rating has hit a low of 37.9%, had lied.
Lee’s office called Kyiv’s statement “false” and said its conduct “seriously damages trust” between the two governments. On Monday, the foreign ministry summoned Ukraine’s chargé d’affaires, demanding an apology at governmental level.
Was there actually an agreement?
South Korea’s foreign ministry told Ukraine’s envoy there had been a “clear agreement”. Asked by the Guardian the same day whether anything had been put in writing, the ministry said only that the two sides “had decided to handle it confidentially”. Ukraine’s embassy in Seoul did not respond to a request for comment.
Has North Korea said anything?
No. South Korea’s unification ministry said it had “not identified any related developments so far” and would continue monitoring.
North Korea has glorified soldiers who killed themselves rather than be captured. The transfer of two who survived and chose the South is “a fatal matter” for Pyongyang, says Cho Han-bum of the Korea Institute for National Unification. Having built a “heroic narrative” around its troops, the regime is unlikely to disclose the transfer domestically, he says.
How big a diplomatic incident is this?
After Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, South Korea condemned Moscow’s actions, joined western sanctions and, in July, pledged a $100m support package. But it has kept the war at arm’s length, refusing to send weapons directly to Kyiv, in line with its practice of not supplying lethal arms to countries at war. Before the war, Russia was one of South Korea’s biggest trading partners. Lee’s government is also keen to improve relations with Pyongyang.
The row has turned that cautious support for Kyiv into open criticism, largely from Lee’s own camp. Kim Byung-joo, a Democratic party lawmaker, said there was “no reason or need” to support Ukraine and has urged the government to review its aid “immediately”.

articles.title: Tehran denounces UK ‘Iranophobia’ over airbase ‘terror case’
articles.body:
Tehran denounces UK ‘Iranophobia’ over airbase ‘terror case’
Iran has denied any ties to the Fairford Airbase incident in the UK, denouncing evidence-free claims that it was involved as “Iranophobia.”
Hours after call from a farmer to the military airbase at RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire, southwestern England, on Saturday night, police arrested five men driving three white vans, on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act.
Britain has ramped up pro-war rhetoric in the last week, with the BBC running an article titled “Are you psychologically prepared for war?” while Sky UK ran a reality show ‘The Wargame’ featuring politicians defining strategy in a ‘war room’ following a hypothetical attack by Russia. London’s belligerent media thus went into overdrive upon reports of a possible incident near the airbase.
Police cordoned off the vicinity of the base and evacuated over 80 homes. According to the BBC, a bomb squad worked at the scene, using a remote-controlled robot to inspect the vans, which were parked in a wooded area.
However, the men were released on bail the following day after “extensive interviews and enquiries,” according to Laurence Taylor, the head of the UK’s National Counter Terrorism Policing. No suspicious materials were found.
Taylor said police had begun investigating whether the offense was “committed by proxies, or individuals either knowingly or unknowingly, working on behalf of a foreign state” including “Russia, Iran or an Islamist state,” according to Reuters citing an anonymous security source.
Iran’s mission in London said in a statement on X on Monday that “The Embassy of the Islamic Republic of Iran in London categorically rejects and strongly condemns the recent unfounded and malicious speculations published by some British individuals and media outlets attempting to link Iran to [the] arrest of five suspects in the vicinity of RAF Fairford base.”
“Such fabricated speculations” would only “fuel Iranophobia propaganda in the UK.”
Although Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) warned in July that the UK would become a “definite and legitimate target” if it supported the US bombing campaign, Tehran has not claimed responsibility for any attacks outside the Middle East.
Iran has fired missiles and drones at Gulf states, which it described as legitimate targets for retaliation because they host American bases used to launch attacks against Iran.

articles.title: Two Russian-installed Donetsk officials suspected of deportation of 31 children to Russia for "treatment"
articles.body:
Two Russian-installed Donetsk officials suspected of deportation of 31 children to Russia for "treatment"
Two officials from the Russian occupation administration in Donetsk have been served with a notice of suspicion in absentia in Ukraine for orchestrating the deportation of 31 Ukrainian children under the guise of medical treatment. Most of the children taken to Russia are still there.
Source: Prosecutor General's Office; Bring Kids Back UA, a Ukrainian government-led effort to bring Ukrainian children home from temporarily Russian-occupied territories
Details: The identities of the suspects were revealed by the Book of Executioners, a Ukrainian project documenting Russian war criminals and those who betrayed Ukraine. They are 52-year-old Donetsk native Oleksii Kulemzin, the so-called head of the "city administration", and 57-year-old Olena Verbovska, a native of Ukrainsk in Donetsk Oblast and the so-called head of Donetsk's "department for children".
Investigators have found that in May 2022, the head of the so-called " Donetsk People's Republic The "Donetsk People's Republic", or "DPR", is a self-proclaimed unrecognised quasi-state formation backed by Russia in Ukraine's Donetsk Oblast " ordered the relocation of children to Russia, ostensibly for medical treatment. The occupation administration in Donetsk implemented the order.
Sixteen boys and 15 girls were brought to the so-called "Children's Social Centre" and taken by bus to Rostov Oblast in Russia. From there, the Ukrainian children were flown to the Polyany sanatorium in Moscow Oblast, which is part of the Children's Medical Centre under the Russian Presidential Administration.
According to the Book of Executioners project, the occupiers used this scheme to take orphans and children deprived of parental care out of Ukraine.
"The children did not require medical treatment outside the region, and there were no hostilities in Donetsk at the time that threatened their lives. Therefore, there were no grounds for their evacuation," the project's creators say.
Once the children were outside Ukraine, the occupation administration decided that they would not be required to return. Instead, they were to be placed under guardianship in Moscow Oblast.
Since then, only six children from this group have been brought back to Ukraine, while the rest remain in Russia.
Kulemzin and Verbovska have now been served with a notice of suspicion of violating the laws and customs of war, committed by a group of persons acting by prior agreement (Articles 28.2 and 438.1 of the Criminal Code). They face between eight and 12 years in prison.
Sanctions have been imposed on both suspects. The Book of Executioners project added that in 2024, other participants in the deportation of the children were also named suspects: so-called "DPR" head Denys Pushylin, his "children's rights adviser" Eleonora Fedorenko, and the director of the "State Service for Children of the DPR", Svitlana Maiboroda.
Quote from the Prosecutor General's Office: "Law enforcement officials are systematically documenting Russia's crimes against Ukrainian children – illegal transfer and deportation, identity changes, militarisation and preparation for service in the Russian armed forces.
An investigation has established that around 6,000 children in temporarily occupied Donetsk Oblast were involved in the Russian military-patriotic movement Yunarmiya between 2019 and 2025. They were taught how to handle weapons and prepared for military service. After reaching adulthood, some of the participants joined the Russian armed forces and took part in the war against Ukraine."
Background: Law enforcement officers previously named two employees of a detention centre in Kursk, Russia, as suspects in a case involving the systematic torture of Ukrainian civilians.
