articles.title: Raytheon expands Sidewinder supplier base in U.S., Europe
articles.body:
The U.S. Navy is paying Raytheon up to $30.2 million to line up additional suppliers for key parts of the AIM-9X Sidewinder air-to-air missile, including the cooling engine for its heat-seeking sensor and its warhead components.
The undefinitized contract modification, announced by the U.S. Department of War, covers engineering work to qualify new manufacturing sources for several AIM-9X components. Naval Air Systems Command at Patuxent River, Maryland, awarded it without competition, and the work is due to be finished in February 2030.
Qualifying a second source means testing and approving another factory to make a part that currently comes from only one supplier, so that production does not stop if that supplier falls behind or shuts down. The notice lists the parts involved: the cryoengine, which cools the missile’s infrared seeker so it can detect a target’s heat; connectors and wiring harnesses; sensor platform and warhead components; components of the optical target detector, which senses when the missile is close enough to its target to detonate; and parts of the inertial measurement unit, which tracks the missile’s movement in flight.
The work will be spread across the United States and Europe. About half, 51%, will take place at Raytheon’s missile plant in Tucson, Arizona. Another 19% is set for Schrobenhausen, Germany, 12% for Anaheim, California, and 8% for Heilbronn, Germany, with smaller shares in Camarillo, California; Delémont, Switzerland; Midland, Ontario; and Logan, Utah.
The modification is a cost-plus-incentive-fee arrangement, meaning the government covers Raytheon’s costs and pays a fee that depends on performance. Because it is undefinitized, work can begin before final prices and terms are agreed, up to a $30.2 million ceiling. The Navy committed $29.6 million in fiscal 2025 weapons procurement funds at the time of award.
The AIM-9X is the latest version of the Sidewinder, a short-range, heat-seeking missile carried by U.S. and allied fighter jets and also fired from the ground by the NASAMS air defense system. The U.S. Navy leads the program jointly with the U.S. Air Force, and more than 35 allied and partner nations use the missile.
In June 2026, the U.S. Navy awarded Raytheon a $1.1 billion contract for more than 1,900 AIM-9X Block II missiles, including 1,653 for U.S. inventories and 336 for foreign customers, with work running through September 2029. That followed another $1.1 billion AIM-9X award in June 2025, then the largest in the program’s history. Raytheon says it is raising AIM-9X production capacity to about 2,500 missiles a year.

articles.title: Estonia slams Russian 'sabotage' after arson attack on defence company Milrem Robotics
articles.body:
European countries have already faced multiple incursions by Russian drones as well as a campaign of covert Russian disruption which began after Putin’s invasion of Ukraine.
NATO chief Mark Rutte urged "calm" on Tuesday over Russia's campaign of sabotage in Europe, saying it was failing to undercut support for Ukraine.
His comments come after Estonia became the latest country to officially blame Russia for such an incident, saying Moscow's "special services" had ordered an arson attack on a defence firm in August.
"Russia continues its reckless campaign of hostile actions against NATO allies. It is trying to weaken our resolve and stop our support for Ukraine. But Russia is failing. It is failing on the battlefield in Ukraine and it is failing to undermine our unity and support for Ukraine," Rutte told journalists.
European governments say Moscow is stepping up a campaign of sabotage and interference against Ukraine's backers as the Kremlin's troops struggle on the front line there, more than four years after their February 2022 invasion.
The Estonian incident came just after the discovery of an explosive-laden drone at an airport in Russia that Berlin pinned on Moscow.
Rutte admitted that Russia's activities "can have an impact and sometimes they have an impact, clearly."
But he urged NATO countries to remain "calm, carry on and support Ukraine."
"We should not be naive... about Russia, but they know we are stronger," Rutte said.
Speaking alongside the NATO chief, Lithuania's Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevicius said intelligence services had no proof Moscow was imminently prepping for something bigger.
"It's a must to say if a threat is there for society, but you can't exaggerate and say something is happening in the upcoming months or weeks," he said.
"The risk remains, but it's not fluctuating...not increasing or decreasing."
Earlier on Tuesday, Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna accused Russia of "sabotage" following an arson attack on the premises of defence company, Milrem Robotics, in August.
"We can conclude with certainty that the arson attack...in Tallinn was an act of sabotage ordered by the special services of the Russian Federation," he wrote in a post on X.
He added that the perpetrators of the attack had been apprehended and "no longer pose a threat" and that Estonia had summoned the Russian ambassador.
"This act of sabotage is part of Russia's broader campaign across Europe, aimed at intimidating us and weakening our support for Ukraine," Tsahkna wrote.
Estonia, an EU and NATO member state along the alliance's eastern flank, has accused Russia of several "hybrid" provocations since the beginning of Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Along with its neighbours, Latvia and Lithuania, it has ramped up its investment in defence in the years since and remains a staunch ally of Kyiv.
News of the attack prompted messages of solidarity from across Europe.
Germany’s Foreign Minister Johan Wadephul slammed what he called “Russia’s reckless act of hostility and said Estonia had full solidarity from Berlin.
French President Emmanuel Macron said in a post on X that "Russia must know that it will not prevail over either our unity or our determination to continue supporting Ukraine."
"The proliferation of these hostile acts reflects a dangerous escalation on the part of Russia, which will only lead it into a dead end," he added.
Sweden’s Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson called the attack “extremely serious.”
“This pattern of attacks is directed against Europe as a whole. The aim is to weaken our support for Ukraine and to intimidate us. It will not work,” he said in a post on X.
And the European Union said it stands by member state Estonia following the "reckless" arson attack and would not be put off supporting Ukraine.
"We stand by Estonia on this reckless attack," European Commission spokesperson Christian Wigand said, expressing "full solidarity" with Tallin.
"Moscow is trying to scare Europe into winding down its support for Ukraine. This will not happen," he added.
The Kremlin rejected what it called Estonia's "baseless" accusation that Russia ordered the arson attack in Tallinn.
"Such statements are baseless, ill-considered, have absolutely no relation to reality and lack any form of reasoning. Consequently, we cannot and will not take such statements seriously," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters.
Putin trying to break NATO support for Ukraine, leaders say
Putin, Stringer said, is “looking at a whole number of things” to try to create division between NATO allies because his campaign in Ukraine is going badly.
Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal likened the Russian leader to a “rat in the corner," who is escalating activity in Europe in an attempt to break Western support for Kyiv at a time when Moscow is under pressure.
Putin is trying to undermine NATO’s collective defence pact by testing nations with covert attacks that are hard to attribute, Michal said.
But the Estonian leader said it's currently “improbable,” that Putin will launch a conventional military attack on Europe because of the threat of a NATO response and because his forces are tied down in Ukraine.
The high level of malign activity from Russia is “here to stay” until Putin changes his military goals, Michal said, adding that the best way to deter him is to “back Ukraine.”

articles.title: First Turkish Pilots Begin Eurofighter Typhoon Training in the UK
articles.body:
The first two Turkish Air Force pilots have begun training in the UK to fly Eurofighter Typhoon fighter jets.
The Royal Air Force (RAF) reported this on September 27.
The training is taking place at RAF Coningsby in Lincolnshire with 29 Squadron of the Royal Air Force, the unit responsible for operational conversion training for Typhoon pilots.
At the first stage, the Turkish pilots will study the fighter’s systems and procedures used in British military airspace. They will then move on to flying Eurofighter aircraft.
The conversion course will last up to nine months. After completing it, the pilots will undergo an additional three months of training to become instructors.
After completing their training, the Turkish pilots will remain with 29 Squadron as instructors.
They will remain there until Turkey receives its first new Eurofighter jets produced by BAE Systems. Ankara expects the first delivery in 2030.
The training is part of a deal worth more than £8 billion between the UK and Turkey.
The main agreement covers the delivery of 20 Eurofighter Typhoon fighter jets to Turkey, along with the necessary weapons, technical support, and personnel training.
On March 25, 2026, the UK and Turkey signed a separate multibillion agreement covering training and long-term support for Turkish Typhoons.
The agreement provides for the training of 10 Turkish pilots and nearly 100 ground handling personnel in the UK, specializing in mechanical systems, avionics, weapons, and task execution systems.
The contract also covers the supply of spare parts and maintenance equipment, simulators, and other support means.
The British defense industry will be involved in producing the Turkish aircraft. Around 37% of each aircraft will be manufactured in the UK, including at facilities operated by BAE Systems, Leonardo, and Rolls-Royce.
Overall, the deal is expected to support around 20,000 jobs in British industry and supply chains.
Militarnyi previously reported that as of August 2026, production of Typhoon fighter jets for the Turkish Air Force had already begun in the UK and Eurofighter consortium partner countries.
The Eurofighter Typhoon is a Gen 4+ multirole supersonic fighter developed jointly by the UK, Germany, Italy, and Spain.
The aircraft is designed for air combat, interception of aerial targets, and strikes against ground targets. The fighters are produced by the Eurofighter GmbH consortium, which includes BAE Systems, Airbus, and Leonardo.
The air forces of the UK, Germany, Italy, Spain, Austria, Saudi Arabia, Oman, Kuwait, and Qatar operate Typhoon aircraft. In service with the Royal Air Force, the aircraft performs airspace patrol, interception, and ground-attack missions.
The Eurofighter can employ a wide range of air-launched weapons. For engaging aerial targets, the aircraft uses the long-range Meteor, medium-range AIM-120 AMRAAM, and short-range ASRAAM missiles. The fighter is also equipped with a 27 mm Mauser automatic cannon.
For strikes against ground targets, the aircraft can carry Storm Shadow cruise missiles, Brimstone 2 guided missiles, and Paveway IV guided bombs.
New weapons are also being considered for and integrated with British Typhoons, including SPEAR 3 missiles.
Turkey also plans to integrate its domestically developed air-launched weapons on the Eurofighter. These include the Gökdoğan and Bozdoğan air-to-air missiles and the SOM cruise missile.
According to BAE Systems, the UK is open to integrating Turkish systems on the fighter jets, but it has not yet announced which weapons will be integrated or the timeline for integration.

articles.title: Lithuania gets its US tank battalion back while the Pentagon weighs pulling up to 40,000 troops from Europe
articles.body:
Lithuania is getting its US troops back although the overall American presence in Europe will shrink, Lithuanian President Gitanas Nausėda said. He tied the wider drawdown to Washington's demand that Europe take more responsibility for its own defense. Lithuania's case, he suggested, is the exception.
While waging all-out war on Ukraine, Russia keeps probing Europe with drones and sabotage that stop just short of open attack. Its small Baltic neighbors are already preparing their people for a possible invasion, and American soldiers on their soil have long been the clearest sign that attacking them means fighting the US. With Washington weighing a pullback and telling Europe to fend for itself, each US unit that stays on Russia's doorstep carries more weight than its size.
"There will be fewer US troops in Europe"
Nausėda spoke in an interview with LNK television on 28 September.
"There will be fewer US troops in Europe. This is partly related to what US President Donald Trump says, to the signals the US administration is sending us that Europe must take on more responsibility itself," he said.
Europe must do more for itself, and it is already doing so, Nausėda added. The US presence in Lithuania matters not only for its military power but also for deterrence, he argued.
"The presence of these troops is precisely what reduces the likelihood of military conflict or military aggression," he told LNK, ELTA reported.
"The heavy battalion will be here"
Nausėda called the decision a kind of encouragement for Lithuania. "As the overall number of US troops in Europe decreases, in Lithuania that number will at least remain, will not decrease, and perhaps will even be slightly larger," he said. "In any case, the heavy battalion will be here."
The battalion will keep its Abrams tanks, but an engineer battalion will replace the artillery battalion, Nausėda said on LRT's Savaitė program. The rotation will again last nine months. The Americans will number roughly as before, over 1,000, Defense Minister Robertas Kaunas said.
Estonia has also secured the return of US troops, at least temporarily, LRT noted.
Trump announces 5,000 US troops to Poland — one week after US froze scheduled combat-team rotation and amid Russia’s threat
More than 1,000 US troops began leaving Lithuania when their rotation ended in early June, and no replacement arrived, LRT said. It was the country's first gap in the US presence since 2020. American heavy battalions have rotated through Lithuania since 2019.
The Pentagon is weighing a withdrawal of about 25,000 US troops from Europe, and possibly as many as 40,000, NBC News reported, adding that no final decision had been made. About 80,000 US troops are now stationed on the continent. Germany, Italy, and Spain would likely be among the countries most affected.

articles.title: AFU General Staff: Russian Kasta radars, UAV control posts and depots hit

"On September 28 and overnight into September 29, units of the Ukrainian Defense Forces struck a number of key military targets belonging to the Russian occupiers," the AFU General Staff said in a Telegram post on Tuesday.

It detects aircraft, helicopters, unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), cruise missiles, and other air attack assets flying at low altitude at ranges of up to 150 km.

articles.title: What to Know About the Pentagon Breach Affecting Millions
articles.body:
A reported monthslong breach in the Defense Department’s human resources database exposed personal information of millions of military personnel and those related to them, including their Social Security numbers and job details.
Unidentified Pentagon officials confirmed to CNN and ABC News that some 2.76 million “living individuals” and 294,000 “deceased individuals” have been affected by the breach at the Defense Manpower Data Center (DMDC).
The breach was first reported by defense-focused news publication Military Times on Thursday, citing a breach notification letter to a person whose information was in the affected files.
It remains unclear what particular files were accessed and who was behind the incident. TIME has requested comment from the Pentagon.
The length of the breach and the amount of personal information exposed present a security risk for many personnel linked with the department, and some experts say it makes other security compromises, like phishing attempts, easier for bad actors.
What we know about the breach
The DMDC collates personnel, manpower, training, financial, and other data for the Defense Department for healthcare, retirement funding, and other administrative needs. Its website says that based on FY2024 data, it has the records of more than 60 million people—including the military, civilians, contractors, family members, retirees, and veterans.
But the Military Times reviewed a Sept. 18 letter from the DMDC notifying its recipient of a data breach. The letter reportedly said it discovered on July 16 a security vulnerability in the center’s file-sharing system.
The notice reportedly details that between October 2025 and the time of discovery, some “unauthorized users” accessed files on a server containing the personal information. The type of personal information varies from names to dates of birth, contact information, and others.
DMDC then said it updated the file-sharing system to address the vulnerability. The letter reportedly added that there has been no indication of misuse of the recipient’s information.
Not the first hack
The latest incident involving Pentagon data emerged as the FBI confirmed it was looking into criminal hacking group ShinyHunters’s apparent attack on its jobs website. The group claimed to have stolen “very sensitive data” on nearly all agents and job applicants in response to an FBI notice about them issued in May. (ShinyHunters were also behind a high-profile hack in May of education platform Canvas.)
It’s still unclear how massive the previous FBI breach was, but a New York Times analysis found that it may have involved the stealing of home addresses, Social Security numbers, and job assignments, on top of other personally identifiable information. Reuters reported last week that the hackers claimed they have obtained about 2-3 terabytes of data. Some of the data Reuters reviewed also revealed details of assignments to specific field offices, as well as FBI units engaged in high-stakes intelligence, security, or counterespionage work, which risks endangering national security.
In a statement to 404 Media and the Times, the FBI said it was “working around the clock to investigate the cyber incident involving FBIJobs.gov and is in regular communication with anyone who may be impacted—including multiple bureau-wide communications within 24 hours of public reporting.”
The FBI incident also follows a breach that may have exposed more than 153 million driver’s licenses in the U.S. and Canada.
What affected personnel can do
Security experts have previously warned that access to troves of records poses a massive security risk, especially if these fall into the hands of foreign actors.
Justin Sherman, a senior associate at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, wrote about the license data breach earlier this month: “It can be tempting to dismiss the next hack of a database as ‘just another data breach.’... But breaches do not exist in a vacuum.”
The DMDC said in its notice to affected personnel that it was offering year-long credit monitoring and identity-restoration services through IDX, a private firm contracted by the department.
According to the Federal Trade Commission, anyone could place a free credit freeze with each of the three major credit bureaus—Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion.
Active duty personnel and National Guard members could also get free electronic credit monitoring to spot problems that could stem from identity theft.

articles.title: Beyond melodrama: Khajepasha on war, childhood and duty of Iranian cinema
articles.body:
Beyond melodrama: Khajepasha on war, childhood and duty of Iranian cinema
TEHRAN- Iranian filmmaker Babak Khajepasha believes cinema should do more than portray suffering. For him, a film dealing with war, the death of children, or a social tragedy should leave audiences with questions rather than simply tears.
Khajepasha, whose “In the Arms of the Tree” was selected as Iran’s submission for the 2025 Academy Awards, has repeatedly turned to children and family in his films. His latest feature, “The Land of Angels”, deals with children in Gaza. The film has also taken part in international events, including the Altyn Minbar Kazan International Film Festival, where it received the Grand Prix for Best Feature Film. Khajepasha is also among the jury members of the 2026 BRICS+ International Film Festival in St. Petersburg.
In an interview with the Tehran Times, he spoke about the possibility of making a film on the recent tragedy in Minab, the difficulty of depicting the death of children without reducing cinema to melodrama, his decision to make films during the 40-day war, and what he saw during a recent visit to Hiroshima. He also discussed the international position of Iranian cinema, his earlier criticism of the Oscars and some major festivals, and why family remains one of the subjects he wants to pursue in his future work.
Looking beyond the tragedy
Speaking about the possibility of making a film about the tragedy in Minab, Khajepasha said he would be more interested in exploring the reasons behind such events than simply depicting their devastating consequences.
“The aspect that I, as a filmmaker, can enter and that deserves to be explored is the reason behind this tragedy,” he said, stressing that society should ask why it has been forced to experience such pain.
The filmmaker pointed to the loss of children in different parts of Iran, including Minab, Lamerd, Tabriz and Kermanshah during the recent war, saying that while addressing the suffering of children is important, cinema should also investigate why children repeatedly become victims of conflict and violence.
This concern, he explained, was also central to his research for “The Land of Angels”. During his research and conversations with Palestinians, he encountered stories that demonstrated the profound psychological impact of losing a child.
Khajepasha recalled speaking with a Palestinian father who had been holding his child when the child was killed. According to the filmmaker, the man later repeatedly returned to the same place, hoping that he too would be killed so that he could join his child. The father said he could not understand why he had been left alive.
For Khajepasha, such stories demonstrate that the killing of a child affects much more than the immediate victim. It leaves a psychological wound on the family and, ultimately, the wider community.
Yet he believes that cinema must be careful not to turn such suffering into an exercise in emotional manipulation.
From tears to questions
That is also why Khajepasha is wary of making films about war and children that rely entirely on emotion.
If simply seeing the suffering of children were enough to change the world's response to violence, he said, the many films and documentaries made about Gaza and other conflicts would already have brought about such a change.
“Just talking about how much pain we are in does not necessarily take us a step forward,” he said. “We have to look at this from an intellectual perspective. We have to search for its causes and ask where this pain is supposed to take us.”
For “The Land of Angels”, he wanted the audience to leave with a question.
A viewer may accept that there are fighters, a military conflict and casualties in a war, he explained. But the death of thousands of children should lead to another question: why are these children being killed?
That question, in his view, can open the door to wider discussions about the position of children in contemporary society, the pressures placed on them and even the declining importance attached to having children in some parts of the world.
Khajepasha prefers this kind of cinema to a film that simply asks its audience to cry.
“I don't want to make a film merely so that audiences cry,” he said. “We have to value the film itself. There have to be other reasons for making it.”
He pointed to techniques used in dramatic literature and epic theater, including distancing, which encourage audiences to think about a work instead of simply surrendering to its emotional effect. A film, he said, should stay with the viewer as a question after the screening.
When filmmaking becomes a duty
The same idea of responsibility was behind Khajepasha's decision to work during the 40-day War.
At the time, Tehran and other parts of the country were facing an extraordinary situation as they came under US and Zionist regime airstrikes. Khajepasha said he saw people from different professions doing more than their normal duties: bakers working additional shifts, doctors and nurses continuing their work in hospitals and other citizens finding ways to contribute.
For him and some of his colleagues, filmmaking became another form of service.
“Sometimes we make films because we are filmmakers. Sometimes, as Iranians, we have another national duty,” he said. “At that point, it is no longer simply about filmmaking. It is a form of service.”
Under ordinary circumstances, he acknowledged, starting a production so quickly and without the usual preparation would not have been logical. But he felt that the circumstances demanded a response.
“As someone working in the arts, I felt I had a responsibility,” he said. “My instrument is cinema and television.”
He began work only a few days after the war started and now looks back on the experience with particular satisfaction.
The reason, he explained, was not necessarily that the films were more successful than his other work. It was the feeling that he was doing something directly for his own people.
“I am happy that, during that period, instead of standing on the sidelines, I was able to take a step,” he said.
Hiroshima: between memory and spectacle
A recent trip to Hiroshima gave Khajepasha another opportunity to think about the way major human tragedies are remembered.
He attended the annual ceremony commemorating the victims of the atomic bombing of Hiroshima and found the gathering visually striking and, from a filmmaker's perspective, fascinating. Yet he said the event left him with mixed feelings.
The scale of the tragedy, he argued, seemed much greater than what was being conveyed by the ceremony.
“I felt that, instead of the truth being fully expressed, I was watching more of a show,” he said.
Khajepasha extended that observation to the way peace is sometimes represented internationally. He questioned the gap that can exist between institutions and governments that publicly promote peace and countries whose policies have contributed to conflicts elsewhere.
But his experience in Japan did not leave him simply pessimistic. He said he encountered ordinary people who appeared genuinely concerned about events beyond their own borders.
When some Japanese people learned that he was Iranian, he recalled, they immediately brought up the victims of the recent tragedy in Minab and other Iranian victims.
He said he had encountered similar reactions in other countries and believes that ordinary people may ultimately understand such tragedies more deeply than political rhetoric suggests.
Iranian cinema and the international festival circuit
Khajepasha also returned to comments he made while “In the Arms of the Tree” was Iran's Oscar submission. At the time, he had questioned whether artistic quality alone determines a film's international success.
His criticism, he explained, was not simply about whether his own film would advance in the Oscar race. He was talking about the broader position of art and cinema.
In his view, political considerations, lobbying and relationships can influence some major international cultural institutions. He also believes that the influence of politics has become particularly visible in some film festivals.
That does not mean he considers the entire international festival circuit politicized.
He mentioned festivals held in South Korea, Morocco, Egypt, Armenia, Russia and Turkey among festivals that continue to offer valuable platforms for filmmakers. Iranian cinema, he stressed, has also received genuine international recognition through films by directors such as Asghar Farhadi and Majid Majidi.
The quality of an individual film, he argued, should not be reduced to the festival at which it appears or the prize it receives.
“A festival award alone cannot determine the value of a film,” he said.
He also believes filmmakers themselves have a responsibility not to allow the desire for international recognition to dictate their artistic choices.
Family at the center
Children feature prominently in both “In the Arms of the Tree” and “The Land of Angels”, but Khajepasha does not see himself primarily as a filmmaker of children's stories.
His deeper interest, he said, is the family.
He usually tries to include children in his films because their presence gives the story another dimension, but he would like to explore the family itself more extensively in future work.
“I would like to make more films about the family itself,” he said, describing it as one of the most important and vulnerable foundations of human societies.
He believes the issue has particular importance in Iran because family relationships are deeply connected to the country's cultural identity.
Iran cannot simply reproduce changes that have taken place in other societies, he argued. Relationships among parents, children and extended family members have a particular cultural meaning in Iranian society.
For that reason, he believes Iranian cinema should address the pressures facing families instead of treating changes in family structures as inevitable.
‘First make a good film’
Khajepasha will soon have an opportunity to examine films from the other side of the filmmaking process, as a jury member of the BRICS+ International Film Festival in St. Petersburg.
At the time of the interview, the festival's films had not yet been sent to the jury, so he had not begun watching them. But he already knew what his first criterion would be.
The film itself comes first.
For Khajepasha, a film needs to have a sound story and plot as well as convincing cinematic elements such as mise-en-scène and visual language. A political or social message cannot make up for weaknesses in the filmmaking.
He is particularly critical of films that appear to have been made primarily to deliver a message.
“If we want to criticize a society, we first have to make a good film,” he said. “If we simply shout our message at the audience, the audience will realize immediately that the filmmaker has an agenda.”
The same principle applies to films carrying messages that he himself agrees with, he added.
“A good film that disagrees with our beliefs can sometimes be less damaging than a bad film that is trying to promote our beliefs,” he said.
As a juror, Khajepasha said his first priority would therefore be cinematic quality.
“Before a film can make an audience believe in its message, it has to make the audience believe in the film itself,” he concluded.
SAB/

articles.title: US tells Lebanon Hezbollah disarmament efforts 'not enough'
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
US tells Lebanon Hezbollah disarmament efforts 'not enough'
Lebanon has received negative signals from the United States over its efforts to bring Hezbollah's weapons under state control, with Washington warning that Israel intends to continue its military operations in the south, The New Arab has learned.
Lebanese Prime Minister Nawaf Salam received several messages while in New York on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly, including warnings from US officials that Israel intends to maintain the security zone it has established in southern Lebanon.
Washington conveyed that Israel would continue its operations "as long as the Lebanese state does not take serious action to disarm Hezbollah", according to information obtained by TNA, and that it remains determined to destroy the group's military infrastructure.
US officials also told Salam that the steps taken by the Lebanese government so far were insufficient and that efforts to bring all weapons under state control must be accelerated.
According to the information obtained by TNA, Washington called for a firmer approach to the issue, warning that the situation could deteriorate further otherwise.
The warnings come as southern Lebanon faces near-daily Israeli escalation, with Israel stepping up its operations and insisting on maintaining the security zone it has established in the south.
Prospects for a solution are meanwhile receding, at least until Israel's parliamentary elections on 27 October.
Salam also received several messages of support, particularly from Arab and European countries, backing the government's decisions and Lebanon's demands for Israel to halt its attacks and withdraw from occupied Lebanese territory.
There was also support for the need to fill any security vacuum in southern Lebanon if the mandate of the United Nations Interim Force in Lebanon (UNIFIL) expires without renewal, with efforts expected to intensify in the coming period to find a solution to the crisis.
Hezbollah sets conditions for weapons talks
Attention is meanwhile turning to Hezbollah and whether the group could enter into a confrontation with Israel, particularly if Israeli military operations intensify.
Such a scenario remains unlikely in the near term, however, as Hezbollah is currently looking to developments between the US and Iran, with Tehran making Lebanon a key issue in its negotiations.
Hezbollah parliamentary sources told The New Arab that the group was "monitoring all developments, and its eyes will remain on the field. Iran remains committed to the Lebanon issue and will not abandon it, which is what should be relied upon rather than direct negotiations with the enemy".
They added that the Lebanese state should return to indirect negotiations with Israel and correct the course of the talks.
The sources said Hezbollah was open to discussing the issue of its weapons domestically and as part of a national defence strategy.
However, they said a complete halt to Israeli attacks and Israel's withdrawal from all Lebanese territory must come first.
Hezbollah Secretary-General Naim Qassem on Sunday renewed his call for Lebanese authorities to end what he described as concessions and review the course of negotiations, calling for direct talks to be suspended in favour of indirect negotiations.
His comments came on the second anniversary of the assassination of former Hezbollah secretary-generals Hassan Nasrallah and Hashem Safieddine.
"Let it be clear, Lebanon without resistance will disappear; the enemy wants all of Lebanon," Qassem said.
"Lebanon can only remain through its liberation and unity and the cooperation of its components. Whoever bets on retaining a part of Lebanon in exchange for abandoning the other part of the land or people is deluded."
Israel steps up attacks on southern Lebanon
Israeli forces carried out a series of attacks on several areas of southern Lebanon in recent hours, including the use of an Apache attack helicopter in a strike for the first time during the latest escalation.
The helicopter struck a commercial centre on the main road between the towns of Shoukine and Mifdoun in the Nabatieh district.
Israeli forces also carried out air strikes on Wadi Zibqin, Talouseh, Mais al-Jabal and the Al-Dabsh area, while artillery fire targeted Wadi Saluki, the outskirts of Kfar Tibnit and Nabatieh al-Fawqa, Al-Mansouri and Wadi Zibqin.
Israeli forces also opened machine-gun fire towards the outskirts of Kfar Shuba in the Azrael area, as well as Sarbin and the Al-Sadana area.
An explosion was also carried out by Israeli forces in Mais al-Jabal, while illumination flares were fired over Hadatha-Haris and Wadi Saluki.
The escalation comes as Israeli media reports suggest southern Lebanon could enter a new phase in the coming days following the completion of what Israel described as "clearing" operations on the Ali al-Taher heights and the destruction of Hezbollah infrastructure in the area.
Direct negotiations remain suspended despite Washington previously announcing that talks would take place in October.

SNEAK PEEK
— Clemens Martin Auer, president of the European Health Forum Gastein, calls for more action ahead of a four-day health conference.

Welcome to Tuesday’s Morning Health Care! It’s the first day of Gastein and Claudia and I will be here all week, so we’re going to need gossip to survive. There are rumors about a place where people dance in a cage to let their hair down; if you know anything, do tell. What happens in Gastein …
A LITTLE LESS CONVERSATION, A LITTLE MORE ACTION: The slow implementation and inefficiency of health policy across Europe is hampering the bloc’s ability to respond to major challenges like climate change, health security, AI and workforce issues, says Clemens Martin Auer, the president of the European Health Forum Gastein. Europe doesn’t have a lack of ideas or technical skills to tackle major problems facing the sector, but rather an implementation problem, he told Morning Health Care in an interview ahead of his last conference as head of the forum, with his final day on Oct. 31. “The older I get, the more impatient I am with the slowness of our policy implementations,” he said.
More action needed: As health experts, industry representatives, and everyone in between descend on Gastein, Austria, for a four-day health conference, Auer is calling for more action. “We are living in really challenging times, and my observation is that we don't do enough to change the situation.”
Pharma: Capricious U.S. health policies, including a push by the Trump administration to reduce domestic drug prices (more on this below), were creating global uncertainty and impacting where drugmakers were investing, Auer said, pointing to increasing investment in China. Health systems in Europe could only be counterbalanced if countries were willing to pay more for products like generics to shore up supply chains, he said. “If you want to safeguard that supply, then you have to be willing to pay more for them.” His comments come as the pharma industry is set to play a major role at the conference across multiple panels, with U.S. policies and European drug prices running as an undercurrent in most major discussions on health security, accessibility, and competitiveness.
Advertisement
Competitiveness: Auer pointed to the Draghi report, which proposed a plan to increase competitiveness more than two years ago. “ Do we see any implementation, substantial implementation? The economic numbers and data are getting worse.”
Health security: Auer also expressed frustration at a lack of action to address the threat to health infrastructure. He called for intelligence sharing and greater cooperation between the defense and health sectors, including shoring up pharmaceutical supply chains to reduce reliance on external sources. “The face of war is changing, the means of war are changing,” he said, pointing to hybrid warfare like cyberattacks and drones. “The security people have to share the information with the health sector, and the health sector has to be open to take it on, act accordingly and put up their measures for more security.”

Rocky negotiations: The report was at the center of controversy over its language on alcohol. “When it comes to cancer, there is no safe level of alcohol consumption,” said the Association of European Cancer Leagues. “By referring to 'levels exceeding scientifically established health recommendations', the report implies there is a safe threshold. That is misleading.”
Rare diseases vote: MEPs want a dedicated law to improve diagnosis of rare diseases, ensure equal access to treatment, and place greater emphasis on patient care, with 33 votes in favor, three against, and five abstentions on a legislative initiative resolution in the health committee. Rare diseases affect tens of millions of people across Europe, with three in four of those living with one being children. The committee’s recommendations and legislative initiative report will be tabled for a vote at the next European Parliament plenary. You can read the full details of the committee’s plan here.

Context: The event, taking place today, is organized by the European Committee of Wine Companies and Socialists & Democrats MEP Dario Nardella. It brings together lawmakers, industry and researchers “to explore how the latest scientific evidence can better inform policymaking and contribute to a more nuanced discussion on the role of wine as part of a healthy lifestyle.”
But to civil societies, it sends the wrong message: “Civil society organisations working to reduce alcohol-related harm in Europe object to events like this, which give commercial interests a seat at the agenda-setting table of EU public health policy,” they wrote in a statement.
Not the time: They also criticize the timing of the event on World Heart Day. “European public health organisations consider it wholly inappropriate that an MEP would give the alcohol industry a platform in a health policy debate, particularly on a day dedicated to raising awareness of cardiovascular disease and its prevention,” they add.
Encouraging an open discussion: “Today's event brings scientists together to discuss evidence on health, diet and longevity, and this kind of debate strengthens prevention,” Nardella told Morning Health Care. “Good public policy needs to be proportionate and evidence-based, and it should distinguish between harmful consumption and moderate consumption within a balanced lifestyle and a traditional food culture like ours. Moderation is the key to the consumption of everything, not just alcohol.” He added that the event falling on World Heart Day was a coincidence.
Coincidence? "On World Heart Day, I would argue this debate is particularly relevant, not inappropriate … an open and transparent dialogue with all relevant stakeholders is an important part of a whole-of-society approach to health," said Ignacio Sánchez Recarte, secretary general of the European Committee of Wine Companies.
Signed: The statement is signed by the Association of European Cancer Leagues, the European Alcohol Policy Alliance, the European Health Alliance on Alcohol, the European Heart Network and the Standing Committee of European Doctors.

WHILE WE'RE TALKING ABOUT HEART HEALTH: The Commission announced Monday it adopted a proposal for a Council recommendation to tackle cardiovascular diseases, which are Europe’s biggest killer, claiming 1.7 million lives a year. The recommendations include more health checks; tackling health inequality by ensuring checks are available and affordable; and encouraging member states to consider personalized prevention and appropriate vaccination advice. Health literacy was also an important tool for empowering Europeans to better understand the value of regular check-ups, the Commission said. The full details are here.
US TARIFFS
D-DAY (AGAIN): Section 232 U.S. tariffs of up to 100% on pharmaceuticals and their ingredients come into effect today for companies that haven’t struck deals with the Trump administration. These deals secure temporary tariff-free access for their products and ingredients while also imposing price controls in the U.S. These so-called most-favored-nation deals also bring U.S. prices for some branded medicines roughly in line with European prices.
Most exposed: Mid-sized European biotech and specialty pharma companies that haven’t signed agreements are the most exposed, according to Diederik Stadig, a health care economist at Dutch bank ING. A handful of biotechs signed agreements last month, bringing the total number of agreements to 26 — so we could expect to see more deals land.
The small print: EU-origin medicines will face a 15% tariff cap under the EU-U.S. Turnberry deal.
Solutions needed: EUCOPE’s Secretary General, Alexander Natz, said there needed to be a sustainable transatlantic solution that safeguarded patient access, investment, and innovation to avoid further trade escalation. Pharma tariffs and the medicine pricing debate “has very real consequences for companies and patients,” he told Morning Health Care. “MFN agreements may provide certainty for individual manufacturers, but they do not resolve the broader challenges facing the European pharmaceutical ecosystem.”
Meanwhile: Generic and biosimilar manufacturers are exempt from all U.S. tariffs that have so far impacted the medicines sector. Adrian van den Hoven, head of generics lobby Medicines for Europe, said tariffs on medicines were counterproductive and called for off-patent medicines to remain exempt.
Advertisement
He pointed out: “Medicines for Europe’s analysis shows that for almost 700 active pharmaceutical ingredients approved in the U.S., Europe is the sole supplier, underlining the importance of maintaining open trade in medicines and pharmaceutical ingredients.”
Remember: A standard zero-tariff rate was agreed upon by World Trade Organization members more than three decades ago for ethical reasons.
And: This comes as the Council of the EU adopted a pharma package aimed at improving patients’ access to medicines and boosting competitiveness. The package includes eight years of data protection for companies that bring new medicines to market, granting them exclusive rights to pre-clinical tests and clinical trials. You can read the full details here.
BIOTECH ACT
WE MEET AGAIN: Shadow rapporteurs will meet to discuss the Biotech Act as they search for compromise amendments on controversial issues like patent extensions. Officials have been meeting for weeks to comb through the legislation line by line and cut through some 3,000 proposed amendments.
Not what we wanted: The meeting brings together industry representatives, experts and European Commission officials for panels on supplementary protection certificates, clinical trial regulations and financing. But some MEPs aren’t happy that the roundtables are being offered in lieu of an independent study.
But, but, but: Although one official previously told us that the EPRS had considered commissioning an external assessment; however, no one had signed off on a tender due to the timeframe and complexity. Catch up on the full story here.
Advertisement
It’s not just some MEPs who raised questions: Civil society groups have criticized the organizers for not including their voices on the panel. “Sidelining civil society, who would be most affected by the new SPC rules, has left us perplexed,” said Ancel·la Santos Quintano, head of one health at BEUC. “Consumer organisations are happy to engage in the discussions about fairer alternatives to measures that risk delaying the arrival of cheaper medicines on the market, instead of playing gooseberry.”
Unfair: A Parliament official told Morning Health Care that it is a “bit unfair to complain,” and that the organizers needed to be more selective due to time concerns. “Given that the panels only last for one hour each, we couldn't include all organisations that have an opinion on the issue,” they said. “We've always tried to create a very broad spectrum to touch every angle possible.”
Our turn next: “European doctors hope the European Parliament will provide an equally meaningful opportunity for civil society to share its views on the development of the Biotech Act,” said Sarada Das, secretary-general of the Standing Committee of European Doctors.
WHAT WE’RE READING
Reuters: Congo’s Ebola outbreak has eclipsed 8,000 cases.

But in its current form, it risks falling short of providing a meaningful and competitive incentive that can influence company investment decisions. A sufficiently broad scope, combined with flexible, workable and non-cumulative eligibility criteria, could make a significant difference. Under the Commission proposal, an estimated 2,200 additional patients could be enrolled in clinical trials, with 2 additional innovative medicines developed over 15 years. With broader scope and eligibility, this could rise to 24,500 additional places for patients in clinical trials and 18 additional medicines developed in the EU. The estimated impact on healthcare spending of a 12-month extension with broad scope and eligibility? Just 0.07%. Read more.**

articles.title: Overnight Russian attack on Kyiv: explosions heard and fires break out
articles.body:
Overnight Russian attack on Kyiv: explosions heard and fires break out
Air-raid warnings were issued in the city of Kyiv and several Ukrainian oblasts on the night of 28-29 September due to the threat of Russian ballistic missiles. Explosions have been heard in the capital and fires have broken out.
Source: Ukraine's Air Force; alerts.in.ua; Kyiv Oblast Military Administration; Kyiv City Military Administration; Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko
Details: Shortly after midnight, the Air Force warned of a threat of ballistic missiles being used.
Air-raid warnings were issued in the capital and several oblasts.
Quote from the Air Force: "Threat of ballistic missiles being used from Kursk."
Details: At 01:21, the Air Force reported "ballistic missiles heading towards Kyiv".
Explosions were heard in Kyiv.
Update: According to Kyiv City Military Administration, debris fell in an open area in the Solomianskyi district. Information about damage and casualties was being confirmed.
Early reports indicated that a fire had broken out in a non-residential building in the Pecherskyi district.
Quote from Klitschko at 01:57: "Missile debris has fallen in the courtyard of a building in the Solomianskyi district. There is no fire.
A fire has broken out in a three-storey non-residential building in the Pecherskyi district. A strike has hit an office building at an infrastructure facility in the Solomianskyi district. There is no fire."
Details: After 02:00, the missile threat in Kyiv changed to a drone threat.
Quote from Klitschko at 02:05: "A strike and a fire in one of the buildings of an educational institution in the Solomianskyi district have been recorded.
Emergency services are heading to the scene."
Update: At around 02:45, explosions were heard in Kyiv again while an air-raid warning was in effect due to a threat from Russian jet-powered drones.
At around 04:40, explosions were also heard in Kyiv amid the threat from Russian jet-powered drones.
After 05:00, Kyiv City Military Administration reported that a three-storey non-residential building had been damaged in the Pecherskyi district.
In addition, a fire broke out on the roof of a five-storey residential building in the Holosiivskyi district after debris fell onto it. Debris fell onto the grounds of a house in the Solomianskyi district.
Background: Two people were killed and 26 injured in Russian attacks on Kyiv on 28 September.

articles.title: Turkmenistan Strengthens Its Air Defense With Chinese FK-2000 Systems
articles.body:
Turkmenistan publicly demonstrated for the first time the new Chinese FK-2000 anti-aircraft missile and artillery systems (AAMS) in service with the country.
The new systems were displayed during a military parade in Ashgabat marking the 35th anniversary of Turkmenistan’s independence.
Based on published footage of the parade, at least eight FK-2000s can be counted in the mechanized column. However, the official number of systems purchased by Turkmenistan has not yet been disclosed.
In an official Turkmen government statement, the FK-2000 was referred to as a system that was recently introduced into the country’s armed forces.
As the mechanized column passed by, the FK-2000s followed behind Chinese air defense systems that have been in service with Turkmenistan since 2016: the FM-90, KS-1A, and FD-2000.
The parade marked the first official confirmation of the FK-2000’s service with the Turkmen armed forces.
The FK-2000 is a Chinese self-propelled air defense missile system designed to destroy cruise missiles, high-precision air-to-ground munitions, air-to-ground missiles, unmanned aerial vehicles, and aircraft.
The system was publicly unveiled for the first time at the Airshow China international aerospace exhibition in Zhuhai in 2021.
The FK-2000 air defense missile system consists of a self-propelled air defense missile launcher on an 8×8 wheeled chassis, equipped with an unmanned combat turret.
The system can engage aircraft at ranges of 1.2 to 25 km and cruise missiles at ranges of 1.2-10 km.
The turret houses 12 anti-aircraft guided missiles with an independent elevation mechanism, while close-in air defense is provided by two 30-mm six-barrel cannons.
Also in January, these anti-aircraft systems were spotted in service with the Sudanese anti-government group Rapid Support Forces (RSF).

articles.title: Mediators push for US-Iran deal as hurdles remain
articles.body:
Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi speaks to the media during the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly at United Nations headquarters, Friday, Sept. 25, 2026. (AP Photo)
Mediators on Sept. 29 continued to work with Iran and the United States on trying to broker a deal to end the fighting and open the Strait of Hormuz, three regional officials and two U.S. officials told the media, but major hurdles remain between the sides.
The indirect talks come as the conflict, which is entering its eighth month, has caused global economic damage and badly battered Iran. Multiple efforts to allow safe shipping on one of the world’s most crucial waterways have failed.
The officials divulged that the behind-the-scenes efforts continue even after U.S. President Donald Trump initially said he spurned an Iranian proposal to reopen the strait in a week if the U.S. agreed to lift its blockade of Iranian ports, release frozen Iranian assets and waive sanctions on Iranian oil sales, among other conditions.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, who stayed in New York after last week’s gathering of world leaders at the U.N. General Assembly, will meet with Qatari mediators on Sept. 28 about the latest discussions, Iranian state media reported Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmail Baghaei as saying.
Despite Trump’s often bellicose rhetoric, he is open to pursuing a non-military resolution to the conflict if one can be achieved, a senior U.S. official said.
But the Trump administration will not reach a deal with Tehran until nuclear issues are addressed, another U.S. official said.
Trump is willing to grant sanctions relief to Iran, along with the release of some frozen funds, for concrete progress on nuclear issues, and while Iran has indicated it is flexible on nuclear issues, the sides are far apart on timing and which side makes the first moves, the official said.
Two of the regional officials speaking to the Associated Press confirmed that mediators are working with both sides on a proposal that would include reopening the strait and lifting the U.S. blockade and then removing sanctions.
According to the draft text being discussed, the strait would reopen in accordance with a separate deal that Iran has been discussing with Oman, on the other side of the strait, and it would include no tolls, something Tehran has pursued.
That deal seeks to temporarily manage shipping traffic on what was seen as an international waterway before the war.
One regional official said the U.S. is seeking Iranian concessions on nuclear issues that include allowing inspectors to enter the country. Under the memorandum of understanding the two sides signed in June that collapsed within days, Iran’s nuclear program was meant to be discussed over a 60-day period.
The U.S. officials say the United States is skeptical about whether Iran can be persuaded to ultimately reach Trump’s conditions for a deal and would be serious about any promises it makes, especially after it broke the interim deal by firing on commercial ships in the Strait of Hormuz.
U.S. officials feel their position is getting stronger as Tehran feels the impact of sanctions.

articles.title: NATO to strengthen lower-cost counter-drone defenses, Rutte says
articles.body:
Necva Tastan Sevinc
29 September 2026•Update: 29 September 2026
NATO will strengthen lower-cost counter-drone defenses so it does not have to deploy advanced fighter jets against inexpensive threats, Secretary General Mark Rutte said Tuesday.
“We will strengthen cheaper counter-drone defenses so we are not using high-end jets against low-cost threats,” Rutte said at a joint news conference with Lithuanian Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevicius at NATO headquarters.
He said repeated drone incidents along the alliance’s eastern flank showed how the threat was evolving. NATO was reinforcing its integrated air and missile defenses through a “multilayered, 360-degree approach” and adapting its posture against drones through initiatives such as Drone Edge, he added.
Rutte cited an incident two weeks ago in which Italian jets deployed by NATO from Lithuania’s Siauliai Air Base shot down a drone that had violated Lithuanian airspace, calling it “collective defense in action.”
Sinkevicius said air defense and preparedness on NATO’s eastern flank were among the main topics of their talks. He said Lithuania remained on track to host a permanently deployed German brigade by the end of 2027.
The two leaders also reaffirmed support for Ukraine. Rutte said Russia’s hostile actions were intended to weaken NATO’s resolve, but pledged that the alliance would “do even more for Ukraine, and not less.”

articles.title: Russia's Kremlin says it does not want Iran to leave nuclear non-proliferation treaty
articles.body:
Russia does not want Iran to quit the nuclear non-proliferation treaty and counts on it remaining a party to the agreement, the Kremlin said on Tuesday.
This follows Iranian Parliament Vice Speaker Ali Nikzad stating that Tehran is considering withdrawing from the NPT, including that the parliament will review a “triple-urgency” motion to do so.
Nikzad reportedly stated that Tehran, which became a party to the treaty in March 1970, has no trust in the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), or IAEA chief Rafael Grossi, because he conducts “merely superficial inspections and submits negative reports against Iran.”
Russia and Iran have close ties under a strategic cooperation treaty.
"Moscow views the NPT as the cornerstone of the nuclear non-proliferation regime and hopes that Tehran remains a responsible party to the treaty," Peskov said, according to Russia's official TASS news agency.
Iran 'has no plans to develop nuclear weapons,' Russia's Peskov says
"Our [Iranian] friends and partners constantly affirm at various levels that Iran is not developing nuclear weapons and has no plans to do so," Peskov added.
"On the contrary, Iran is committed to its obligations under the non-proliferation regime. At the same time, it remains committed to developing such an important economic sector as peaceful nuclear energy within the country," Peskov stated.

articles.title: Pentagon awards RTX's Raytheon $20.7 billion contract for AMRAAM missiles amid stockpile concerns
articles.body:
Pentagon awards RTX’s Raytheon $26.4 billion contract for AMRAAM missiles amid stockpile concerns
- The Pentagon awarded RTX’s Raytheon a $26.4 billion contract to speed up AMRAAM missile production amid concerns over depleted stockpiles from Middle East and Ukraine conflicts.
- AMRAAM missiles support air-to-air combat and air defence systems like NASAMS, used by the US and over a dozen allied countries, including Ukraine and Qatar.
- The deal aims to increase output as part of the "Arsenal of Freedom" initiative, with RTX planning to produce at least 1,900 missiles annually from 2026, pending Congressional funding.
AI generated
WASHINGTON - The Pentagon awarded RTX’s Raytheon business a provisional multiyear contract worth US$20.7 billion (S$26.44 billion) to accelerate production of AMRAAM missiles, as the military pushes to replenish stockpiles depleted by conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine.
The US has supplied large quantities of weapons to allies while also using munitions in its own military operations in Iran, raising concerns about inventories of key air defence and precision-guided weapons.
The AMRAAM is used in air-to-air jet fighter combat as well as in the National Advanced Surface-to-Air Missile System (NASAMS), which is used to defend the Washington area and is used by more than a dozen other countries, including Ukraine, Oman and Qatar.
The prospective AMRAAM deal is the latest in a series of large munitions contracts the Pentagon has pursued this year to pressure contractors into ramping output up faster.
The award follows a similar pattern to a US$58.6 billion Patriot interceptor deal awarded to Lockheed Martin in July, a seven-year procurement plan running through fiscal 2032.
As with that contract, industry executives have cautioned that Congress has not yet appropriated the funding needed to support the full multiyear commitment, meaning contractors may be unable to invest at scale in components and facilities until lawmakers act.
The production agreements are designed to entice contractors to move faster on increasing output, part of a broader push by the Trump administration to prioritise weapons production over shareholder returns.
The contract, if Congress ultimately appropriates the funds, would let RTX continue to invest in its workforce, supply chain and facilities as US demand surges.
The company said it nearly doubled AMRAAM production in 2025, compared with the prior year.
The deal would be part of the Pentagon’s “Arsenal of Freedom” initiative.
RTX said earlier in 2026 it would set an annual production goal of at least 1,900 AMRAAM missiles. REUTERS

articles.title: WATCH: IDF strikes in Gaza, killing Hamas Northern Brigade commander, top military financer
articles.body:
The IDF and Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency) eliminated Hamas Northern Gaza Brigade commander Izz al-Din Beik in a strike in the northern Gaza Strip overnight Tuesday, the military announced on Tuesday.
Beik had served as commander of the brigade since the elimination of his predecessor, Ahmed Ghandour, and had previously served as the brigade’s military intelligence chief, according to the IDF.
In his role, Beik was responsible for managing the activities of Hamas terrorists in northern Gaza and directing efforts to carry out attacks against IDF troops and Israeli civilians, the military said. He was also involved in efforts to rebuild the brigade’s capabilities after they were severely damaged during the war.
The IDF said Beik posed an immediate threat to IDF troops and Israeli civilians and was eliminated in a precise aerial strike.
Prior to the strike, the military said it took steps to mitigate the risk to civilians, including using precise munitions and aerial surveillance.
Predecessor killed shortly after October 7
Ghandour, Beik’s predecessor, was killed in an Israeli strike in November 2023. He had been a member of Hamas’s military council and was responsible for directing the terrorist organization’s activities in northern Gaza. His death was part of a broader operation that targeted senior commanders in Hamas’s Northern Gaza Brigade.
Additionally, the IDF carried out a separate strike against a Hamas financial operative in Gaza City.
The IDF said it eliminated Shadi Abu Hasira, a key money exchanger for Hamas’s military wing, in an aerial strike on Monday.
According to the military, Abu Hasira headed the “Geneva” money exchange network, which transferred tens of millions of shekels in foreign currency to Hamas’s military wing.
The funds were used to finance terrorists, restore military infrastructure, and advance attacks against IDF troops, the IDF said.
Abu Hasira was also involved in commercial activity in the Gaza Strip and managed a company called Gardena Professional, which the military said facilitated his money-transfer operations.
The IDF said Abu Hasira had recently been involved in advancing attacks against IDF troops and Israeli civilians and in efforts to restore Hamas’s capabilities, which the military described as a systematic violation of the ceasefire.
As in the strike targeting Beik, the military said it used precise munitions and aerial surveillance to mitigate harm to civilians before targeting Abu Hasira.

articles.title: Europe’s businesses are paying for Russia’s hybrid war
articles.body:
Police investigators work on the tarmac with a robot that is capable, among other things, of defusing explosives, near a Ukrainian Antonov cargo plane at Leipzig/Halle Airport in Germany on Aug. 5, 2026. | Jens Schlueter/Getty Images
Elisabeth Braw is a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council, author of the award-winning “Goodbye Globalization” and a regular columnist for POLITICO. Her new book, “The Undersea War,” is out Oct. 8.
Plots against defense executives, a series of arson attacks against private companies and warehouses, and explosive drones at Germany’s Leipzig/Halle Airport.
Had any of these worked as intended, they would have caused immense damage, not to mention claimed lives.
Advertisement
This is the situation plaguing Europe today, faced as it is with a proliferation of gray-zone attacks. And while a definitive response from the continent is yet to materialize, the bloc has finally started to name and address the hybrid war it’s been pulled into. No, summits and statements won’t thwart attacks, but acknowledgement is famously the first step to recovery.
It was only a miracle that saved workers at Leipzig airport when, on Aug. 4, an approaching drone landed poorly and lost its load of explosives. Had things gone to plan, it would have exploded next to a Ukrainian Antonov plane ready for departure, causing immense damage to a busy airport servicing the people and businesses of large parts of Germany. (Investigators later found a second drone laden with military-grade explosives right next to the airport.)
But who would want to maim and kill airport users? On Sept. 1, the German government announced it had determined Russia was behind the attack.
German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt and Saxony’s Interior Minister Armin Schuster arrive for a news conference at Leipzig/Halle Airport on Aug. 5, 2026. | Jens Schlueter/Getty Images
Years ago, European governments would have preferred not to publicly attribute such reckless incidents because with attribution comes the need to respond. But this time Germany openly identified the Kremlin as the instigator, showing just how seriously Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s government is taking the incident.
That’s because the failed drone explosion is only the latest in a series of sinister activity of which Germany has been a particular target.
Just before the country’s national election in 2025, the exhaust pipes of hundreds of cars were sabotaged across the country, and stickers calling for people to vote for the Greens attached to their windows. While that last touch suggested environmental activists were behind the campaign, the perpetrators were later identified as agents working on Russia’s behalf.
Advertisement
A couple of months earlier, a parcel — which turned out to contain a bomb — caught fire at DHL’s depot at Leipzig/Halle Airport. The perpetrators of this event, too, were later found to be working for Russia. And a few months before that, German authorities uncovered a Russian assassination plot against arms manufacturer Rheinmetall’s CEO.
You all know about these cases, not just because I’ve written about them on these pages but because they were so brazen. And Germany is not the only country to see all manner of businesses — and even business executives — targeted by geopolitically linked strikes. The U.K. has been hit by arson, as have Poland, the Czech Republic and other European countries.
In September 2025, objects in the skies above airports in Denmark and Norway forced temporary closures. Drones keep appearing around Scottish offshore installations. Numerous Swedish communication masts have sustained suspicious damage. And in the Baltic Sea, there has been a string of suspicious cable and pipeline incidents.
The Eagle S oil tanker is escorted by a tugboat to the Port of Kilpilahti in the Gulf of Finland on Dec. 28, 2024. | Vesa Moilanen/Lehtikuva/AFP via Getty Images
So far, none of these incidents have caused devastating damage — though a 2024 arson attack subsequently attributed to Russia destroyed Poland’s largest shopping mall. But each attempt costs the affected businesses money. Each piece of sabotaged infrastructure incurs repair costs and operational losses. Each disruption causes delays and further expenses. In fact, most targeted companies have seen their operations disrupted, which means additional financial hits.
In the case of the undersea cables struck by anchors, the owners were left with significant repair bills. For power cables, repairs typically run into the tens of millions of euros. Each incident also costs personnel time. Had the Leipzig drones or parcel bombs exploded, the financial losses — and, of course, the human losses — would have been extremely painful.
Even a relatively small incident can leave the target facing significant damage: Last month WB Group, a Polish drone-component manufacturer, was subject to an arson attack and incurred losses of at least €3.5 million. Polish prosecutors believe the attack was, again, instigated by Russia.
Advertisement
But when all this happens, who foots the bill?
If the companies are lucky, their insurers will. However, standard insurance only covers standard perils. It doesn’t cover war-like acts, which is what geopolitically linked acts of harm amount to. At least that’s what many standard insurers are unsurprisingly contending. And while specialized war insurers do offer coverage for war, doing so involves having to decide what exactly constitutes war-like acts.
The most detailed discussion of this fundamental question isn’t taking place at think tanks or universities. They’re taking place in the insurance industry, as vast amounts of money are at stake. And this — rendering European companies’ operations financially unsustainable — may, in fact, be Russia’s objective.
Surveillance drone models from WB Group are displayed during the MSPO International Defence Industry Exhibition in Kielce, Poland on Sept. 8, 2026. | Omar Marques/Getty Images
Credit to the German government for convening the Baltic Sea Security Summit in August to accelerate European nations’ response to a discreditable and dangerous form of geopolitical score-settling, and for calling the Kremlin out.
Now, how will these subversive attacks on European companies continue to unfold? You will have to find out without me, as this is my farewell as a columnist for POLITICO. It has been an immense pleasure and honor to have your company. Arrivederci!
POLITICO occasionally publishes opinion pieces from guest authors to offer our readers a range of perspectives on the intersection of power and politics. The views expressed are those of the authors and do not reflect the views of POLITICO.

Iranian women take up arms amid US threats (VIDEO)
Iranian women have been flocking to Imam Hossein Square in central Tehran to receive basic military and first-aid training as part of the ‘Sacrifice for Iran’ campaign.

The number of civilian volunteers, including dozens of women, enrolling in the training course has risen recently amid renewed threats from US President Donald Trump, RT’s Saman Kojouri reports from Tehran.

articles.title: Airmen, Guardians Told to Select Religion Code from New Consolidated List
articles.body:
Active-Duty Airmen and Guardians have until mid-October to update their personnel records with their religious preference using the Pentagon’s new consolidated list of Religious Affiliation Codes, according to a recent Department of the Air Force announcement.
The new list of codes—ordered by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth—slashed the number of religions specified in the Pentagon’s HR systems from more than 200 to roughly 30. Officials said in June that the consolidation was necessary to streamline the number of religious preferences for service members and shape the chaplain corps to support them.
The consolidation process collapsed roughly 170 denominations of Christianity down to 21 and includes widespread non-Christian religions such as Buddhism, Hindu, Islam, and Judaism, among other faiths. It removes Wicca, paganism, and other nontraditional faiths from the list, replacing them with an “Other Religious” category.
The department directs all Active-Duty members of the Air Force and Space Force to select their new Religious Affiliation Code in the Virtual Military Personnel Flight system and certify their record of emergency data is accurate by Oct. 16, the announcement states. Members of the Air Force Reserve and Air National Guard have until Nov. 9 to update their records.
“Transitioning to these standardized codes ensures our chaplain corps has the accurate demographic data they need to provide tailored resources and support to our service members, while continuing to respect their individual convictions,” Richard Anderson, assistant secretary of the Air Force for manpower and reserve affairs, said in the announcement.
Airmen and Guardians who fail to update their RAC before the deadline will have their records automatically updated to a selection that aligns with the new RAC list. For example, paganism would likely fall under the “Other Religions” category, according to an Air Force official.
Individual Airmen and Guardians, however, will not be limited by the new RAC list for the purposes of identifying their religious preference on the ID tags or “dog tags” they wear around their necks. The tags can be vital for helping chaplains determine the religious needs of service members wounded in battle.
Hegseth announced the effort to consolidate the list of religious preferences in a March 24 video on social media, calling the older list of Faith and Belief Codes “impractical and unusable.” Hegseth also directed chaplains to replace their rank insignia with their appropriate religious affiliation insignia in an effort to make them more approachable to younger service members. The announcement came six months after Hegseth singled out paganism in September 2025 because some troops have petitioned for religious exemptions so they could grow beards.
“If you want a beard, you can join Special Forces,” Heseth told hundreds of general officers at Quantico, Va., last Sept. 30. “If not, then shave. We don’t have a military full of Nordic pagans, but unfortunately, we have had leaders who either refuse to call BS and enforce standards, or leaders who felt like they were not allowed to enforce standards.”
Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell has argued the new consolidated RAC list is not intended to provide a list of “officially approved” religions. Rather it is “designed to allow chaplains to quickly look at the religious composition of their units and determine how they structure resources to best provide for warfighters of all faith groups,” Parnell wrote in a June 5 social media post.

articles.title: British authorities continue to investigate a suspected terrorist plot; foreign involvement not ruled out
articles.body:
British police have announced an investigation into whether other countries were involved in the alleged planning of a terrorist attack against a Royal Air Force (RAF) base, noting that the suspects are being released on bail, Reuters reports.
All five suspects are British citizens living in London, aged over 20; they were detained early on the morning of the 27th of September after a local farmer alerted police to three suspicious vans heading toward the RAF base. The Fairford base is also used by the US Air Force, serving as a stopover for American military aircraft en route to Iran. In July, the Iranian military stated that the base was a legitimate target.
Laurence Taylor, head of the British police counter-terrorism unit, stated that the men have been released under strict bail conditions. Speaking to reporters, Taylor emphasized that this does not mean the investigation has ended; it is ongoing and proceeding along multiple lines of inquiry. US President Donald Trump told reporters at the White House on the 28th of September that the incident could be linked to Iran, adding that he would not have released the detained men. US Senator Marco Rubio stated—without providing further details—that foreign agents of influence were involved. He told Fox News that the events that nearly unfolded in Great Britain over the weekend constituted a very serious situation and that foreign involvement was evident.
A source close to the investigation told Reuters that an Iran-related motive is considered the most likely, though Russian-orchestrated sabotage or an Islamist terrorist plot has not been ruled out. The Iranian Embassy in London has categorically denied Tehran’s involvement, condemning the speculation as baseless and malicious.
Taylor did not explicitly mention Iran but acknowledged significant interest in whether the current geopolitical climate is linked to the incident. He stated that
the matter is being examined from every possible angle,
including the possibility that the incident involved proxies or individuals acting—knowingly or unknowingly—on behalf of another state. Taylor reported that three white vans are undergoing a comprehensive search, with support provided by army and forensic experts, and a large police presence remains at the scene.
On the 27th of September, Trump stated that the suspects had intended to cause significant harm, and their role is being investigated by both British and American authorities. However, doubts have been raised in the British media regarding the quality of surveillance, given that the men managed to get so close to the base. A source linked to the investigation noted that, although security levels around the RAF base are high, the arrests were not led by intelligence agencies, suggesting that authorities were unaware of an elevated risk.
The farmer who alerted the police said she saw a group of men wearing hoods and face masks running across a field. She believes she saw up to ten individuals at the scene. British Defence Secretary Wes Streeting noted that she had witnessed only part of the incident but did not provide further details. He added that he is aware of the desire of Iran and its allies to cause harm, and that he knows Tehran hates democracy. Following the arrests at Fairford, the US Embassy issued a security alert, advising US citizens to exercise heightened caution and remain vigilant regarding their personal safety. Security levels have been raised at other US-used bases in the UK.
