articles.title: Denmark Purchases Batch of Dropla 4×4 UGVs from Ukrainian-Danish Company
articles.body:
Denmark has purchased nine Dropla 4×4 unmanned ground vehicles to train unmanned systems operators.
According to the Danish Ministry of Defense, the new vehicles were delivered to the Danish Defence Drone Centre (Forsvarets Dronecenter), where they will be used, among other things, to train conscripts operating unmanned systems.
The supplier was the Danish company Dropla, founded by Ukrainians. The company operates in Denmark and has activities and partnerships in Ukraine.
The procurement is part of a Danish Ministry of Defense Acquisition and Logistics Organization (FMI) program to test unmanned ground vehicles and gain operational experience with them.
Earlier this year, the agency purchased eight more UGVs for the Royal Danish Army, which were tested in various operational scenarios.
Before being selected, the Dropla 4×4 underwent intensive testing in Denmark.
In particular, on September 1, 2026, Ukrainian unmanned systems manufacturers took part in Innovation Day 2026 at the Hevring training range in Denmark.
The Ukrainian-Danish company Dropla Tech also participated in the event. Viacheslav Shvaidak, its co-founder and CEO, shared that the company participated in Innovation Day and Range Day.
Denmark plans to use the Dropla 4×4 for more than just training. Drawing on Ukrainian combat experience and the results of UGV testing in Denmark, FMI is already exploring the possibility of equipping the vehicles with additional equipment.
This includes remotely controlled weapon stations and communications equipment.
The agency says the new vehicles will help Denmark gain experience operating unmanned ground systems and determine how to use them in the military in the future.
The Dropla 4×4 universal unmanned ground vehicle is designed to perform logistics, evacuation, and specialized missions in hazardous environments.
The robot features an electric powertrain and a welded self-supporting steel structure. The UGV can carry up to 150 kg of cargo. Its modular platform allows it to transport equipment, ammunition, engineering tools, and other cargo. The system is also designed for casualty evacuation.
For route monitoring, the robot has independent digital front- and rear-view cameras. An onboard computing module is installed, while ELRS, LTE, and Starlink Mini provide communications. Starlink Mini integration enables operation via a beyond-line-of-sight (BLOS) satellite communications link.
According to the stated specifications, the Dropla UGV has a range of at least 40 km and can operate continuously for at least four hours. Its maximum speed is at least 20 km/h on roads and 15 km/h off-road. The robot has a clearance of up to 340 mm.
The UGV measures 1,580 × 1,120 × 1,570 mm and weighs 350 kg. It is equipped with a 180 Ah LiNiCoMnO₂ battery in a 14S configuration.
The developers identify the UGV’s main applications as logistical support for forward units, casualty evacuation, transportation of EW and communications equipment, deployment of reconnaissance and sensor systems, and delivery of ammunition and engineering equipment.
The robot can also operate in mined, dangerous, or exposed areas where using conventional vehicles or deploying service members would create additional risks.

articles.title: Denmark buys Ukrainian-founded firm’s ground drones
articles.body:
- Denmark bought nine Dropla 4x4 unmanned ground vehicles to train drone operators, including conscripts, at the Danish Defence Drone Center.
- The vehicles were delivered without weapon mounts, and Denmark is studying adding remote weapon stations and communications equipment.
Denmark’s armed forces have taken delivery of nine unmanned ground vehicles built by Dropla, a Danish company founded by Ukrainians, to train drone operators, including conscripts, at the country’s military drone center.
Denmark’s defense procurement agency, known by its Danish initials FMI, bought the Dropla 4×4 vehicles for the Danish Defence Drone Center, the agency said Sept. 28. An unmanned ground vehicle, or UGV, is a vehicle that drives itself or is steered remotely with no crew aboard. The agency did not disclose the price of the order or when the vehicles arrived.
The Danish version of the Dropla 4×4 was delivered without a weapon mount. FMI said it is already studying how to fit the vehicles with extra equipment such as a remotely operated weapon station, which lets a soldier aim and fire a machine gun from a safe distance, and new communications gear. The agency said those plans draw on lessons from the war in Ukraine and on its own trials of other UGVs in Denmark.
Colonel Thomas Øgendahl Knudsen, who heads FMI’s land division, said unmanned systems are developing quickly, so the Danish military needs to build experience with them and bring them into soldier training now. He said the new vehicles let the drone center work with ground drones while exploring how the technology could be used across the armed forces in the future.
The purchase is FMI’s second batch of UGVs this year. Earlier in 2026, the agency bought eight unmanned ground vehicles for the Danish Army, which FMI said have since been tested in a range of operational scenarios with strong results.
Dropla Tech was founded in 2023 by four Ukrainian entrepreneurs and is headquartered in Odense, Denmark, with its engineering and operations teams working in Ukraine. The company is best known for Blue Eyes, an artificial intelligence system that detects mines, improvised explosive devices and loitering drones without needing a cloud connection. Dropla says the system has confirmed more than 5,000 explosive threats in Ukraine.
The company builds two modular UGV platforms, the Dropla 4×4 and Dropla 6×6. Both can be configured for casualty evacuation, cargo delivery, reconnaissance, remote weapon stations and counter-drone missions. Dropla has also signed an agreement with Ukrainian company Frontline Robotics to integrate its Burya weapon turret onto the vehicles.
The Danish military has worked with Dropla before. During a six-month innovation project that ended this summer, the armed forces tested a Dropla prototype built for evacuation and logistics. That vehicle started out with four wheels but was fitted with two more on the military’s recommendation to make it more stable.
Dropla raised €2.4 million ($2.7 million) in 2025 from investors including Denmark’s state Export and Investment Fund, and in July 2026 it received an undisclosed investment from U.S.-Ukrainian group MITS Capital. The company says it wants to scale production to as many as 3,000 UGVs a year.

articles.title: UK police release men on bail for airbase incident, US surprised
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
UK police release on bail five men held over airbase incident, 'surprising' the US
British police said Monday five men arrested near an airbase used by the United States were released on bail, as Washington asserted a "foreign actor" was involved in the suspected bomb plot.
US President Donald Trump, speaking in Washington, said he was "surprised that they released them", adding that "I wouldn't have done that".
For his part, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Monday that a suspected bomb plot near a UK airbase used by the United States was the work of a "foreign actor."
"It's one that clearly involves the hands of a foreign actor," Rubio told Sean Hannity on broadcaster Fox News in an interview Monday, adding that he would not go into further detail.
The release of the five—all London-based Britons in their mid-20s—came as British Prime Minister Andy Burnham announced an emergency meeting of top officials to ensure they have "the full picture".
Earlier, Iran had denied involvement in any plot to target the Royal Air Force (RAF) Fairford base in Gloucestershire, southwest England, following the security scare there early Sunday.
Here's what we know so far:
Counter-terror probe
UK counter-terror police are leading the investigation after authorities received reports Sunday of three "suspicious" white vans near the airbase, which has been used by the United States to bomb Iran.
Police said in their latest update Monday that the five men held, who all live in inner London boroughs, were being released on bail.
"This does not mean the investigation is over," Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor, the head of Counter Terrorism Policing, said, adding the five would be subject to "stringent" bail conditions.
He said officers were "considering this from every possible angle, including that this may be activity committed by proxies, or individuals either knowingly or unknowingly, working on behalf of a foreign state".
The men were arrested on suspicion of explosives offences and "preparation of a terrorist act" under UK anti-terrorism laws, according to police.
They had been travelling in the three suspect vehicles, which have since been subject to "extensive examination, with the support of military assets and forensic experts".
Bomb-disposal team
Authorities have not confirmed details of the threat but bomb-disposal experts were seen working at the scene.
The Daily Mail and Press Association both reported late Monday they understood from sources that tests on materials in the back of the vans established they were "not viable explosives".
A farmer living in the village of Whelford near the airbase said she rang the police after seeing the vans blocking a road and a group of masked men.
The anonymous woman told media on Monday that she believed the police had "dropped the ball" on the threat.
But UK Defence Minister Wes Streeting said the farmer only had a "partial picture".
Iran denies involvement
Trump said on Sunday that Britain and United States had had the suspects "under investigation" for a while and alleged "they were looking to do big damage to our fort".
After hearing news of their bail, Trump said Monday the case "might be" linked to Iran but declined to elaborate.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the incident "clearly involves the hands of a foreign actor", without giving further details.
Iran's embassy in London said on X that it "categorically rejects and strongly condemns" the "unfounded and malicious speculations" that Tehran was involved.
US bombers
Britain gave the United States permission in March to use Fairford for "specific defensive operations into Iran" to destroy Iranian missiles at source.
US bombers and other planes have since been seen taking off and landing from the base—the only one on Britain's mainland used for this purpose.
Residents in the rural Cotswolds area surrounding Fairford said the site, which hosts a range of US military equipment and personnel, had seen increased activity and security in recent months.
Authorities evacuated around 85 households from the village early on Sunday, and they were allowed to return home the next day.
Tehran has previously warned London against allowing its bases to be used by the United States in operations against Iran.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has accused London of "putting British lives in danger" by allowing the bases to be used "for aggression against Iran".

articles.title: Iran nearing completion of key rail link key for India’s gateway to Eurasia
articles.body:
Iran nearing completion of key rail link key for India’s gateway to Eurasia
Iran has completed laying track on the southern stretch of the Chabahar-Zahedan railway, closing a key gap in a route designed to connect the port of Chabahar on the Gulf of Oman to Zahedan near the Afghan border. 
Iranian railway official Abbas Khatibi said last week that tracks had been laid for the crucial 480km stretch between Chabahar and Khash, and currently the priority is to complete the stations on the route, Tasnim news agency reported. 
The Chabahar–Zahedan link stretches 630 km, or 735 km including branch lines. With the northern sections already linked to the existing rail network, the Iranian authorities are now preparing it for operation. 
The Chabahar–Zahedan link is an extension of the larger International North–South Transport Corridor (INSTC), backed by India, Iran and Russia. The project has been in the making for decades because of its huge infrastructure requirements and has also been slowed by Western sanctions on both Iran and Russia. 
The milestone comes as the Middle East conflict has disrupted traditional transport and energy routes across the region. Chabahar has direct access to the Indian Ocean without requiring ships to pass through the Strait of Hormuz, a major chokepoint affected by the conflict.
Strategic Step: Iran Completes Chabahar-Zahedan Rail Link – Connecting Central Asia to Indian Ocean
The major infrastructure project looks set to become fully operational within 3-4 months with final safety checks for the route underway. (Economic Times)
The route connects… pic.twitter.com/pUKsSzJEJq
For India, the Chabahar-Zahedan link strengthens a trade route that reaches Afghanistan and Central Asia without transiting Pakistan. Cargo arriving by sea at Chabahar would be able to move inland through Iran’s rail and road network toward landlocked regional markets. 
India’s role in Chabahar is complicated by US sanctions. A conditional waiver covering the project, in which India invested around $120 million, expired in April. New Delhi maintained it was discussing the issue with both Tehran and Washington, describing the regional conflict as a “complicating factor.” 
In July, the conflict touched Chabahar itself, when US forces struck a surveillance tower at the neighboring Shahid Kalantari terminal linked to the project. India said the terminal was not damaged.

articles.title: Sudan demands UN action against external backers of rebels
articles.body:
Sudan demands UN action against external backers of rebels
Sudan has called for international action against foreign parties supporting the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) opposing the government, and accused the UN Security Council of failing to identify and condemn the group’s sponsors.
Sudanese Foreign Minister Mohieldin Salim Ahmed Ibrahim made the appeal at the UN General Assembly in New York on Monday, saying external support for the RSF was prolonging the war.
“Pressure must be exerted on the regional sponsors and certain neighboring states,” Ibrahim said.
The foreign minister accused unnamed countries of allowing weapons and supplies to reach the RSF through their territory and enabling attacks by the paramilitary group and mercenaries to be launched from outside Sudan’s borders. He also claimed hospitals had been established in neighboring states to treat wounded RSF fighters.
Ibrahim said the UN Security Council had failed to identify and condemn the RSF’s sponsors, which he accused of recruiting foreign mercenaries, providing political backing to the paramilitary group and financing media platforms spreading what he described as “disinformation” against the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF).
Sudan has previously accused the United Arab Emirates (UAE) of providing military support to the RSF, allegations Abu Dhabi has repeatedly denied. Khartoum has also accused neighboring Ethiopia of allowing its territory to be used for drone attacks against Sudan, a claim Addis Ababa has rejected.
The accusations come weeks after a UN fact-finding mission found reasonable grounds to believe that a transnational network had supplied the RSF with weapons, logistics, training and foreign personnel. Investigators identified private entities and intermediaries operating from countries including the UAE, with transit routes through Chad, southeastern Libya and Somalia.
Ibrahim said peace would require the RSF to be disarmed and its weapons to remain under the control of state institutions. He also called for attacks on civilians and infrastructure to end.
Sudan plunged into a civil war three years ago after a struggle for power broke out between the SAF and the RSF.
Sudan descended into chaos in April 2023 when fighting erupted between the national army (Sudanese Armed Forces, SAF) and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF). This occurred after months of tension between their commanders, army generals Abdel Fattah al-Burhan and Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo ‘Hemedti’, respectively, over a planned transition to civilian rule. What began in the capital, Khartoum, as a power struggle has devastated the country, killing tens of thousands and displacing millions.
Regional and international peace efforts, including African Union mediation and Saudi–US talks in Jeddah, have repeatedly stalled. Sudanese officials have named Colombians and Ukrainians among mercenaries backing the RSF against the army. Officials have also accused Ukraine and the United Arab Emirates of involvement and recently claimed the European Union has an “incomplete understanding of the complex situation” in the country.
Khartoum has also accused authorities in neighboring Kenya of backing the RSF and has broken ties with the East African grouping IGAD amid mistrust of regional mediation. In July, TASIS, a political coalition aligned with the paramilitary, announced the formation of a rival government months after its members signed a charter in Nairobi. It named Gen. Dagalo as chairman of a 15-member presidential council, a move rejected by the UN and AU.
The RSF was originally established by the Sudanese government under former President Omar al-Bashir in 2013, drawing heavily on the Janjaweed militias that Khartoum had used to fight rebels in Darfur. Its status was later formalized by law before tensions with the regular army erupted into open warfare.
Diplomatic efforts to end the war have intensified on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York. Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov discussed ways to resolve the conflict with his Sudanese counterpart last week, while the African Union and the US called for an immediate humanitarian truce followed by a durable ceasefire and a Sudanese-led political process.
Washington does not regard either side as representing legitimate constitutional rule in Sudan. Khartoum strongly rejected the US position, calling for respect for the country’s sovereignty and national institutions and warning against legitimizing the RSF through force.

articles.title: Poland eases rules; will shoot down airspace violators more quickly
articles.body:
On the 28th of September, Polish Deputy Defense Minister Cezary Tomczyk announced that Poland plans to simplify the procedure for shooting down objects that have entered its airspace without authorization, Politico reports.
Tensions between Warsaw and Moscow are palpable following repeated Russian violations of Polish airspace in recent weeks, and this decision could cause them to escalate further. Speaking to reporters, Tomczyk explained that pilots currently must not only rely on radar readings but also establish visual contact with an object before shooting it down; this entails flying up to the target to identify exactly what it is.
Now, the Polish Ministry of Defense plans to scrap the visual identification requirement. Tomczyk noted that, once the changes are implemented, a pilot or commander will be able to decide whether to shoot down an object based solely on radar data. The new rules will save time, meaning
Polish fighter jets will be able to shoot down drones and missiles coming from Russia more quickly.
On the 23rd of September, a Russian Mi-8 helicopter briefly entered Polish airspace from the Königsberg region. It penetrated about 300 meters into Polish airspace and remained there for 42 seconds. Poland responded by scrambling fighter jets. The Polish Operational Command commented on the incident, noting that Russia was once again testing the readiness of Poland’s air defenses.
Poland has previously shot down drones that entered its airspace. Around this time last year, Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski stated that Poland would shoot down Russian fighter jets if they crossed the airspace border, adding that the Russians had been warned.

articles.title: BNN IN FOCUS | Political party review: Latvia First – it has the votes, but will it find coalition partners?
articles.body:
Ainārs Šlesers’ Latvia First (LPV) is among the parties that do not have to worry about entering the 15th Saeima. In the September SKDS poll, 9.2% of surveyed Latvian citizens said they would vote for LPV. This is the third-highest result, behind the United List and Sovereign Power/Young Latvians. Equally important is the fact that LPV has candidates capable of appealing to different groups of voters. However, no matter how strong its polling numbers may be, they do not automatically translate into a place in government.
LPV is heading into the election with parliamentary experience and politicians who, so to speak, “know the ropes”. Among its most prominent parliamentary initiatives during the 14th Saeima – proposals that are also included in its current election programme – are allowing people to withdraw their second-pillar pension savings; abolishing property tax on a person’s only home; introducing a reduced VAT rate not only for vegetables but also for bread, milk, meat and sausages; reducing VAT on infant formula and nappies; and introducing a 5,000-euro benefit for every newborn child, among other measures.
Although these initiatives did not receive support in the Saeima, they demonstrated that LPV consistently promotes its key issues and values, including traditional family values, and is capable of maintaining a high public profile. However, if LPV becomes a governing party and wants to deliver on its promises, the ability to criticise will no longer be enough. It will have to secure majority support, agree on the order in which decisions are implemented and take into account the limits of the state budget.
It should be recalled that in the 2025 Riga City Council election, LPV won 18.17% of the vote and 13 seats – more than any other list. Yet Šlesers’ party remained in opposition even in the capital. This result highlights the party’s main problem: despite strong voter support, it struggles to find partners with whom it can form a majority.
A brief look at how the party emerged
Ainārs Šlesers has been involved in the creation of several political parties: the New Party (1998), Latvia’s First Party (2000), For a Good Latvia (2010), Šlesers’ Reform Party LPP/LC (2011), and United for Latvia, which Šlesers joined in 2014 and subsequently became its leader.
LPV was founded on the 16th of August, 2021, at a time when Covid-19 restrictions were deeply dividing society. For Šlesers, it marked a return to politics after a break of approximately seven years.
The party name was new, but its leadership brought together a number of already familiar politicians and public figures, including Linda Liepiņa, Vilis Krištopans, Edmunds Zivtiņš, Ilze Stobova and others.
Jūlija Stepaņenko and Ļubova Švecova, meanwhile, were expelled after they declined to join LPV in condemning Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Conservative values and major economic promises
LPV’s political niche can be described as populist, socially conservative and business-friendly. The party contrasts entrepreneurial people and ordinary citizens with a slow and bureaucratic government and promises a rapid change of course.
On the economy, LPV promises lower taxes, investment, transit development and major infrastructure projects. On social issues, it advocates Christian values and the concept of the natural family, wants Latvia to withdraw from the Istanbul Convention and seeks to enshrine the definition of family in the Constitution.
At the same time, it promises to unite residents regardless of their native language, pursue a close alliance with the United States and support Ukraine’s accession to the European Union.
This combination allows LPV to appeal to several audiences: people expecting an economic breakthrough, socially conservative voters, those dissatisfied with previous governments, and voters from different language groups who place greater importance on wages, prices and the way public administration treats them.
At the same time, Šlesers has faced public criticism over what critics describe as his desire to preserve the possibility of eventually resuming trade with Russia. For years, he has defended the importance of ports, railways and eastbound cargo flows to Latvia’s economy.
Even after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, he has said that relations with Russia will eventually have to be rebuilt after the war and that sanctions could one day be lifted.
Critics see this as a willingness to return too quickly to a business model that made Latvia dependent on Russian cargo. Šlesers himself describes his position as a pragmatic defence of Latvia’s economic interests and has condemned Russia’s attack on Ukraine.
The party’s “faces”
The party’s central figure is unquestionably Ainārs Šlesers, who heads its Riga list. Support for “Šlesers’ party” is largely based on voters’ belief in his ability to deliver results, even though LPV has not yet been part of a national government where this could be put to the test.
Linda Liepiņa, leader of the LPV parliamentary group in the 14th Saeima, heads the party’s Vidzeme list. She took over leadership of the LPV parliamentary group after Šlesers moved to Riga City Council. According to the Saeima’s summary of the 2026 spring session, she was among the MPs who spoke most frequently in debates, with 18 appearances.
Edmunds Zivtiņš is the number one candidate in Zemgale. As a former head of the Traffic Police, Zivtiņš gives the party a law-and-order profile.
The Latgale list is headed by former Rēzekne mayor Aleksandrs Bartaševičs. In the 2025 municipal election, the joint LPV and Together for Latvia list he represented won eight of the 13 seats on the city council, and Bartaševičs was the elected councillor who received the strongest voter support. While some see him as a defender of Rēzekne’s interests, others associate him with the city’s financial crisis.
Andrejs Klementjevs is also near the top of the Riga list, benefiting from name recognition dating back to his time with Harmony. Much the same can be said of Regīna Ločmele.
Ainars Baštiks, number three on the Riga list, is pastor of the Matejs Baptist congregation and a former Minister for Children and Family Affairs. His candidacy serves to some extent as a guarantee of LPV’s promises to support families and Christian values.
Former Freeport of Riga chief Leonīds Loginovs, meanwhile, is running in the final, 42nd position on the Riga list. The party has named him as its candidate for transport minister. This allows LPV to argue that its promises concerning the development of ports and transit are backed by someone with experience managing the sector.
In this way, the party can appeal to people working in ports, railways, transport and related businesses for whom the future of these industries is personally important.
Strong polling numbers and programme promises
LPV was among the leaders in opinion polls during the summer. According to SKDS data, support among all respondents stood at 10% in July, fell to 8.5% in August and rose again to 9.2% in September.
Among voters who had already decided which party to support, LPV had 16.7% backing in September, placing it third in the rankings.
Meanwhile, in a September poll conducted by Latvijas Fakti in cooperation with Faktu logs, LPV was supported by 8.6% of all Latvian citizens surveyed. At the end of August, the figure was 8.3%, meaning support increased by 0.3 percentage points over the month.
Among respondents who had already chosen a party, the Latvijas Fakti poll put LPV at 12.9%, in second place behind the United List at 23.8%. Another 20% of respondents had not yet decided how they would vote.
LPV has an easily recognisable leader, a clear opposition message and a demonstrated ability to attract votes, as shown by the Riga election. The party offers simple and easily understood answers to complex problems: lower taxes, a lower cost of living, more jobs and less bureaucracy.
At the same time, its programme combines extensive tax cuts, a 5,000-euro benefit for every newborn child, higher healthcare spending and projects worth several billion euros. These promises help sustain voter support, but the question of where the money for all of them would come from remains unanswered.
Among other measures, LPV’s election programme promises a 10% tax rate for the self-employed, corporate income and capital gains; reduced VAT on several goods and sectors; the abolition of property tax on a person’s only home; the right to withdraw second-pillar pension savings; a directly elected president; and a lower threshold for initiating referendums.
The party also proposes reviewing the implementation of Rail Baltica, attracting US partners for the construction of a nuclear power plant, and investing in major road and other infrastructure projects. As noted above, some of these proposals have already appeared in the party’s parliamentary initiatives during the current Saeima term.

articles.title: Vivaldi counteroffensive advanced after Ukraine took Russia’s drones out of the fight, ISW assesses
articles.body:
Ukraine likely neutralized Russia's drone defenses north of Lyman before sending armor into the third phase of its Vivaldi counteroffensive, the Institute for the Study of War (ISW) assessed. An intermediate-range strike campaign against Russian logistics and electronic warfare paved the way, the think tank said.
Drones have made this front so deadly that armor now mostly fights from kilometers back. That is what makes Ukraine's armored push onto fortified positions near Lyman stand out. Russia has already shifted its effort south toward Sloviansk after losing the Lyman pincer.
Armor reached Russian bunkers without drawing drone strikes
To break the strongest Russian fortifications, Ukraine used old Soviet BTR-60 armored personnel carriers rebuilt as remote-controlled explosive vehicles, the 3rd Army Corps says.
Ukrainian forces drove them up to heavy Russian fortifications without coming under Russian drone strikes, ISW noted. The think tank said this indicates Ukraine neutralized or otherwise negated Russia's drone defenses in the area.
New Vivaldi tactic: Ukraine’s ground robots, each carrying two Bullspike grenade launchers, attack Russian positions and then detonate inside their shelters
Strikes on fuel starved Russia's jammers
Ukraine achieved tactical drone overmatch through extensive shaping operations and an intermediate-range strike campaign, ISW said. Those strikes targeted the Russian drones and electronic warfare (EW) systems that would otherwise have hunted the advancing vehicles.
The 3rd Army Corps reported on 17 September that strikes on Russian logistics in occupied Luhansk Oblast had degraded Russian fuel supplies to the front, ISW wrote that day. The corps said that strained Russia's ability to use drones and EW against Ukrainian drones. EW systems consume a lot of power, and Russian troops run them on diesel generators, ISW explained.
Deputy corps commander Maksym Zhorin credited strict information silence and a "Protective Drone" system of EW assets, according to the same assessment. He said it helped neutralize around 20,000 Russian drones. The corps had earlier described mapping Russian command posts and striking them to sow panic.
Ukraine’s Vivaldi counteroffensive near Lyman just got help from behind Russian lines: partisans say they cut rail supply to three Russian regiments, no explosion needed
Five settlements and 2,000 Russian losses
The corps liberated Nove, Ridkodub, and Katerynivka and restored control over Karpivka and Novomykhailivka, it said on 28 September. The phase added 51 km², bringing the total since the offensive began to 176 km².
Russian losses reached 2,000 personnel, and more than 250 Russians were taken prisoner, according to the corps. Corps commander Andrii Biletskyi said a feint from Shandryholove toward Zelena Dolyna drew Russian reserves away from the real target, Nove.
The first two phases had reportedly cleared more than 125 km² north of Lyman.

articles.title: Russia attacks Kyiv again with missiles and drones, sparking fires at an educational facility and the roof of a five-story apartment building
articles.body:
Russia attacks Kyiv again with missiles and drones, sparking fires at an educational facility and the roof of a five-story apartment building
Russian forces attacked Kyiv with missiles and drones overnight on September 29, Ukraine’s Air Force said. Several districts were hit, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said.
In the Solomianskyi district, missile “debris” fell into the courtyard of a residential building. One of the buildings at an educational institution was hit, sparking a fire. Klitschko also said an administrative building at an infrastructure facility was hit. He did not identify the educational institution or the facility.
In the Pecherskyi district, a three-story nonresidential building caught fire after the attack. In the Holosiivskyi district, the roof of an apartment building caught fire as a result of “falling debris.”
”One person was injured in the Holosiivskyi district, according to Ukraine’s State Emergency Service. Rescuers evacuated 10 people from the damaged building.
In the Bucha district of the Kyiv region, a Russian drone strike set a private home and the roof of a neighboring building on fire. Two people were taken to hospitals.
Russian forces have struck Kyiv both day and night for several days. On September 28, a building belonging to Ukraine’s National Academy of Sciences was among the sites hit, and a fire broke out there. According to Kyiv authorities, two people were killed and 26 injured in Monday’s attacks. Eight of those injured remain hospitalized.
